chapters.title: Book II: Old And Young — Chapter XIII
paragraphs:
FIRST GENTLEMAN. How would you classify your man? Better than most,
Or worse beneath the cloak of seeming better?
A saint or rogue, a pilgrim or a hypocrite?

SECOND GENTLEMAN. First tell me how you classify your books,
Those relics washed together from all ages.
You might as well arrange them by their size and dress:
Vellum, tall volumes, ordinary calfskin
Will scarcely hide more difference than the clever labels
You devise to sort the authors
You have never read.

After hearing Fred's account, Mr. Vincy decided to speak to Mr. Bulstrode in his private room at the Bank at half past one, when he was usually free of other visitors. But someone had arrived at one, and Mr. Bulstrode had so much to say to him that their interview was unlikely to end within half an hour. The banker spoke fluently, but at length, and his short, thoughtful pauses consumed an appreciable amount of time. Do not picture his sickly appearance as yellow skin and black hair: he had pale, fair skin, thinning brown hair sprinkled with gray, light-gray eyes, and a broad forehead. Loud men described his quiet voice as an undertone, sometimes suggesting that it showed a lack of openness. Yet there seems no reason why a loud man should not conceal anything except his voice, unless Scripture can be shown to locate honesty in the lungs. Mr. Bulstrode also leaned forward respectfully when listening, with a seemingly unwavering attention in his eyes. People who considered themselves worth listening to assumed that he was trying to gain the greatest possible benefit from their conversation. Those who expected to make less of an impression disliked having this moral lantern turned upon them. If you are not proud of your wine cellar, there is no pleasure in watching a guest raise his glass to the light with the air of a judge. Such pleasures are reserved for those who know their own merits. Consequently, Mr. Bulstrode's close attention did not please the publicans and sinners of Middlemarch. Some blamed it on his being a Pharisee, others on his being an Evangelical. The deeper thinkers wanted to know who his father and grandfather had been, pointing out that twenty-five years earlier no one in Middlemarch had ever heard of a Bulstrode. His present visitor, Lydgate, was indifferent to that searching look. He merely formed an unfavorable opinion of the banker's physical constitution and concluded that he lived intensely within himself, with little enjoyment of material things.

“I would be very grateful if you would come and see me here from time to time, Mr. Lydgate,” the banker said after a short pause. “If, as I venture to hope, I have the privilege of finding in you a valuable colleague in the important business of hospital management, there will be many questions for us to discuss privately. As for the new hospital, which is almost finished, I shall consider what you have said about the advantages of reserving it for fever cases. The decision rests with me. Lord Medlicote has supplied the land and building timber, but he has no wish to give the matter his personal attention.”

“Few things would better repay the effort in a provincial town like this,” said Lydgate. “A good fever hospital, alongside the old infirmary, could become the basis of a medical school once our medical reforms come through. And what could do more for medical education than establishing such schools across the country? A man born outside London who has a little public spirit as well as a few ideas ought to do what he can to resist the rush towards the capital of everything that rises above the ordinary. Serious professional ambitions can often find greater freedom in the provinces, even if the rewards are smaller.”

Among Lydgate's gifts was a voice generally deep and resonant, but capable of becoming very soft and gentle when the occasion called for it. His usual manner had a certain dash: a fearless expectation of success, a confidence in his abilities and integrity strengthened considerably by his contempt for petty obstacles and temptations he had never encountered. Yet an expression of sincere goodwill made this proud openness attractive. Perhaps Mr. Bulstrode liked him better for the contrast between their voices and manners; certainly, like Rosamond, he liked him better for being a stranger in Middlemarch. So much can begin with a new acquaintance! One can even begin to be a better man.

“I shall be delighted to give your enthusiasm a wider field,” Mr. Bulstrode replied. “I mean by entrusting you with the supervision of my new hospital, if closer acquaintance supports that arrangement. I am determined that so important an undertaking shall not be held back by our two physicians. Indeed, I feel encouraged to regard your arrival in this town as a gracious sign that a more evident blessing is now to attend my efforts, which have so far met with much resistance. At the old infirmary we have achieved the first step: your election. Now I hope you will not hesitate to provoke a certain amount of jealousy and dislike among your fellow practitioners by presenting yourself as a reformer.”

“I won't claim to be brave,” said Lydgate with a smile, “but I admit I rather enjoy a fight. I should have no interest in my profession if I didn't believe that better methods could be discovered and put into practice there, as everywhere else.”

“The profession's standard in Middlemarch is low, my dear sir,” said the banker. “In knowledge and skill, I mean, rather than social standing. Most of our medical men have connections with respectable local families. My own poor health has led me to study, to some extent, the means of relief that divine mercy has put within our reach. I have consulted eminent men in London, and I am painfully aware of how far medical treatment in our provincial districts lags behind.”

“Yes. Given our present medical regulations and training, we must be content to encounter a reasonably competent practitioner now and then. As for the larger questions that determine where a diagnosis should begin—the principles on which medical evidence rests—even a glimmer of understanding requires a scientific education of which country practitioners usually know as little as the man in the moon.”

Mr. Bulstrode, leaning forward and looking intently at him, found that Lydgate had expressed his agreement in terms he could not quite understand. In such circumstances a sensible man changes the subject and moves to ground where his own gifts may be more useful.

“I am aware,” he said, “that medical expertise naturally inclines towards material remedies. Nevertheless, Mr. Lydgate, I hope we shall agree about a measure in which you are unlikely to be actively involved, but where your sympathetic support could assist me. You acknowledge, I hope, that your patients have spiritual interests?”
“Certainly. But those words can mean different things to different people.”

“Exactly. And in these matters false teaching is as fatal as no teaching at all. One change I am particularly anxious to secure concerns the clergy's attendance at the old infirmary. The building stands in Mr. Farebrother's parish. Do you know Mr. Farebrother?”
“I've met him. He voted for me. I must call and thank him. He seems a very lively, pleasant little fellow. And I understand he studies natural history.”
“Mr. Farebrother, my dear sir, is a man whose case gives me deep pain. I doubt there is a clergyman anywhere in the country with greater talents.” Mr. Bulstrode paused, looking thoughtful.
“So far I haven't been troubled by finding too much talent in Middlemarch,” Lydgate said bluntly.

“What I wish,” Mr. Bulstrode continued, his face growing still more serious, “is to replace Mr. Farebrother's visits to the hospital with the appointment of a chaplain—Mr. Tyke, to be precise—and to allow no other spiritual assistance to be brought in.”

“Speaking as a doctor, I couldn't offer an opinion without knowing Mr. Tyke. Even then, I would need to know the cases in which he was to be prescribed.” Lydgate smiled, but he intended to tread carefully.

“Naturally, you cannot yet judge all the merits of the proposal. But”—here Mr. Bulstrode began to emphasize each word more distinctly—“the matter will probably be referred to the infirmary's medical board. What I hope I may ask is that, in view of the cooperation between us to which I now look forward, you will not allow my opponents to influence your part in this business.”
“I hope to stay out of disputes between clergymen,” said Lydgate. “The course I've chosen is to do good work in my own profession.”

“My responsibility is wider, Mr. Lydgate. For me this is a matter of sacred duty, while I have good reason to say that my opponents see it as an opportunity to indulge their worldly hostility. But I shall not surrender the smallest part of my convictions on that account, or cease to stand beside the truth that an evil generation hates. I have devoted myself to improving hospitals, but I will frankly tell you, Mr. Lydgate, that hospitals would hold no interest for me if I thought they existed merely to cure bodily disease. My actions have another foundation, and persecution will not make me hide it.”
As Mr. Bulstrode spoke those last words, his voice had risen to a loud, agitated whisper.

“On that point we certainly disagree,” said Lydgate. Still, he was glad when the door opened and Mr. Vincy was announced. Since meeting Rosamond, he had taken more interest in that ruddy, sociable gentleman. He had not, as she had, been imagining a future in which their lives were joined; but a man naturally remembers an attractive girl with pleasure and is willing to dine somewhere he may see her again. Before Lydgate left, Mr. Vincy had extended the invitation he had been “in no hurry about.” At breakfast Rosamond had mentioned that she thought her uncle Featherstone had taken a great liking to the new doctor.
Once alone with his brother-in-law, Mr. Bulstrode poured himself a glass of water and opened a box of sandwiches.
“Can I not persuade you to follow my diet, Vincy?”

“No, no. I don't think much of that system. Life needs padding,” said Mr. Vincy, unable to leave out the theory he carried everywhere with him. “However,” he continued, stressing the word as though to dismiss everything irrelevant, “I've come to talk about a little matter concerning that young rascal of mine, Fred.”
“You and I are likely to disagree as much about that, Vincy, as we do about diet.”

“I hope we won't this time.” Mr. Vincy was determined to remain good-humored. “The fact is, it's one of old Featherstone's whims. Someone has spitefully invented a story and taken it to the old man to turn him against Fred. He's very fond of Fred and will probably do something generous for him. In fact, he's practically told Fred that he intends to leave him his land, and that makes other people jealous.”

“Vincy, I must say again that you cannot expect me to approve of the course you have taken with your eldest son. It was entirely worldly vanity that made you intend him for the Church. With three sons and four daughters, you had no justification for spending so much on an education whose only result has been to give him idle, extravagant habits. You are now suffering the consequences.”

Pointing out other people's mistakes was a duty Mr. Bulstrode seldom avoided, but Mr. Vincy was less ready to be patient. When a man is about to become mayor and is prepared to take a firm position on politics generally in the interests of commerce, he naturally feels himself important to the whole arrangement of things. Questions of private conduct then seem rather secondary. This particular rebuke irritated him more than any other. He had no need whatever to be told that he was suffering the consequences. But he felt Bulstrode's yoke upon his neck, and although he usually enjoyed kicking against it, he was anxious to deny himself that relief.

“As for that, Bulstrode, there's no use going over the past. I'm not one of your model men, and I don't pretend to be. I couldn't foresee everything that would happen in the trade. There wasn't a better business in Middlemarch than ours, and the boy was clever. My poor brother went into the Church and would have done well—he'd already been promoted—but that gastric fever carried him off. Otherwise he might have been a dean by now. I think I had every right to try what I did for Fred. If we're going to talk religion, it seems to me a man shouldn't insist on weighing out his portion to the ounce beforehand. You must put some trust in Providence and be generous. Wanting to raise your family a little is a sound British instinct. I think a father has a duty to give his sons a good chance.”
“I am acting only as your best friend, Vincy, when I say that everything you have just said is a mixture of worldliness and contradictory nonsense.”

“Very well,” said Mr. Vincy, kicking despite his resolutions. “I never claimed to be anything but worldly. What's more, I don't see anyone else who isn't. I don't suppose you run your business on what you call unworldly principles. The only difference I can see is that one kind of worldliness is a little more honest than another.”
“This discussion leads nowhere, Vincy,” said Mr. Bulstrode. Having finished his sandwich, he had leaned back in his chair and covered his eyes, as if tired. “You had some more specific business.”

“Yes, yes. To come to the point, someone has told old Featherstone, quoting you as their authority, that Fred has been borrowing money, or trying to borrow it, on the expectation of inheriting his land. Naturally, you never said any such nonsense. But the old fellow insists that Fred bring him a denial in your own handwriting. Just a short note saying you don't believe a word of it—that he either borrowed or tried to borrow in such a foolish way. I don't suppose you can object to that.”

“Excuse me, but I do object. I am by no means certain that your son, in his recklessness and ignorance—I will use no harsher word—has not tried to raise money on the strength of his future expectations. Nor am I certain that someone has not been foolish enough to lend to him on so uncertain a prospect. The world has plenty of careless moneylending, as it has plenty of other follies.”

“But Fred gives me his word of honor that he never borrowed money by claiming there was any agreement about his uncle's land. He's no liar. I don't want to make him out better than he is. I've given him a thorough dressing-down; nobody can say I turn a blind eye. But he's no liar. And I would have thought—though perhaps I'm mistaken—that no religion forbids a man to think the best of a young fellow when he knows nothing worse. It seems a poor sort of religion that would put obstacles in his way by refusing to say you don't believe something bad about him when you've no good reason to believe it.”

“I am far from sure I should be doing your son a kindness by making it easier for him to inherit Featherstone's property. I cannot consider wealth a blessing for those who use it merely to reap the rewards of this world. You dislike hearing these things, Vincy, but I feel obliged on this occasion to tell you that I have no reason to encourage the disposal of property you describe. I will say plainly that it would serve neither your son's eternal welfare nor the glory of God. Why, then, should you expect me to write this sort of sworn declaration, whose only purpose is to sustain a foolish favoritism and secure a foolish legacy?”

“If you mean to stop anyone having money except saints and evangelists, you'll have to give up some profitable partnerships. That's all I can say,” Mr. Vincy burst out bluntly. “It may serve the glory of God, but it does nothing for the glory of Middlemarch trade when Plymdale's firm uses those blue and green dyes from the Brassing factory. They rot the silk; that's what I know. Perhaps people would like it better if they knew how much of the profit went to God's glory. But I don't make much of that. I could stir up quite a row if I chose.”

Mr. Bulstrode waited a moment before replying. “It pains me deeply to hear you speak like this, Vincy. I do not expect you to understand my reasons. It is hard enough to guide one's principles through the complications of the world, let alone to make their course clear to careless people and scoffers. Please remember that I extend my tolerance towards you as my wife's brother. It ill becomes you to complain that I withhold material assistance in maintaining your family's worldly position. I must remind you that your place in the trade has not been preserved by your own prudence or judgment.”

“Very likely not, but you haven't lost by my business yet,” said Mr. Vincy, thoroughly nettled—a condition his earlier good intentions seldom delayed for long. “And when you married Harriet, how could you expect our families not to hang from the same nail? If you've changed your mind and want my family to come down in the world, you'd better say so. I haven't changed. I'm a plain Churchman now, just as I was before all these doctrines came along. I take the world as I find it, in business and everything else. I'm content to be no worse than my neighbors. But if you want us brought down, say so. Then I'll have a better idea what to do.”
“You are being unreasonable. Will your family come down in the world for lack of this letter about your son?”

“Whether we will or not, I think it's very shabby of you to refuse it. Conduct like that may have religion for its lining, but from the outside it looks nasty and selfish. You might as well slander Fred yourself. It comes close enough when you refuse to say you didn't start the slander. This is the sort of thing—that domineering spirit, wanting to be bishop and banker everywhere—that gives a man a bad name.”
“Vincy, if you insist on quarreling with me, it will cause Harriet great distress, as well as myself,” said Mr. Bulstrode, a little more anxious and pale than usual.

“I don't want a quarrel. It's in my interest—and perhaps yours too—that we stay friends. I've no grudge against you. I think no worse of you than of anyone else. A man who half starves himself and goes as far as you do with family prayers and all the rest believes in his religion, whatever it may be. You could turn your money over just as quickly while cursing and swearing; plenty of men do. You like being master, there's no denying it. You'll have to rank first in heaven or you won't enjoy it much. But you're my sister's husband, and we ought to stand together. If I know Harriet, she'll blame you if we quarrel because you make such a fuss over a trifle and refuse to help Fred. And I don't pretend I shall take it well. I call it shabby.”
Mr. Vincy got up, began buttoning his overcoat, and looked steadily at his brother-in-law, silently demanding a definite answer.

This was not the first time Mr. Bulstrode had begun by lecturing Mr. Vincy and ended by seeing a most unsatisfactory reflection of himself in the coarse, unflattering mirror that the manufacturer's mind held up to the subtler lights and shadows of other people. Experience might have warned him how the scene would end. But a well-fed fountain pours out its water generously even in the rain, when it is worse than useless; and a fine fountain of moral advice is apt to prove just as impossible to stop.

It was not in Mr. Bulstrode's nature to give way immediately because of uncomfortable suggestions. Before altering his course, he always had to reshape his motives until they agreed with his usual standard. At last he said:
“I shall consider it a little, Vincy. I shall speak to Harriet about it. I shall probably send you a letter.”
“Very well. As soon as possible, please. I hope it will all be settled before I see you tomorrow.”

chapters.title: Book II: Old And Young — Chapter XIV
paragraphs:
Here is the precise recipe
For the sauce served with delicate meat,
Called Idleness, which many prefer
And declare wonderfully sweet:
First, like a hound, watch for scraps;
Mix in insults, stirring them well
With thick oil of flattery; froth the whole
With low, self-praising lies.
Serve warm. The vessels you must use
To keep it in are dead men's shoes.

Mr. Bulstrode's discussion with Harriet appeared to have produced the result Mr. Vincy wanted. Early the next morning a letter arrived that Fred could take to Mr. Featherstone as the required evidence.

Because of the cold weather, the old gentleman was staying in bed. Mary Garth was not in the sitting room, so Fred went straight upstairs and handed his uncle the letter. Comfortably supported by a backrest, Mr. Featherstone was as capable as ever of enjoying his own wisdom in distrusting and thwarting mankind. He put on his spectacles to read, pursing his lips and pulling down the corners of his mouth.

“‘Under the circumstances I will not refuse to state my conviction’—tchah! Listen to his fine language! He's as grand as an auctioneer—‘that your son Frederic has received no advance of money against legacies promised by Mr. Featherstone’—promised? Who said I'd promised anything? I promise nothing. I'll go on adding codicils to my will as long as I please—‘and that, given the nature of such a transaction, it is unreasonable to suppose that a young man of sense and character would attempt it’—ah, but he doesn't say you ARE a young man of sense and character. Mark that, sir!—‘As for my own connection with any such report, I state distinctly that I never said your son had borrowed money against property he might inherit on Mr. Featherstone's decease’—bless my soul! Property, inherit, decease! Lawyer Standish is nothing beside him. He couldn't put it more finely if he wanted a loan himself. Well,” Mr. Featherstone said, looking over his spectacles at Fred and handing the letter back with a scornful gesture, “you don't suppose I believe a thing just because Bulstrode writes it down in fine language, do you?”
Fred flushed. “You asked for the letter, sir. I should think Mr. Bulstrode's denial is worth as much as the authority who told you the thing he's denying.”
“Every bit as much. I never said I believed either of them. And what do you expect now?” Mr. Featherstone asked sharply. He kept his spectacles on but withdrew his hands under the bedcovers.
“I expect nothing, sir.” Fred struggled to hold back his irritation. “I came to bring the letter. If you wish, I'll say good morning.”
“Not yet, not yet. Ring the bell. I want missy.”
A servant answered the bell.
“Tell missy to come!” Mr. Featherstone said impatiently. “What business did she have going away?” His tone was no different when Mary appeared.
“Why couldn't you stay here till I told you to go? I want my waistcoat now. I've told you always to leave it on the bed.”

Mary's eyes were rather red, as if she had been crying. Clearly Mr. Featherstone was in one of his most irritable moods that morning. Although Fred could now hope to receive the badly needed gift of money, he would have preferred the freedom to turn on the old tyrant and tell him that Mary Garth was too good to be ordered about by him. Fred had stood up when she entered, but she scarcely acknowledged him. She looked as if her nerves were trembling in expectation of something being thrown at her. In fact, she never had anything worse than words to fear. As she reached for the waistcoat on its peg, Fred went over and said, “Let me.”

“Leave it alone! You bring it, missy, and put it here,” said Mr. Featherstone. When she had laid the waistcoat beside him, he added, “Now go away again till I call.” He habitually added flavor to his pleasure in favoring one person by being especially unpleasant to another, and Mary was always available to provide the seasoning. He treated her better when his own relatives visited. Slowly he took a bunch of keys from the waistcoat pocket; slowly he brought out a tin box from beneath the bedclothes.
“Expecting me to give you a little fortune, eh?” he said, peering over his spectacles and pausing as he opened the lid.

“Not at all, sir. You kindly mentioned giving me a present the other day. Otherwise, of course, I wouldn't have thought of it.” But Fred was naturally hopeful. He had imagined a sum just large enough to free him from a particular anxiety. Whenever he went into debt, it seemed highly likely to him that something would happen—he need not imagine exactly what—to enable him to pay on time. Now that this providential event apparently lay within reach, it would have been absurd to suppose that the supply might fall short of the need. As absurd as having faith in half a miracle because one lacked the strength to believe in a whole one.

The deeply veined hands felt through banknote after banknote, laying each flat again, while Fred leaned back in his chair, too proud to look eager. He considered himself a gentleman at heart and disliked flattering an old man for his money. At last Mr. Featherstone looked over his spectacles again and offered a small bundle of notes. Their nearer edges fanned out towards Fred, showing him plainly that there were only five. But each could be worth fifty pounds. He took them, saying:
“I'm very much obliged to you, sir,” and was about to roll them up as though their value had not occurred to him. This did not suit Mr. Featherstone, who was watching him closely.
“Come, aren't they worth counting? You take money like a lord. I suppose you lose it like one too.”
“I thought I shouldn't look a gift horse in the mouth, sir. But I'll gladly count them.”

After counting them, however, Fred was considerably less glad. They had actually committed the absurdity of amounting to less than his hopeful imagination had decided they must. What could the fitness of things mean, except their fitting a man's expectations? Without that, absurdity and atheism yawn behind him. Fred suffered a severe collapse on discovering that he held only five twenty-pound notes. His participation in the country's higher education did not seem to help him. Nevertheless, as the color changed rapidly in his fair face, he said:
“That's very generous of you, sir.”

“I should think it is,” said Mr. Featherstone, locking and putting away his box, then slowly removing his spectacles. At length, as if private reflection had strengthened his conviction, he repeated, “I should call it generous.”
“I assure you I'm very grateful, sir,” said Fred, who had had time to regain his cheerful manner.

“And so you ought to be. You want to make a show in the world, and I reckon Peter Featherstone is the only person you've got to depend on.” The old man's eyes shone with a strange mixture of satisfaction: this smart young fellow relied on him, and the smart young fellow was rather a fool to do so.

“Yes, indeed. I wasn't born with very splendid prospects. Few men have been more restricted than I have,” Fred said, feeling a little surprised at his own virtue in the face of such hard treatment. “It really seems unfair to have to ride a hunter with damaged lungs, while men who aren't half such good judges of horses can throw away any amount of money on bad bargains.”
“Well, now you can buy a fine hunter. Eighty pounds should do it, I reckon. And you'll have twenty left to get you out of any little scrape,” said Mr. Featherstone with a slight chuckle.
“You're very kind, sir,” said Fred, keenly aware of the contrast between his words and his feelings.
“Yes, a better uncle than your grand uncle Bulstrode. I doubt you'll get much from his speculations. He's got a pretty strong cord tied round your father's leg, from what I hear, eh?”
“My father never tells me about his business, sir.”

“Well, he shows some sense there. But people find things out without his telling them. HE won't have much to leave you. Most likely he'll die without making a will—he's the sort to do it—however much they make him mayor of Middlemarch. And you won't get much from his dying without a will, even if you ARE the eldest son.”
Fred thought Mr. Featherstone had never been so disagreeable. Admittedly, he had never given him quite so much money at one time either.
“Shall I burn Mr. Bulstrode's letter, sir?” Fred asked, getting up with it as if to put it into the fire.
“Yes, yes. I don't want it. It's worth nothing to me.”

Fred took the letter to the fire and drove the poker through it with considerable relish. He longed to leave, but both his own conscience and his uncle's presence made him a little ashamed to run off as soon as he had pocketed the money. Presently the farm manager came upstairs to report to his employer. To Fred's enormous relief, he was dismissed with instructions to come again soon.

He had wanted not only to escape his uncle but also to find Mary Garth. She was now in her usual place by the fire, sewing, with a book open on the little table beside her. Her eyelids were less red, and she had recovered her customary composure.
“Am I needed upstairs?” she asked, half rising when Fred came in.
“No. I've simply been sent away because Simmons has gone up.”
Mary sat back down and resumed her sewing. She was certainly more indifferent to Fred than usual. She did not know how affectionately indignant he had felt on her behalf upstairs.
“May I stay a little, Mary, or would I bore you?”
“Please sit down,” said Mary. “You won't be as great a bore as Mr. John Waule, who came yesterday and sat down without asking my permission.”
“Poor fellow! I think he's in love with you.”

“I hadn't noticed. To me, one of the most hateful things in a girl's life is that there always has to be some idea of falling in love between her and any man who is kind to her and earns her gratitude. I would have thought I, at least, might be safe from all that. I've no reason for the ridiculous vanity of imagining that every man who comes near me is in love with me.”
Mary had not meant to reveal any emotion, but despite herself her voice ended in a tremor of irritation.

“Damn John Waule! I didn't mean to make you angry. I didn't know you had any reason to be grateful to me. I'd forgotten what a great service you consider it when someone trims a candle for you.” Fred had his pride too and would not admit that he knew what had provoked Mary's outburst.

“Oh, I'm only angry with the ways of the world. I do like being spoken to as though I had common sense. I often feel I could understand a little more than I ever hear, even from young gentlemen who've been to college.” Mary had recovered herself. Beneath her words ran a suppressed ripple of laughter that was pleasant to hear.
“You can laugh at me as much as you like this morning,” said Fred. “I thought you looked so sad upstairs. It's a shame you have to stay here and be bullied like that.”

“Oh, my life is easy, comparatively. I've tried teaching, and I'm not suited to it. My mind likes wandering off on its own too much. I think any hardship is better than pretending to do the work you're paid for and never really doing it. Everything here I can do as well as anyone else could—perhaps better than some people. Rosy, for example. Though she's just the sort of beautiful creature who gets imprisoned with ogres in fairy tales.”
“ROSY!” Fred exclaimed, with profound brotherly skepticism.
“Come now, Fred!” Mary said firmly. “You've no right to be so critical.”
“Do you mean something in particular, at this moment?”
“No. Something general, at all times.”
“Oh, that I'm idle and extravagant. Well, I'm not suited to being poor. I wouldn't have turned out badly if I'd been rich.”
“You would have done your duty in the station of life to which God has not been pleased to call you,” Mary said, laughing.
“Well, I couldn't do my duty as a clergyman any more than you could as a governess. You ought to feel a little sympathy there, Mary.”
“I never said you should become a clergyman. There are other kinds of work. It seems a miserable thing not to choose a course and follow it.”
“I could, if—” Fred stopped and stood up, leaning against the mantelpiece.
“If you knew you weren't going to inherit a fortune?”
“I didn't say that. You want to quarrel. It's unfair to judge me by what other people say.”

“How could I want to quarrel with you? It would be like quarreling with all my new books,” said Mary, lifting the volume from the table. “However badly you behave towards other people, you're good to me.”
“Because I like you better than anyone. But I know you despise me.”
“Yes, a little,” Mary said, nodding and smiling.
“You'd admire some extraordinary fellow with wise opinions on every subject.”

“Yes, I would.” Mary sewed quickly and seemed irritatingly in command of the situation. Once a conversation has taken a wrong turn for us, we sink further and further into the swamp of awkwardness. That was how Fred Vincy felt.
“I suppose women never fall in love with someone they've known for as long as they can remember, the way men often do. It's always some new fellow who catches a girl's attention.”

“Let me think,” said Mary, the corners of her mouth turning up mischievously. “I must review my experience. There's Juliet. She seems to support what you say. But Ophelia had probably known Hamlet for a long time. And Brenda Troil had known Mordaunt Merton since they were children—though he seems to have been a respectable young man. Then again, Minna was even more deeply in love with Cleveland, a stranger. Waverley was new to Flora MacIvor, but she didn't fall in love with him. There's Olivia and Sophia Primrose, and Corinne: you could say they fell in love with new men. Taken altogether, my experience is rather mixed.”

Mary looked up at Fred with a touch of mischief. He loved that look, though her eyes were merely clear windows through which a laughing observer watched. He was certainly affectionate. As he grew from boyhood into manhood, his love for his old playmate had grown too, despite the share of higher education that had raised his expectations of social rank and income.
“When a man isn't loved, there's no point in telling someone he could be better—could do anything, I mean—if only he knew she loved him back.”
“No point at all in saying he COULD be better. Might, could, would: they're contemptible helping verbs.”
“I don't see how a man can amount to much unless some woman loves him dearly.”
“I think he should become worthy before he expects that.”
“You know better, Mary. Women don't love men because they're good.”
“Perhaps they don't. But when they love them, they never think they're bad.”
“It's hardly fair to call me bad.”
“I haven't said anything about you.”
“I'll never amount to anything, Mary, unless you'll tell me you love me—unless you'll promise to marry me. When I'm able to marry, I mean.”
“Even if I loved you, I wouldn't marry you. I certainly wouldn't promise ever to marry you.”
“I think that's positively wrong, Mary. If you love me, you ought to promise.”
“On the contrary, I think it would be wrong of me to marry you, even if I loved you.”
“You mean as I am now, with no way of supporting a wife. Naturally. I'm only twenty-three.”
“That last circumstance will change. I'm less certain anything else will. My father says an idle man ought not to exist, let alone marry.”
“So I'm to shoot myself?”
“No. On balance, I think you'd do better to pass your examination. I've heard Mr. Farebrother say it's shamefully easy.”
“That's all very well. Everything is easy for him. Not that intelligence has anything to do with it. I'm ten times cleverer than plenty of men who pass.”

“Good heavens!” said Mary, unable to hold back her sarcasm. “That explains curates like Mr. Crowse. Divide your intelligence by ten, and the result—good heavens!—can get a degree. But it only proves you're ten times lazier than the others.”
“Well, if I passed, you wouldn't want me to enter the Church?”
“What I want you to do isn't the question. I suppose you have a conscience of your own. Look! There's Mr. Lydgate. I must go and tell my uncle.”
“Mary,” Fred said, catching her hand as she got up, “if you won't give me any encouragement, I'll grow worse instead of better.”
“I won't encourage you,” Mary said, flushing. “Your family would disapprove, and so would mine. My father would think I'd disgraced myself by accepting a man who ran into debt and refused to work!”
Stung, Fred let go of her hand. She went to the door, then turned. “Fred, you've always been so kind and generous to me. I'm not ungrateful. But never speak to me like that again.”

“Very well,” said Fred sulkily, picking up his hat and whip. His face was blotched pale pink and dead white. Like many an idle young gentleman who had failed his examinations, he was thoroughly in love—and with a plain girl who had no money! Still, with Mr. Featherstone's land in the background and a conviction that, whatever Mary said, she really did care for him, Fred was not entirely in despair.
At home he gave his mother four of the twenty-pound notes and asked her to keep them. “I don't want to spend this money, mother. I need it to pay a debt. Keep it safely out of my fingers.”

“Bless you, my dear,” said Mrs. Vincy. She adored her eldest son and her youngest daughter, a child of six, whom other people considered her two naughtiest children. A mother's partiality does not always blind her. She, at least, is best placed to judge which child is tender and loving towards her. And Fred certainly loved his mother. Perhaps his affection for someone else also made him particularly anxious to protect the hundred pounds from his own tendency to spend. The creditor to whom he owed a hundred and sixty had a stronger safeguard: a promissory note signed by Mary's father.

chapters.title: Book II: Old And Young — Chapter XV
paragraphs:
“You've left dark eyes behind, you say,
And blue eyes cannot charm you;
Yet you seem more absorbed today
Than ever we remember.

“Oh, I pursue the fairest beauty
Through new places of delight;
Footprints here and echoes there
Lead me to my treasure.

“Look! She turns: immortal youth
Shaped into a mortal figure,
Fresh as starlight's ancient truth—
Nature, with her many names!”

A great historian, as he insisted on calling himself, had the good fortune to be dead a hundred and twenty years ago, and so to join those giants beneath whose enormous legs our present-day littleness is seen to walk. He takes particular pride in his plentiful comments and digressions as the hardest part of his work to imitate, especially the opening chapters of the successive books of his history. There he seems to pull his armchair to the front of the stage and chat with us in all the hearty ease of his splendid English. But Fielding lived when days were longer—for time, like money, is measured by our needs—when summer afternoons stretched wide and the clock ticked slowly through winter evenings. We historians who have arrived late must not linger as he did. If we tried, our conversation would probably sound thin and hurried, as though we were speaking from a folding stool in a parrot house. I, at least, have so much to do in disentangling certain human lives and tracing how they were woven together that I must focus all the light at my disposal on this particular web, instead of scattering it across that tempting collection of related subjects called the universe.

For now I must make the newcomer Lydgate better known to anyone interested in him than he could possibly be even to those who have seen most of him since his arrival in Middlemarch. Surely everyone must acknowledge that a man can be advertised and praised, envied, mocked, counted on as a useful instrument, and fallen in love with—or at least chosen as a future husband—while remaining almost entirely unknown. His neighbors may know him merely as a collection of signs to which they attach their mistaken assumptions. There was, however, a general impression that Lydgate was no ordinary country doctor. In Middlemarch at that time, such an impression meant that great things were expected of him. Everyone's own family doctor was remarkably clever, of course, credited with immeasurable skill in taming the most skittish or vicious diseases. The evidence for his ability belonged to the higher order of intuition: the unshakable convictions of his female patients. Nothing could challenge it except the existence of equally strong contrary convictions. Every lady who found medical truth in Wrench and his “strengthening treatment” regarded Toller and his “lowering system” as medical ruin. The heroic age of plentiful bleeding and blistering had not yet passed, still less the age of sweeping theories in which disease in general received some bad name and was treated accordingly, without hesitation. Call it insurrection, for example, and you must not fire blank cartridges at it: you must draw blood at once. Strengtheners and lowerers alike were “clever” men in someone's opinion, which is really as much as can be said for any living talent. Nobody had imagined that Mr. Lydgate might know as much as Dr. Sprague and Dr. Minchin, the two physicians. They alone could offer hope in extreme danger, when the slightest hope was worth a guinea. Still, as I say, people generally felt that Lydgate was rather more unusual than any other general practitioner in Middlemarch. And they were right. He was only twenty-seven, an age at which many men remain uncommon: hopeful of achievement, determined to avoid compromise, convinced that Mammon will never put a bit in their mouths and climb onto their backs. Rather, if they have anything to do with that god of wealth, he will pull their chariot.

He had become an orphan soon after leaving public school. His father, an army officer, had left little provision for his three children. When young Tertius asked for a medical education, his guardians found it easier to grant his wish by apprenticing him to a country practitioner than to object on grounds of family dignity. He belonged to that rarer class of boys who discover a definite inclination early and decide there is something particular they want to do for its own sake, rather than because their fathers did it. Most of us who love a subject can recall some morning or evening when we climbed onto a high stool to reach an unfamiliar volume, or sat listening open-mouthed to a new speaker, or, for lack of books, began listening to the voices within. That is the earliest beginning of our love we can trace. Something like this happened to Lydgate. A quick-minded boy, he would fling himself into a corner, still hot from play, and within five minutes be deep in whatever book lay to hand. Rasselas or Gulliver was preferable, but Bailey's Dictionary would do, or the Bible with the Apocrypha. When he was not riding his pony, running, hunting, or listening to men talk, he had to read something. All this was true by the time he was ten. He had already read “Chrysal, or the Adventures of a Guinea,” which was neither milk for infants nor a chalky mixture meant to pass for it, and had already begun to suspect that books were rubbish and life was dull. School did little to change his opinion. He worked through his classics and mathematics without excelling in either. People said Lydgate could do anything he chose, but he had certainly not yet chosen to do anything remarkable. He was a vigorous young animal with a quick understanding; no spark had yet ignited an intellectual passion. Knowledge seemed superficial and easy to master. Judging by the conversation of his elders, he apparently possessed more already than adult life required. This was probably no unusual result of expensive schooling in that age of short-waisted coats and other fashions that have not yet returned. Then, one holiday, a wet day drove him to the small library at home to look once more for a book that might offer something new. It seemed hopeless, unless he tried a dusty row of volumes in gray paper covers with dingy labels: an old encyclopedia he had never touched. Disturbing them would at least be a novelty. They stood on the highest shelf, and he climbed onto a chair to reach them. He opened the first volume he took down; somehow we often begin reading in an improvised position, precisely where it seems inconvenient. The page was headed Anatomy, and the first passage to catch his eye concerned the valves of the heart. He knew little of valves of any kind, but he knew that valvae meant folding doors. Through that crack a sudden light entered, startling him with his first vivid sense of the body's finely adjusted machinery. His liberal education had, naturally, left him free to read the indecent passages in the classical authors studied at school. But apart from a vague association of his internal organs with secrecy and obscenity, it had left his imagination entirely uninformed. For all he knew, his brains lay in little bags at his temples. He had no more thought of picturing his circulation than of explaining how paper took the place of gold. Yet the moment of vocation had arrived. Before he climbed down from the chair, the world had become new through his glimpse of endless processes filling vast regions previously boarded out of sight by the wordy ignorance he had mistaken for knowledge. From that hour, an intellectual passion began to grow in Lydgate.

We never hesitate to tell, again and again, how a man falls in love with a woman and marries her, or is tragically separated from her. Is it an excess of poetry or of stupidity that makes us tireless in describing what King James called a woman's “form and beauty,” tireless in listening to the twang of the old troubadour strings, while taking comparatively little interest in that other kind of form and beauty which must be courted through diligent thought and the patient surrender of small desires? That passion also has its varying histories: sometimes a glorious marriage, sometimes frustration and final separation. Often enough its catastrophe is entangled with the other passion, the one the troubadours sang about. Among the crowds of middle-aged men whose daily professional routine has become as fixed as the way they tie their cravats, there are always many who once intended to direct their own actions and change the world a little. The story of how they were shaped into average men, fit to be packed by the dozen, is scarcely ever told, even in their own minds. Perhaps their enthusiasm for generous, unpaid labor cooled as imperceptibly as other youthful loves, until one day their former self walked like a ghost through its old home and made the new furniture look ghastly. Nothing could be subtler than that gradual change. At first they breathed it in without knowing. You and I may have helped infect them with our breath when we spoke our conformist untruths or reached our foolish conclusions. Or perhaps it entered with the vibrations of a woman's glance.

Lydgate did not intend to become one of those failures. There was greater hope for him because his scientific interest soon developed into enthusiasm for a profession. He had a young man's faith in the work by which he would earn his bread, a faith that survived the schooling in makeshift methods called his apprenticeship. He went on to study in London, Edinburgh, and Paris, convinced that medicine, as it could be practiced, was the finest profession in the world. It offered the most perfect exchange between science and practical art, the most direct union between intellectual discovery and social benefit. Lydgate's nature required that combination. He was a man of feeling, with a flesh-and-blood sense of fellowship that survived all the abstractions of specialized study. His concern was not merely for “cases,” but for John and Elizabeth—especially Elizabeth.

His profession had another attraction: it needed reform. A man could indignantly resolve to reject its purchasable honors and other nonsense, and acquire genuine qualifications even where none were required. He went to Paris determined that, on returning, he would settle in a provincial town as a general practitioner. For the sake of both his own scientific work and general progress, he would resist the irrational separation of medical from surgical knowledge. He would avoid London's intrigues, jealousies, and social servility, and win distinction, however slowly, as Jenner had done, through the independent value of his work. We must remember that this was an unenlightened period. Venerable colleges labored to keep knowledge pure by keeping it scarce, and to exclude error by strict exclusiveness over fees and appointments. Yet very ignorant young gentlemen still won advancement in town, and many more gained the legal right to practice across large stretches of the countryside. Nor did the high standard displayed to the public by the College of Physicians—with its special approval for the expensive, highly rarefied medical training of Oxford and Cambridge graduates—prevent quackery from flourishing. Professional treatment consisted chiefly of administering large quantities of drugs. The public therefore concluded that it might do still better with even more drugs, if only they could be bought cheaply, and swallowed vast volumes of medicine prescribed by unscrupulous ignorance without degrees. Statistics had not yet calculated how many ignorant or sanctimonious doctors must inevitably exist, whatever changes occurred. To Lydgate, therefore, changing the individual units seemed the most direct way to change the totals. He intended to be a unit that made a difference towards a spreading improvement which would one day visibly affect the averages, while meanwhile enjoying the satisfaction of benefiting his own patients' internal organs. Yet he wanted more than a sounder practice than most. He hoped for a wider influence. He was fired by the possibility of proving an anatomical theory and adding a link to the chain of discovery.

Does a Middlemarch surgeon dreaming of becoming a discoverer seem incongruous? Most of us know little about the great pioneers until they have been placed among the stars and already govern our destinies. But Herschel, for instance, who “broke through the barriers of the heavens”—did he not once play a provincial church organ and teach fumbling pianists? Every one of those shining figures had to walk the earth among neighbors who may have thought much more about his walk and his clothes than about anything that would earn him lasting fame. Each had his small, local, personal history, dotted with petty temptations and sordid worries that created friction on his path towards the immortals. Lydgate saw the danger of such friction, but he had abundant confidence in his determination to avoid it as far as possible. At twenty-seven, he considered himself experienced. He would not expose his vanity to the capital's glittering worldly successes. Instead, he would live among people who could offer no rivalry to his pursuit of a great idea, which would stand beside diligent medical practice as his twin purpose. He found it fascinating to hope that the two pursuits would illuminate each other. The careful observation and reasoning of his daily work, and the use of a lens to assist his judgment in particular cases, would sharpen his thinking for larger investigations. Was this not the special excellence of his profession? He would be a good doctor in Middlemarch and, through that very work, stay on the path of far-reaching research. At this stage of his career, he fairly deserves credit on one point. He did not intend to imitate those model philanthropists who profit from poisonous pickles while campaigning against adulterated food, or hold shares in a gambling den to buy themselves leisure to defend public morality. He meant to begin with specific reforms in his own practice, reforms certainly within reach and far less difficult than proving an anatomical theory. One was to act firmly on a recent legal decision and write prescriptions without dispensing medicines himself or taking a commission from chemists. For a general practitioner in a country town this was an innovation, and his colleagues would feel it as an insulting criticism. But Lydgate also meant to innovate in treatment. He was wise enough to see that his best protection in practicing honestly according to his beliefs was to remove the regular temptations to do otherwise.

Perhaps observers and theorists had more cause for cheer then than they do now. We tend to imagine the beginning of America's discovery as the world's finest age, when a bold sailor might land in a new kingdom even through shipwreck. Around 1829, the dark territories of pathology offered a splendid America to a spirited young adventurer. Above all, Lydgate wanted to help enlarge the scientific and rational foundations of his profession. The more closely he studied particular questions of disease, such as the nature of fever or fevers, the more urgently he felt the need for basic knowledge of bodily structure. That knowledge had been illuminated at the beginning of the century by the brief, brilliant career of Bichat, who died at thirty-one but, like another Alexander, left a realm large enough for many heirs. This great Frenchman was the first to develop the idea that living bodies are not fundamentally collections of organs to be understood by studying them separately and then, as it were, in federation. They must instead be understood as consisting of certain basic webs or tissues from which the different organs—brain, heart, lungs, and the rest—are formed, just as the different parts of a house are built from varying proportions of wood, iron, stone, brick, zinc, and other materials, each with its own composition and properties. Clearly, no one can understand or assess the whole structure or any of its parts, its weaknesses or its repairs, without knowing the materials. Bichat's idea, worked out through his detailed study of different tissues, necessarily transformed medical questions as the lighting of gas lamps would transform a dim street lit by oil. It revealed new connections and previously hidden structural facts that had to be considered in interpreting symptoms and the effects of medicines. But results that depend on human conscientiousness and intelligence arrive slowly. At the end of 1829, most medical practice was still strutting or shuffling along the old roads, and scientific work remained that might have seemed the immediate next step after Bichat. That great visionary treated tissues as the final facts of the living organism, the furthest point of anatomical analysis. Another mind might ask whether these structures shared some common basis from which all had developed, as sarsenet, gauze, net, satin, and velvet all come from the raw cocoon. That would provide another light, as powerful as an oxyhydrogen flame, exposing the very grain of things and revising every earlier explanation. Lydgate was in love with this extension of Bichat's work, already stirring through many currents of European thought. He longed to demonstrate the deeper relationships of living structure and help bring human understanding into closer accord with the true order of things. The work remained undone, though the groundwork was there for those who knew how to use it. What was the primary tissue? That was how Lydgate framed the question—not quite in the form the waiting answer required, but many seekers miss the right word. He counted on seizing quiet intervals in which to resume the threads of research, and on gathering many clues through diligent use of both scalpel and microscope. Researchers had begun to put renewed and enthusiastic trust in the latter. Such was Lydgate's plan for his future: useful small work for Middlemarch, and great work for the world.

He was certainly a fortunate fellow then: twenty-seven, with no settled vices, generously determined to do good, and with ideas that made life interesting quite apart from the worship of horses and other mysterious rituals expensive to observe. The eight hundred pounds he had left after buying his practice would not have gone far towards those. He stood at the beginning of a career that would make an excellent subject for betting, if any gentlemen fond of that amusement could assess the complicated odds of a difficult ambition: all the ways circumstances might hinder or help, all the delicate internal balances by which a man swims towards his goal or is swept headlong away. Even close knowledge of Lydgate's character would leave the risk unresolved, for character itself develops and unfolds. The man was still being made, no less than the Middlemarch doctor and the immortal discoverer. His virtues and faults alike could shrink or grow. I hope his faults will not make you lose interest in him. Do we not all have some valued friend who is a little too confident and scornful, whose distinguished mind is spotted with ordinary failings, whose inborn prejudices pinch him here and bulge out there, or whose better energies may flow into the wrong channel under a passing temptation? All these things could be said of Lydgate. But they are the polite circumlocutions of a preacher who speaks of Adam rather than risk troubling those who pay for their pews. The particular faults distilled into these delicate generalities have their own recognizable faces, speech, accents, and grimaces, and play roles in very different dramas. Our vanities differ as our noses do. Conceit is not always the same conceit; it varies with the minute differences in our mental construction. Lydgate's conceit was arrogant: never simpering, never pert, but grand in its claims and benevolently contemptuous. He would do a great deal for fools, feeling sorry for them and entirely certain they could have no power over him. In Paris he had considered joining the Saint Simonians in order to turn them against some of their own doctrines. All his faults bore related marks. They belonged to a man with a fine baritone voice, clothes that sat well on him, and an air of inborn distinction even in his ordinary gestures. Where, then, were these spots of commonness? asks a young lady in love with his careless grace. How could there be anything ordinary in someone so well bred, so eager for social distinction, so generous and unusual in his sense of social duty? As easily as there can be stupidity in a genius surprised on the wrong subject. Or a man most sincerely wishing to bring about a social paradise may imagine its lighter pleasures very poorly, unable to rise above Offenbach's music or the sparkling puns of the latest burlesque. Lydgate's commonness lay in the character of his prejudices. Despite his noble intentions and sympathies, half of them were those of any ordinary man of the world. The distinction of mind behind his intellectual passion did not extend to his feelings and judgments about furniture, women, or the desirability of people's knowing—without his telling them—that his birth was superior to other country surgeons'. He did not intend to think about furniture yet. But when he did, there was reason to fear that neither biology nor plans for reform would raise him above the vulgar conviction that anything less than the best would be unfitting.

As for women, he had already been carried headlong into one impulsive folly, which he intended to be his last. Marriage at some distant date would, of course, be free of impulsiveness. Anyone wishing to know Lydgate should learn what that folly was, since it illustrates both the sudden swerves of passion to which he was prone and the chivalrous kindness that helped make his character lovable. The story does not require many words. It happened while he was studying in Paris, when, besides his other work, he was conducting experiments with electricity. One evening, tired and unable to establish the facts he needed, he gave his frogs and rabbits a rest from the distressing, mysterious rule of unexplained shocks under which they lived. He went to spend the rest of the evening at the Porte Saint Martin theater. A melodrama was playing there which he had already seen several times, drawn not by the ingenuity of its collaborating authors but by an actress whose character stabbed her lover, mistaking him for the play's scheming duke. Lydgate loved the actress as a man loves a woman he never expects to speak to. She came from Provence and had dark eyes, a Greek profile, and a full, majestic figure, with the kind of beauty that carries a sweetly maternal quality even in youth. Her voice was a soft cooing. She had only recently arrived in Paris and had a virtuous reputation. Her husband played the unfortunate lover. It was her acting, rather than her morals, that was questionable, but the audience was satisfied. Lydgate's only recreation now was to go and look at her, as he might have rested for a while on a bank of violets in the gentle southern breeze, without doing any harm to the electrical experiments to which he would soon return. That evening, however, the old drama acquired a new catastrophe. At the moment when the heroine was supposed to pretend to stab her lover and he was supposed to fall gracefully, the wife really stabbed her husband, and he fell as death dictated. A wild scream pierced the theater, and the woman from Provence fainted. The play required both a scream and a faint, but this time the faint was real too. Lydgate leaped and climbed onto the stage, scarcely knowing how, and set about helping. His introduction to his heroine consisted of discovering a bruise on her head and lifting her gently in his arms. All Paris talked of the death. Was it murder? Some of the actress's most enthusiastic admirers inclined to believe her guilty and admired her more for it—such was the taste of the period. Lydgate did not. He fiercely defended her innocence. His former distant, impersonal passion for her beauty had become personal devotion and tender concern for her fate. Murder was an absurd idea. No motive could be found; the young couple were believed to adore each other. Nor was it unheard of for an accidental slip to have such terrible consequences. The legal investigation ended with Madame Laure's release. By then Lydgate had seen her many times and found her increasingly adorable. She spoke little, which only added to her charm. She was sad and seemed grateful. Her presence was enough, like evening light. Lydgate became desperately anxious to win her affection, jealous that another man might gain it and ask her to marry him. But instead of returning to the Porte Saint Martin, where the fatal incident would have made her still more popular, she left Paris without warning and abandoned her little court of admirers. Perhaps none of them pursued their inquiries far except Lydgate. For him all science had stopped while he pictured the unhappy Laure wandering, pursued by wandering sorrow, with no faithful comforter. Actresses in hiding, however, are easier to discover than certain other hidden facts. Before long Lydgate found signs that Laure had taken the road to Lyons. At last he found her acting with great success in Avignon, under the same name, looking more majestic than ever as an abandoned wife carrying a child in her arms. He spoke to her after the performance. She received him with her usual quiet manner, which seemed as beautiful to him as clear, deep water, and allowed him to call the following day. He was determined then to tell her he adored her and ask her to marry him. He knew this resembled a madman's sudden impulse and was out of keeping even with his usual weaknesses. No matter. It was the one thing he meant to do. Apparently he had two selves within him; they must learn to accommodate each other and endure the obstacles each created for the other. How strange that some of us can glance quickly beyond our infatuations, and even while raving on the heights see the wide plain where our enduring self has stopped to wait.
To approach Laure with anything less than tender reverence would have contradicted everything he felt for her.

“You came all the way from Paris to find me?” she asked the next day. She sat facing him, arms folded, her eyes showing the wondering look of a wild animal quietly chewing its cud. “Are all Englishmen like that?”
“I came because I couldn't live without trying to see you. You're alone. I love you. I want you to agree to be my wife. I'll wait, but I want your promise that you'll marry me and no one else.”
Laure watched him silently, a melancholy radiance shining beneath her magnificent eyelids, until joyful certainty filled him and he knelt beside her knees.
“I'll tell you something,” she said in her cooing voice, her arms still folded. “My foot really did slip.”
“I know, I know,” Lydgate said, wanting to spare her the recollection. “It was a fatal accident, a terrible misfortune that only bound me more closely to you.”
Laure paused again, then said slowly, “I meant to do it.”
Strong as he was, Lydgate went pale and began to tremble. Moments seemed to pass before he got up and moved away from her.
“There was a secret, then,” he said at last, almost fiercely. “He treated you brutally. You hated him.”
“No. He bored me. He loved me too much. He insisted on living in Paris instead of my own country, and I didn't like that.”
“Great God!” Lydgate groaned in horror. “And you planned to murder him?”
“I didn't plan it. The idea came during the play. I meant to do it.”
Lydgate stood speechless, unconsciously putting on his hat as he looked at her. He saw this woman, the first to receive his youthful adoration, among the crowd of stupid criminals.
“You're a good young man,” she said. “But I don't like husbands. I'll never have another.”

Three days later Lydgate was back at his electrical experiments in his Paris rooms, convinced that he had finished with illusions. His abundant kindness and his belief that human life could be improved saved him from becoming hardened. But now that his judgment was so experienced, he had still more reason to trust it. From this point on he would take a strictly scientific view of women and entertain only expectations justified in advance.

No one in Middlemarch was likely to imagine anything resembling even this faint sketch of Lydgate's past. Indeed, the respectable townspeople were no more eager than most human beings to form an accurate picture of what lay beyond their own senses. Not only the town's young unmarried women but its gray-bearded men hurried to imagine how a new acquaintance could serve their purposes. They were content with the vaguest knowledge of how life had been shaping him for the use they intended. Middlemarch, in fact, expected to swallow Lydgate and digest him quite comfortably.

chapters.title: Book II: Old And Young — Chapter XVI
paragraphs:
“Everything adored in women
I find in your fair self;
For all their sex can offer
Is beauty joined with kindness.”
—SIR CHARLES SEDLEY.

Whether Mr. Tyke should become the hospital's paid chaplain was an absorbing question in Middlemarch. The discussions Lydgate heard revealed much about Mr. Bulstrode's power in the town. The banker clearly ruled, but there was an opposition party. Even some supporters let it be known that their support involved a compromise. They freely expressed their belief that the general arrangement of the world, and especially the hazards of trade, obliged a man to hold a candle to the devil.

Mr. Bulstrode's power came from more than his position as a provincial banker who knew most local tradesmen's financial secrets and could influence their credit. It was strengthened by a generosity at once prompt and exacting: prompt to place others under an obligation, exacting in watching the results. Industrious and always at his post, he had acquired a leading share in managing the town's charities. His private charitable acts were both numerous and attentive to small details. He would take great trouble to apprentice the shoemaker Tegg's son, and keep watch on Tegg's attendance at church. He would defend Mrs. Strype, the washerwoman, against Stubbs's unfair demands over her drying ground, and personally investigate a slander against Mrs. Strype. He made many small private loans, but examined the borrower's circumstances closely, both before and afterwards. In this way a man acquires territory in his neighbors' hopes and fears as well as their gratitude. Once power enters that subtle region, it multiplies, spreading far beyond its outward resources. Mr. Bulstrode made it a principle to acquire as much power as possible so that he could use it for God's glory. He endured much spiritual struggle and inward debate in arranging his motives and establishing for himself what God's glory required. Yet, as we have seen, people did not always appreciate those motives correctly. Middlemarch had many crude minds whose scales of reflection could only weigh things in a lump. They strongly suspected that, since Mr. Bulstrode could not enjoy life as they did—eating and drinking so little and worrying over everything—his sense of mastery must provide a sort of vampire's feast.

The chaplaincy came up when Lydgate dined at Mr. Vincy's. He noticed that the family's connection with Mr. Bulstrode did not prevent frank criticism, even from the host. Mr. Vincy's objections, however, rested entirely on his dislike of Mr. Tyke's sermons, which were all doctrine, and his preference for Mr. Farebrother, whose sermons were untainted by it. He quite approved of paying the chaplain a salary, provided it went to Farebrother: as good a little fellow as ever lived, the best preacher anywhere, and excellent company too.
“What position will you take, then?” asked Mr. Chichely, the coroner, who often went hare-coursing with Mr. Vincy.

“Oh, I'm extremely glad I'm no longer a Director. I'll vote to leave it to the Directors and the Medical Board together. I'll shift some responsibility onto your shoulders, Doctor,” said Mr. Vincy, looking first at Dr. Sprague, the town's senior physician, then at Lydgate opposite him. “You medical gentlemen must decide which black draught to prescribe, eh, Mr. Lydgate?”

“I know little about either man,” said Lydgate. “But appointments generally depend too much on personal liking. The man best suited to a particular post isn't always the nicest or most agreeable. Sometimes the only way to bring about a reform would be to pension off the good fellows everyone likes and remove them from consideration.”

Dr. Sprague was considered the physician with the greatest “weight,” although Dr. Minchin was usually credited with greater “insight.” As Lydgate spoke, Sprague emptied his broad, heavy face of expression and looked at his wineglass. Whatever about this young man was not uncertain and suspect—his rather showy display of foreign ideas, for instance, and his inclination to reopen questions his elders had settled and forgotten—was definitely unwelcome to a physician whose reputation had been established thirty years earlier by a treatise on meningitis. At least one copy of that work, marked “personal copy,” had been bound in calfskin. I feel some sympathy for Dr. Sprague. Self-satisfaction is a form of untaxed property, and it is very unpleasant to hear its value questioned.
Lydgate's observation, however, did not suit the company. Mr. Vincy said that, if HE had his way, he would put disagreeable fellows nowhere at all.

“Damn your reforms!” said Mr. Chichely. “There's no greater humbug. Whenever you hear of a reform, it means some trick to bring in new men. I hope you're not one of the Lancet's people, Mr. Lydgate, wanting to take coroners' posts away from lawyers. Your remarks seem to point that way.”

“Nobody disapproves of Wakley more than I do,” Dr. Sprague interjected. “He's a malicious fellow who would sacrifice the profession's respectability—which everyone knows depends on the London Colleges—just to make himself notorious. Some men don't care if they're kicked black and blue as long as people talk about them. But Wakley is sometimes right,” the Doctor added judiciously. “I could name one or two points on which he's right.”
“Well,” said Mr. Chichely, “I don't blame anyone for standing up for his own profession. But as a matter of argument, I'd like to know how a coroner can assess evidence without legal training.”

“In my view,” said Lydgate, “legal training only makes a man less competent in matters requiring a different kind of knowledge. People speak of evidence as though a blind Justice could actually weigh it on scales. No one can judge what counts as good evidence on a subject without knowing that subject well. A lawyer is no more useful than an old woman at a postmortem. How can he know what a poison does? You might as well claim that learning to scan verse teaches you to inspect potato crops.”
“I assume you know that a coroner doesn't conduct the postmortem. He simply hears the medical witness's evidence,” Mr. Chichely said with some scorn.

“And the witness is often nearly as ignorant as the coroner,” said Lydgate. “Questions of medical law shouldn't depend on the chance that a medical witness happens to know his business. A coroner ought not to be someone who will believe that strychnine destroys the stomach lining just because an ignorant practitioner tells him so.”
Lydgate had genuinely forgotten that Mr. Chichely was His Majesty's coroner. He ended innocently, “Don't you agree, Dr. Sprague?”

“Up to a point—in densely populated districts and in London,” said the Doctor. “But I hope it will be a long time before this part of the country loses my friend Chichely's services, even if the finest man in our profession could replace him. I'm sure Vincy agrees.”

“Yes, yes. Give me a coroner who enjoys a good day's coursing,” Mr. Vincy said cheerfully. “And I think you're safest with a lawyer. Nobody can know everything. Most deaths are ‘acts of God.’ As for poisoning, what you need to know is the law. Come, shall we join the ladies?”

Privately, Lydgate thought Mr. Chichely might be precisely the coroner without preconceptions about the stomach lining, but he had not intended a personal attack. This was one difficulty of moving in good Middlemarch society: insisting on knowledge as a qualification for any paid office was dangerous. Fred Vincy had called Lydgate a prig; now Mr. Chichely inclined to call him conceited and forward. Especially when, in the drawing room, he seemed to be making himself exceptionally agreeable to Rosamond, whom he had easily secured for a private conversation while Mrs. Vincy presided at the tea table. She surrendered none of her domestic duties to her daughter. Her blooming, good-natured face, the two fluttering pink ribbons at her handsome throat, and her cheerful manner with husband and children were among the Vincy household's great attractions—attractions that made falling in love with the daughter still easier. The touch of unpretentious, harmless vulgarity in Mrs. Vincy heightened Rosamond's refinement, which exceeded Lydgate's expectations.

Small feet and beautifully shaped shoulders certainly help create an impression of refined manners. The right remark seems astonishingly right when accompanied by exquisite curves of lip and eyelid. And Rosamond knew how to say the right thing. Hers was the intelligence that catches every tone except humor. Fortunately she never tried to joke, perhaps the clearest proof of her cleverness.

Conversation came easily between them. He regretted missing her singing at Stone Court the other day. Towards the end of his stay in Paris, listening to music had been the only pleasure he allowed himself.
“I suppose you've studied music?” Rosamond asked.

“No. I know many birds' calls, and I know plenty of tunes by ear. But music I know nothing about delights me—moves me. How foolish the world is not to make more use of a pleasure so readily available!”
“Yes, and you'll find Middlemarch very unmusical. There are hardly any good musicians. I know only two gentlemen who sing at all well.”
“I suppose the fashion is to sing comic songs in rhythm and leave the listener to imagine the tune, much as though it were being tapped on a drum?”
“Ah, you've heard Mr. Bowyer,” said Rosamond, giving one of her rare smiles. “But we're being very unkind about our neighbors.”

Lydgate almost forgot his duty to keep the conversation going as he contemplated her loveliness. Her dress seemed made from the palest blue sky. She herself was so perfectly fair that she might just have been revealed by the opening petals of some enormous flower; yet her childlike fairness came with such ready, self-possessed grace. Since Laure, Lydgate had lost all taste for large-eyed silence. The divine cow no longer appealed to him, and Rosamond was her exact opposite. But he recalled himself.
“I hope you'll let me hear some music tonight.”

“You may hear my attempts if you wish,” said Rosamond. “Papa is sure to insist that I sing. But I shall be nervous before someone who has heard the best singers in Paris. I've heard very little. I've only been to London once. Our organist at St. Peter's is a good musician, though, and I still study with him.”
“Tell me what you saw in London.”
“Very little.” A less sophisticated girl would have said, “Oh, everything!” Rosamond knew better. “A few of the usual sights that inexperienced country girls are always taken to see.”

“Do you consider yourself an inexperienced country girl?” Lydgate asked, looking at her with an involuntary emphasis of admiration that made her blush with pleasure. Yet she kept a simply serious expression, turned her long neck a little, and raised a hand to her extraordinary braids. It was a habitual gesture, as pretty as any movement of a kitten's paw. Not that Rosamond resembled a kitten in the least. She was a sylph caught young and educated at Mrs. Lemon's.
“My mind is certainly inexperienced,” she said at once. “I pass well enough in Middlemarch. I'm not afraid to talk to our old neighbors. But I really am afraid of you.”

“An accomplished woman nearly always knows more than we men do, although her knowledge is of a different kind. I'm sure you could teach me a thousand things, as an exquisite bird could teach a bear if they had a language in common. Fortunately women and men do share a language, so the bears can learn.”

“Oh, Fred has started banging away! I must stop him before he ruins your nerves,” said Rosamond, crossing the room. At his father's request Fred had opened the piano so that she could play, and was filling the interval with a one-handed performance of “Cherry Ripe!” Capable men who have passed their examinations sometimes do this too, no less than Fred, who had failed.
“Fred, please leave your practice until tomorrow. You'll make Mr. Lydgate ill,” said Rosamond. “He has a musical ear.”
Fred laughed and played his tune to the end.
Turning to Lydgate with a gentle smile, Rosamond said, “You see, the bears aren't always willing to learn.”
“Now then, Rosy!” said Fred, jumping off the stool and spinning it higher for her, with a wholehearted expectation of enjoyment. “Give us some good lively tunes first.”

Rosamond played beautifully. At Mrs. Lemon's school, near a county town whose memorable past survived in church and castle, her teacher had been one of those excellent musicians scattered through the provinces who could stand comparison with many a famous musical director in a country offering more opportunities for musical distinction. With a performer's instinct, Rosamond had absorbed his manner of playing. She reproduced his expansive interpretations of noble music with the precision of an echo. To hear her for the first time was almost startling. An unseen soul seemed to pour from her fingers. And indeed it did: souls live on in endless echoes, and every fine expression originates somewhere in an act of creation, even if only an interpreter's.
