Lydgate was captivated and began to believe she was exceptional. After all, he thought, one need not be surprised to find rare combinations of nature in apparently unfavorable circumstances. Wherever they occur, they depend on conditions that are not obvious. He sat looking at her without getting up to compliment her. His admiration had deepened, and he left compliments to the others.

Her singing was less remarkable, but it too was well trained, as sweet to hear as bells perfectly in tune. Admittedly she sang “Meet Me by Moonlight” and “I've Been Roaming.” Mortals must follow the fashions of their time; only the ancients can always be classical. But she could also sing “Black-eyed Susan” effectively, or Haydn's canzonets, or “Voi, che sapete,” or “Batti, batti.” She only needed to know what her audience preferred.

Her father looked round the room, delighted by everyone's admiration. Her mother sat like Niobe before her sorrows, the youngest little girl on her lap, gently moving the child's hand up and down to the music. Fred, despite his usual skepticism about Rosy, listened with complete loyalty and wished he could do the same on his flute. It was the most pleasant family gathering Lydgate had encountered since coming to Middlemarch. The Vincys' readiness for enjoyment, their rejection of anxiety, and their belief that life was a merry business made theirs an unusual home in most county towns then. Evangelicalism had cast a suspicion almost of plague infection over the few amusements left in provincial life. At the Vincys' there was always whist. The card tables already stood ready, making some guests secretly impatient with the music. Before it ended, Mr. Farebrother arrived: a handsome man of about forty, broad in the chest but otherwise small, dressed in very worn black. All the brightness was in his quick gray eyes. He entered like a pleasant change in the light, stopping little Louisa with fatherly nonsense as Miss Morgan led her from the room, greeting each person with an individual remark, and seeming to pack more conversation into ten minutes than the whole evening had held. He reminded Lydgate of his promise to visit. “I can't let you escape, you know. I've some beetles to show you. We collectors take an interest in every new acquaintance until he's seen everything we have to exhibit.”
Soon, however, he turned to the whist table, rubbing his hands. “Come, now, let's be serious! Mr. Lydgate? You don't play? Ah, you're too young and frivolous for this sort of thing.”

Lydgate reflected that the clergyman whose abilities caused Mr. Bulstrode such pain seemed to have found a pleasant refuge in this decidedly unlearned household. He could partly understand it. The good humor, the good looks of young and old, and the arrangements for passing time without intellectual effort might make the house attractive to people who had no particular use for their spare hours.

Everything seemed flourishing and cheerful except Miss Morgan, who was brown, dull, and resigned: altogether, as Mrs. Vincy often remarked, exactly the right sort of person to be a governess. Lydgate did not intend to make many such visits himself. They wasted evenings terribly. After a little more conversation with Rosamond, he meant to excuse himself and leave.
“I'm sure you won't like us here in Middlemarch,” she said once the whist players had settled. “We're very dull, and you're accustomed to something quite different.”

“I imagine country towns are much alike,” said Lydgate. “But I've noticed that people always think their own town duller than any other. I've decided to accept Middlemarch as I find it, and I'll be grateful if the town accepts me in the same spirit. I've certainly discovered some attractions far greater than I expected.”
“You mean the rides towards Tipton and Lowick. Everyone likes those,” Rosamond said innocently.
“No. I mean something much closer to me.”
Rosamond got up to fetch her netting, then asked, “Do you enjoy dancing? I'm never quite sure whether clever men dance.”
“I'd dance with you, if you'd let me.”
“Oh!” Rosamond gave a slight, modest laugh. “I only meant that we sometimes have dances, and I wondered whether you'd be offended if we invited you.”
“Not on the condition I mentioned.”

After this exchange Lydgate thought he was leaving. But as he approached the whist tables, he became interested in Mr. Farebrother's masterly play, and in his face, which strikingly combined shrewdness and gentleness. Supper arrived at ten, as was customary in Middlemarch, and people drank punch. Mr. Farebrother took only a glass of water. He was winning, and there seemed no reason the games should stop. At last Lydgate said goodbye.

It was not yet eleven, so he decided to walk through the brisk air towards the tower of St. Botolph's, Mr. Farebrother's church, which rose dark, square, and massive against the starlit sky. It was Middlemarch's oldest church, although the vicarage brought in barely four hundred pounds a year. Lydgate had heard that figure and now wondered whether Mr. Farebrother cared about his card winnings. “He seems a very pleasant fellow,” he thought, “but Bulstrode may have good reasons.” A great many things would become easier for Lydgate if Mr. Bulstrode proved generally justified. “What do his religious doctrines matter to me if he brings some useful ideas along with them? One must use the brains available.”

These really were Lydgate's first reflections on leaving Mr. Vincy's. I fear many ladies will therefore consider him scarcely worth their attention. Rosamond and her music came second. Once her turn arrived, he dwelt on her image for the rest of his walk, but without agitation or any feeling that a new current had entered his life. He could not marry yet; he did not want to marry for several years. Consequently, he was unwilling to entertain the idea of being in love with a girl he happened to admire. He admired Rosamond enormously, certainly. But he did not think the madness that had seized him over Laure was likely to return with any other woman. If falling in love had been under consideration, it would surely have been quite safe with a creature like Miss Vincy. She had exactly the intelligence one would wish for in a woman: polished, refined, teachable, capable of perfection in all life's delicate accomplishments. It was housed in a body that expressed those qualities so convincingly that no further evidence was needed. Lydgate felt certain that, if he ever married, his wife would have that feminine radiance, that distinctive womanhood to be classed with flowers and music: a beauty virtuous by its very nature, shaped only for pure and delicate pleasures.

But since he had no intention of marrying within five years, the more urgent business was Louis's new book on Fever. It particularly interested him because he had known Louis in Paris and attended many anatomical demonstrations intended to establish the specific differences between typhus and typhoid. He went home and read well into the first small hour of the morning. He brought a far more searching attention to details and relationships in this study of disease than he had ever thought necessary for the complexities of love and marriage. On those subjects he considered himself amply instructed by literature and the traditional wisdom passed down through men's agreeable conversation. Fever, by contrast, had obscure causes and conditions. It offered that delightful labor of imagination which is no mere whim but a disciplined exercise of power: combining and constructing with the clearest regard for probability and complete submission to knowledge, then, in an even more energetic partnership with impartial Nature, stepping back to invent tests of its own work.

Many men have won praise for vivid imagination simply by producing great quantities of mediocre pictures or cheap stories: accounts of very poor conversation on distant planets; portraits of Lucifer on his evil errands as a large, ugly man with bat's wings and bursts of phosphorescent light; or exaggerated sensuality that reflects life like a feverish dream. Lydgate thought such inspiration rather vulgar and wine-soaked beside the imagination that reveals subtle processes invisible through any lens. That imagination follows them through the outer darkness along long paths of necessary sequence, using an inward light that is Energy's ultimate refinement, able to bathe even the ethereal atoms in the space it illuminates in thought. He had discarded all the cheap inventions in which ignorance feels capable and comfortable. He loved the difficult invention that is the very eye of research: provisionally forming its object and correcting it towards ever more exact relationships. He wanted to penetrate the darkness surrounding the minute processes that prepare human misery and happiness; those invisible passages where anguish, madness, and crime first lie hidden; the delicate balances and transitions that determine whether consciousness grows happy or unhappy.

He put down his book, stretched his legs towards the embers, and clasped his hands behind his head. In that pleasant afterglow of excitement, thought relaxes from examining a particular object into a spreading awareness of its connections with the rest of existence. It seems to roll onto its back after vigorous swimming and float, resting without exhaustion. Lydgate felt triumphant pleasure in his studies, and something like pity for less fortunate men outside his profession.

“If I hadn't taken that turn as a boy,” he thought, “I might have landed in some dull dray-horse occupation and spent my life in blinkers. I could never have been happy in work that didn't demand the greatest intellectual effort while keeping me in warm contact with other people. Nothing equals medicine for that. One can lead the solitary scientific life that reaches into the distance and still befriend the old fogies of the parish. It's harder for a clergyman. Farebrother seems an exception.”

That last thought brought back the Vincys and the evening's scenes. They drifted pleasantly through his mind, and as he picked up his bedroom candle his lips formed the beginning of the smile that agreeable memories often bring. He was a passionate man, but for now his passion was absorbed in his work and in the ambition to have his life recognized as a contribution to humanity's better future, like other scientific heroes who had begun with nothing but an obscure country practice.

Poor Lydgate! Or should I say poor Rosamond? Each inhabited a world unknown to the other. Lydgate had not imagined himself the subject of Rosamond's eager reflections. She had no reason to place marriage in the distant future, and no studies in pathology to draw her from the habit of dwelling on things: that inward rehearsal of looks, words, and phrases which occupies so much of most girls' lives. He had intended no more admiration or compliments in his looks and conversation than a man inevitably offers a beautiful girl. Indeed, he thought his enjoyment of her music had been almost silent; he had feared being rude by expressing how surprised he was at her accomplishment. But Rosamond had recorded every look and word and valued them as the opening events of a romance already imagined, events made precious by the development and climax she foresaw. Her romance required little imagination of the hero's inward life or serious work in the world. Naturally he had a profession and was clever, as well as handsome enough. But Lydgate's special attraction was his good birth, which distinguished him from every Middlemarch admirer. Marriage offered advancement in rank, a step towards that heavenly earthly condition in which she would have nothing to do with vulgar people. Perhaps she would at last mix with relatives quite equal to the county families who looked down on Middlemarch. One part of Rosamond's cleverness was her delicate perception of the faintest trace of rank. Once, seeing the Miss Brookes with their uncle at the county assizes, seated among the aristocracy, she had envied them despite their plain clothes.

If you find it incredible that thinking of Lydgate as well born could produce thrills of satisfaction connected with her feeling of being in love, I ask you to use comparison a little more effectively. Have red military coats and epaulets never produced a similar effect? Our passions do not live separately in locked rooms. Dressed in their small wardrobe of ideas, they bring their supplies to a common table and eat together, each feeding from the shared store according to its appetite.

Rosamond was, in fact, entirely occupied not quite with Tertius Lydgate himself, but with his relation to her. A girl accustomed to hearing that all young men might, could, would, or did love her could be forgiven for immediately assuming he was no exception. His looks and words meant more than other men's because she cared more about them. She considered them diligently and worked just as diligently at perfecting her appearance, manners, feelings, and every other elegance. In Lydgate those perfections would find a more appreciative admirer than she had yet known.

For although Rosamond never did anything she disliked, she was industrious. Now more than ever she busied herself with sketches of landscapes, market carts, and portraits of friends; practiced her music; and spent morning to night living up to her own idea of a perfect lady. She always had an audience in her own awareness of herself, sometimes pleasantly supplemented by the more changeable outside audience of the household's many visitors. She also found time to read the best novels, and even the second best, and knew a great deal of poetry by heart. Her favorite poem was “Lalla Rookh.”

“The finest girl in the world! The man who wins her will be lucky!” was the opinion of the older gentlemen who visited the Vincys. Young men she had rejected thought of trying again, as they tend to do in country towns where the horizon is not crowded with approaching rivals. Mrs. Plymdale, however, considered Rosamond's education absurdly elaborate. What use were accomplishments that would all be abandoned after marriage? Her aunt Bulstrode, loyal to her brother's family as a sister should be, had two sincere wishes for Rosamond: that she might develop a more serious mind, and that she might find a husband whose wealth matched her habits.

chapters.title: Book II: Old And Young — Chapter XVII
paragraphs:
“The learned gentleman smiled and said,
Promise was a lovely girl,
But poor, and so she died unwed.”

The Reverend Camden Farebrother, whom Lydgate visited the following evening, lived in an old stone parsonage venerable enough to match the church it overlooked. The furniture was old too, though of a different vintage: it belonged to the generations of Mr. Farebrother's father and grandfather. White-painted chairs bore gilding and wreaths, and remnants of red silk damask survived with splits in them. Engraved portraits of Lord Chancellors and other celebrated lawyers of the previous century hung there, reflected in old pier mirrors, along with little satinwood tables and sofas that resembled extended uncomfortable chairs. All stood out against dark wooden paneling. Such was the appearance of the drawing room into which Lydgate was shown. Three ladies received him, equally old-fashioned and possessed of a faded but genuine respectability. Mrs. Farebrother, the Vicar's white-haired mother, wore frills and a kerchief with dainty cleanliness; upright and bright-eyed, she was not yet seventy. Her sister, Miss Noble, was a tiny old woman of gentler appearance, her own frills and kerchief noticeably more worn and mended. Miss Winifred Farebrother, the Vicar's older sister, was good-looking like him, but pinched and subdued as unmarried women often become when they spend their lives continually subject to their elders. Lydgate had not expected so quaint a group. Knowing only that Mr. Farebrother was a bachelor, he had imagined being shown into a snug room furnished chiefly with books and natural-history specimens. The Vicar himself looked somewhat different, as most men do when acquaintances first see them at home. Some resemble actors known for genial roles unfortunately cast as misers in a new play. That was not Mr. Farebrother's case. He was simply a little gentler and quieter. His mother did most of the talking, while he occasionally added a good-humored qualification. The old lady plainly considered it her habit and duty to tell visitors what to think; no subject was entirely safe without her guidance. Miss Winifred attended to all her small wants, leaving her free to perform this function. Meanwhile, little Miss Noble carried a basket on her arm. Into it she slipped a piece of sugar, first dropping it into her saucer as though by accident, then glancing furtively round and returning to her tea with a small innocent sound like that of a tiny, timid animal. Please do not think badly of Miss Noble. The basket held little portions saved from her more portable food for the children of poor friends whom she trotted off to visit on fine mornings. Caring for and indulging every needy creature delighted her so spontaneously that she regarded it almost as an enjoyable vice to which she was addicted. Perhaps she knew herself tempted to steal from those who had plenty in order to give to those who had nothing, and bore in her conscience the guilt of that suppressed desire. One must be poor to know the luxury of giving!

Mrs. Farebrother welcomed the guest with brisk formality and precision. Soon she informed him that the household seldom needed medical assistance. She had raised her children to wear flannel and not to overeat; overeating, in her view, was the chief reason people required doctors. Lydgate spoke on behalf of those whose parents had overeaten, but Mrs. Farebrother considered that a dangerous view. Nature was more just than that. Any criminal could easily claim that his ancestors should have been hanged instead of him. If people with bad parents were themselves bad, they were hanged for their own badness. There was no need to reach back into what you could not see.
“My mother resembles old George the Third,” said the Vicar. “She disapproves of metaphysics.”

“I disapprove of what is wrong, Camden. Hold fast to a few plain truths, I say, and make everything agree with them. When I was young, Mr. Lydgate, there was never any dispute about right and wrong. We knew our catechism, and that was enough. We learned our creed and our duty. Every respectable member of the Church held the same opinions. Now you may quote the Prayer Book itself and still be contradicted.”
“That must make life quite pleasant for people who enjoy defending their own opinion,” said Lydgate.
“But my mother always gives in,” said the Vicar slyly.

“No, no, Camden. You mustn't give Mr. Lydgate a false impression of ME. I shall never disrespect my parents by abandoning what they taught me. Anyone can see where changing leads. Change once, and why not twenty times?”
“A man might find good reasons to change once without finding reasons to change again,” said Lydgate, amused by the decisive old lady.

“Excuse me. If you rely on arguments, a man without a steady mind will always find plenty. My father never changed. He preached plain moral sermons without arguments, and he was a good man—few were better. When you can produce a good man out of arguments, I'll produce a good dinner by reading you the cookbook. That's my opinion, and I think anyone's stomach will support it.”
“Certainly about the dinner, mother,” said Mr. Farebrother.

“It's the same principle, whether a dinner or a man. I'm nearly seventy, Mr. Lydgate, and I rely on experience. I'm not likely to follow new lights, though there are plenty here as elsewhere. They came in, I say, with those mixed fabrics that neither wash nor wear properly. It wasn't like that when I was young. A Churchman was a Churchman, and you could be fairly sure a clergyman was a gentleman, if nothing more. Now he may be no better than a Dissenter and try to push my son aside on some pretext of doctrine. But whoever wants to push him aside, I'm proud to say, Mr. Lydgate, that he can stand comparison with any preacher in the kingdom, let alone this town. That's a low enough standard—at least to my mind, since I was born and raised in Exeter.”
“Mothers are never biased,” said Mr. Farebrother with a smile. “What do you suppose Tyke's mother says about him?”
“Ah, poor woman! What indeed?” said Mrs. Farebrother, her sharpness momentarily blunted by her faith in mothers' judgments. “Depend on it, she tells herself the truth.”
“And what is the truth?” Lydgate asked. “I'd be interested to know.”
“Oh, nothing bad,” said Mr. Farebrother. “He's a zealous fellow. Not very learned, and not very wise, I think—because I disagree with him.”
“But Camden!” said Miss Winifred. “Only today Griffin and his wife told me Mr. Tyke said they would receive no more coal if they came to hear you preach.”

Mrs. Farebrother put down the knitting she had resumed after her modest portion of tea and toast, and looked at her son as if to say, “Do you hear that?” Miss Noble murmured, “Oh, poor things, poor things!” Probably she meant the double loss of sermons and coal. But the Vicar answered calmly:
“That's because they aren't my parishioners. And I don't think my sermons are worth a load of coal to them.”

“Mr. Lydgate,” said Mrs. Farebrother, unable to let that pass, “you don't know my son. He always undervalues himself. I tell him he's undervaluing the God who made him, and made him an excellent preacher.”
“I think that's my cue to take Mr. Lydgate to the study, mother,” the Vicar said, laughing. Turning to Lydgate, he added, “I promised to show you my collection. Shall we go?”

All three ladies protested. Mr. Lydgate must not be hurried away without the chance of another cup of tea. Miss Winifred had plenty of good tea in the pot. Why was Camden so eager to drag a visitor to his den? There was nothing there but preserved vermin and drawers full of bluebottles and moths, and not even a carpet. Mr. Lydgate must forgive it. A game of cribbage would be much better. In short, a vicar could plainly be adored by the women of his household as the king of men and preachers while still being thought greatly in need of their guidance. With the usual shallowness of a young bachelor, Lydgate wondered why Mr. Farebrother had not taught them better.

“My mother isn't used to visitors taking an interest in my hobbies,” said the Vicar as he opened his study door. The room was indeed as bare of bodily comforts as the ladies had suggested, unless one counted a short porcelain pipe and a tobacco box.

“Men in your profession don't usually smoke,” he said. Lydgate smiled and shook his head. “Nor in mine, properly speaking, I suppose. You'll hear Bulstrode and Company count that pipe against me. They don't know how pleased the devil would be if I gave it up.”
“I understand. You're excitable and need something calming. I'm more sluggish; it would make me lazy. I'd fling myself into idleness and stagnate with all my strength.”

“And you intend to give all that strength to your work. I'm ten or twelve years older and have reached a compromise. I feed a weakness or two to keep them from clamoring. Look,” the Vicar continued, opening several small drawers. “I believe I've made a complete study of the district's insects. I'm continuing with both animals and plants, but at least I've done the insects properly. We're unusually rich in orthoptera. I don't know whether—ah! You've picked up that glass jar. You're looking at that instead of my drawers. You don't really care for these things?”

“Not compared with this wonderful specimen without a brain. I've never had time to devote much attention to natural history. Structure caught my interest early, and it lies directly within my profession. I have no other hobby. There's an entire sea for me to swim in there.”

“Ah, you're a fortunate man,” said Mr. Farebrother, turning on his heel and beginning to fill his pipe. “You don't know what it is to need tobacco for the spirit: bad corrections of ancient texts, or little notes on a variety of Aphis Brassicae, signed with the familiar name Philomicron, for the Twaddler's Magazine. Or a learned study of insects in the Pentateuch, including all those not mentioned but probably encountered by the Israelites crossing the desert; with a monograph on Solomon's treatment of the ant, demonstrating the agreement between Proverbs and modern research. You don't mind being smoked, do you?”

Lydgate was more surprised by this frankness than by its implication that the Vicar felt he had not quite found his proper calling. The neatly fitted drawers and shelves and the bookcase full of expensive illustrated works on natural history made him think again of the card winnings and where they went. But he was beginning to wish that the most favorable interpretation of everything Mr. Farebrother did would prove the true one. The Vicar's candor did not seem the repellent kind that arises from an uneasy conscience trying to anticipate other people's judgment. It seemed simply the relief of wanting as little pretense as possible. Apparently he realized that he might seem to be speaking too freely so soon, for presently he said:

“I haven't told you that I have an advantage, Mr. Lydgate: I know you better than you know me. Do you remember Trawley, who shared your rooms in Paris for a while? We corresponded, and he told me a good deal about you. When you first arrived, I wasn't certain you were the same man. I was very pleased to discover you were. But I haven't forgotten that you've had no similar introduction to me.”

Lydgate sensed a delicacy of feeling behind this, but scarcely understood it. “What has become of Trawley, by the way?” he asked. “I've lost touch entirely. He was enthusiastic about French social theories and talked of going to the American backwoods to found a sort of Pythagorean community. Did he go?”
“Not at all. He's practicing at a German spa and has married a wealthy patient.”

“Then my ideas have lasted better so far,” said Lydgate with a short, scornful laugh. “He insisted that medicine was inevitably a system of humbug. I said the fault lay with the men who bowed to lies and foolishness. Rather than denouncing the humbug from outside the walls, it might be better to install some disinfecting equipment inside. In short, since I'm reporting my own conversation, you may be sure all the good sense was on my side.”

“Your plan is considerably harder to carry out than a Pythagorean community, though. You face not only the old Adam within yourself, but all the descendants of the original Adam who make up the society around you. You see, I've paid twelve or thirteen years more than you for my knowledge of difficulties. But—” Mr. Farebrother paused, then added, “you're looking at that glass jar again. Would you like an exchange? You won't get it without a fair trade.”
“I have some sea mice, excellent specimens, preserved in spirits. And I'll add Robert Brown's new work, ‘Microscopic Observations on the Pollen of Plants,’ unless you already have it.”

“Considering how much you want the specimen, I might ask more. Suppose I make you examine my drawers and agree with me about all my new species?” While he spoke, the Vicar alternated between walking about with his pipe in his mouth and returning to hover affectionately over his drawers. “Good training for a young doctor who has to please patients in Middlemarch. You must learn to be bored, remember. Still, you may have the specimen on your own terms.”

“Don't you think men exaggerate the need to indulge everyone's nonsense until the very fools they indulge despise them?” said Lydgate. He moved beside Mr. Farebrother and looked rather distractedly at the insects, arranged in fine gradations and labeled in exquisite handwriting. “The shortest way is to make people feel your value. Then they have to put up with you, whether you flatter them or not.”

“I agree entirely. But you must be sure you have that value, and you must remain independent. Very few men manage it. Either you slip out of service altogether and become useless, or you wear the harness and are pulled a long way in the direction your teammates take. But do look at these delicate orthoptera!”
In the end Lydgate had to examine every drawer. The Vicar laughed at himself but persisted with the display.

“About what you said of wearing a harness,” Lydgate began when they were seated, “I decided some time ago to wear as little as possible. That's why I resolved not to attempt anything in London, for many years at least. I disliked what I saw while studying there: so much empty self-importance and obstructive maneuvering. People in the country make fewer claims to knowledge and offer less companionship, but for that very reason they touch one's pride less. One breeds less resentment and can follow one's own course more peacefully.”

“Yes, well, you've made a good beginning. You're in the right profession, doing the work you feel best suited for. Some people miss that and regret it too late. But don't be too certain you'll keep your independence.”
“Do you mean family ties?” Lydgate asked, imagining that those might press rather heavily on Mr. Farebrother.

“Not entirely. They certainly make many things harder. But a good wife, a good woman without worldly ambitions, can really help a man and preserve his independence. One of my parishioners is a fine fellow, but he would scarcely have pulled through as he has without his wife. Do you know the Garths? I don't think they were Peacock's patients.”
“No, though there's a Miss Garth at old Featherstone's in Lowick.”
“Their daughter. An excellent girl.”
“She's very quiet. I've hardly noticed her.”
“You may be certain she's noticed you.”
“I don't understand,” said Lydgate. He could hardly say, “Of course.”
“Oh, she takes everyone's measure. I prepared her for confirmation. She's a favorite of mine.”

Mr. Farebrother smoked silently for a few moments. Lydgate had no desire to hear more about the Garths. At last the Vicar put down his pipe, stretched out his legs, and turned his bright eyes towards Lydgate with a smile.
“But we Middlemarch people aren't as tame as you imagine. We have our intrigues and factions. I belong to a faction, for example, and so does Bulstrode. If you vote for me, you'll offend him.”
“What is there against Bulstrode?” Lydgate asked emphatically.
“I didn't say there was anything against him except that. Vote against him, and you'll make an enemy of him.”

“I don't know that I need worry about that,” said Lydgate rather proudly. “But he seems to have good ideas about hospitals and spends large sums on useful public causes. He could help me considerably in carrying out my plans. As for his religious beliefs—well, as Voltaire said, incantations will kill a flock of sheep if accompanied by a certain quantity of arsenic. I'm looking for the man who will supply the arsenic. His incantations don't concern me.”

“Very well. But then you mustn't offend your arsenic supplier. You won't offend me, you know,” said Mr. Farebrother with complete sincerity. “I don't turn my own convenience into other people's duties. I disagree with Bulstrode on many things. I dislike his circle. They're narrow and ignorant, and do more to make their neighbors uncomfortable than to improve them. Their system is a kind of clique combining worldly and spiritual interests. They really regard the rest of humanity as a condemned carcass on which they can feed themselves for heaven. But,” he added with a smile, “I'm not saying his new hospital is a bad thing. As for his wanting to push me out of the old one, if he thinks I'm harmful, he's only returning the compliment. And I'm no model clergyman, merely a tolerable substitute.”

Lydgate was not certain the Vicar was judging himself unfairly. A model clergyman, like a model doctor, ought to consider his profession the finest in the world and treat all knowledge as nourishment for his understanding and treatment of moral disease. He merely asked, “What reason does Bulstrode give for replacing you?”

“That I don't teach his opinions, which he calls spiritual religion, and that I have no time to spare. Both are true. But I could make time, and I would welcome the forty pounds. That's the plain truth. Still, let's drop it. I only meant to say that, if you vote for your arsenic supplier, you mustn't avoid me afterwards. I can't spare you. You're like a traveler who has circled the world and settled among us; you'll keep alive my belief that the other side of the globe exists. Now tell me all about Paris.”

chapters.title: Book II: Old And Young — Chapter XVIII
paragraphs:
“Oh, sir, the highest hopes on earth
Take their chances with the lowest. Heroic hearts,
Breathing foul air, may catch the plague;
Or, without lime juice when they cross the equator,
May waste away with scurvy.”

Several weeks passed after this conversation before the chaplaincy became a practical concern for Lydgate. Without admitting why, he put off deciding how to vote. It would really have been a matter of complete indifference to him—meaning he would have chosen the convenient side and voted for Tyke without hesitation—if he had not personally cared for Mr. Farebrother.

But his affection for the Vicar of St. Botolph's increased as he knew him better. Understanding that Lydgate was a newcomer with professional aims of his own, Mr. Farebrother had taken pains to discourage rather than secure his support. This showed an unusual delicacy and generosity to which Lydgate was acutely sensitive. It accompanied other exceptionally fine qualities of conduct, making the Vicar's character resemble a southern landscape divided between natural grandeur and human untidiness. Few men could have shown such devoted and chivalrous care towards the mother, aunt, and sister whose dependence had shaped his life in many ways uncomfortable for himself. Few men pressed by small necessities are so nobly determined not to disguise their inevitably self-interested wishes as higher motives. In these matters he knew his life could bear the closest examination. Perhaps that knowledge encouraged a little defiance towards the strict criticism of people whose close relations with heaven did not seem to improve their manners at home, and whose actions required no lofty ambitions to explain them. His preaching, too, was inventive and concise, like the preaching of the English Church in its vigorous age, and he delivered his sermons without a text before him. People came from outside the parish to hear him. Since filling a church was always the hardest part of a clergyman's work, this gave him another reason for an easy sense of superiority. Besides, he was likable: good-tempered, quick-witted, and frank, without smiles of concealed bitterness or other conversational seasonings that make half of us a burden to our friends. Lydgate liked him wholeheartedly and wanted his friendship.

With this feeling uppermost, Lydgate kept setting the chaplaincy aside. He persuaded himself not only that it was none of his proper business, but that he probably would never be troubled by having to vote. At Mr. Bulstrode's request he was drawing up plans for the new hospital's internal arrangements, and the two often consulted together. The banker continually assumed that he could count on Lydgate's general cooperation, but did not specifically return to the approaching choice between Tyke and Farebrother. Then the Infirmary's General Board met, and Lydgate learned that the chaplaincy had been referred to a council of directors and medical men, to meet the following Friday. Irritated, he realized he must decide this trivial Middlemarch business. An unmistakable inward voice declared that Bulstrode was prime minister and the Tyke question meant holding office or losing it. Equally unmistakable was his dislike of surrendering the prospect of office. Everything he observed confirmed Mr. Farebrother's warning that the banker would not overlook opposition. “Damn their petty politics!” was one of his reflections during three mornings' shaving, as he began to feel he must truly bring the matter before the court of his conscience. There were certainly sound objections to choosing Mr. Farebrother. He already had too much to do, especially given the time he devoted to activities outside his clerical duties. And the Vicar's obvious interest in winning money at cards repeatedly jarred against Lydgate's respect for him. He enjoyed the game, certainly, but clearly also enjoyed something it paid for. Mr. Farebrother defended all games in principle and said Englishmen's wits stagnated for lack of them. Yet Lydgate was certain he would play much less without the money. The Green Dragon had a billiard room which some anxious mothers and wives considered Middlemarch's chief temptation. The Vicar was an excellent billiard player. He did not frequent the Green Dragon, but reports said he had sometimes visited by day and won money. Nor did he pretend to want the chaplaincy for anything except its forty pounds. Lydgate was no Puritan, but he did not enjoy gambling, and winning money that way had always seemed mean to him. Moreover, his ideal of life made him thoroughly dislike conduct governed by the pursuit of small sums. His own needs had always been supplied without effort on his part. His first instinct was to give half-crowns freely, as trifles beneath a gentleman's concern; he had never thought of devising a way to earn half-crowns. He had always known, generally, that he was not rich, but he had never felt poor. He could not imagine how lack of money directs men's actions. Money had never been his motive. He was therefore unwilling to excuse this deliberate pursuit of small gains. It repelled him altogether, and he never calculated the relation between the Vicar's income and his more or less unavoidable expenses. Possibly he would not have made that calculation even for himself.

Now that the vote approached, this repellent fact weighed more heavily against Mr. Farebrother than before. How much easier decisions would be if people's characters were more consistent, and particularly if our friends were always suited to whatever posts they wanted! Lydgate felt certain that, without a valid objection to Mr. Farebrother, he would have voted for him regardless of Bulstrode's feelings. He had no intention of becoming Bulstrode's dependent servant. On the other hand stood Tyke, wholly devoted to his clerical work, merely a curate at an outlying chapel in St. Peter's parish, and with time for additional duties. Nobody had anything against him except that they could not stand him and suspected his piety of being cant. From his own point of view, Bulstrode was thoroughly justified.

Yet whichever way Lydgate leaned, something made him wince. Being proud, he was irritated at having to wince at all. He disliked frustrating his best purposes by falling out with Bulstrode. He disliked voting against Farebrother and helping deprive him of work and income. Might not the extra forty pounds free the Vicar from that undignified concern with card winnings? Lydgate also disliked knowing that a vote for Tyke would favor the side most obviously convenient to himself. But would his own convenience really be the object? Others would say so. They would claim he was courting Bulstrode to increase his own importance and get ahead. What of it? He knew that, had only his personal prospects been involved, he would not have cared a rotten nut whether the banker was friend or enemy. What he really wanted was a setting for his work, a means of carrying out his ideas. Was he not, after all, obliged to put the creation of a good hospital, where he could demonstrate the distinctions between fevers and test treatments, ahead of every other consideration connected with the chaplaincy? For the first time he felt the restricting, threadlike pressure of small social circumstances and their frustrating complexity. When he finally set out for the hospital after this inward debate, he was really hoping the discussion might somehow put the question in a new light and tip the balance enough to spare him a vote. I think he also relied a little on the energy circumstances generate: some feeling might rush warmly through him and make resolution easy, where cool debate had only made it harder. Whatever the case, he did not clearly tell himself how he would vote. All the while he resented being forced into this dependence. Earlier it would have seemed absurdly illogical that a man with his uncompromising independence and chosen aims should find himself, at the very start, trapped between petty alternatives equally distasteful to him. In his student rooms he had planned his dealings with society quite differently.

Lydgate set out late, but Dr. Sprague, the other two surgeons, and several directors arrived early. Mr. Bulstrode, the treasurer and chairman, was still absent. Conversation suggested that the result remained uncertain; a majority for Tyke was less secure than people had assumed. Astonishingly, the two physicians were united—or rather, though they thought differently, they would act together. Dr. Sprague, solid and formidable, supported Mr. Farebrother, as everyone expected. The Doctor was strongly suspected of having no religion at all. Somehow Middlemarch tolerated that deficiency as if he were a Lord Chancellor. Indeed, people probably believed all the more in his professional authority. The ancient association of cleverness with the devil remained powerful, even among female patients with the strictest ideas about frills and proper feelings. Perhaps the Doctor's unbelief led his neighbors to call him hard-headed and dry-witted, qualities of texture also considered favorable for storing judgments about drugs. At any rate, a medical man arriving in Middlemarch with a reputation for definite religious opinions, frequent prayer, and other displays of active piety would certainly have faced a general suspicion of his medical skill.

In that respect Dr. Minchin was professionally fortunate that his religious sympathies were broad. They offered a distant medical blessing to all serious feeling, Anglican or Dissenting, rather than allegiance to particular doctrines. When Mr. Bulstrode insisted, as he often did, that the Lutheran doctrine of justification determined whether a Church stood or fell, Dr. Minchin replied that man was certainly no mere machine or accidental collection of atoms. When Mrs. Wimple insisted that Providence concerned itself particularly with her stomach complaint, Dr. Minchin liked to keep the windows of the mind open and opposed fixed boundaries. When the Unitarian brewer joked about the Athanasian Creed, Dr. Minchin quoted Pope's “Essay on Man.” He disliked Dr. Sprague's rather free style of anecdote, preferring respectable quotations and refinement of every kind. Everyone knew he was related to a bishop and sometimes spent his holidays at “the palace.”

With his soft hands, pale face, and rounded shape, Dr. Minchin could have passed for a gentle clergyman. Dr. Sprague, by contrast, was unnecessarily tall. His trousers creased at the knees and exposed too much boot in an age when trouser straps seemed essential to a dignified appearance. You could hear him entering, leaving, and going upstairs and down as if he had come to inspect the roof. In short, he had weight and could be expected to wrestle a disease to the ground. Dr. Minchin might be better at detecting it in hiding and outmaneuvering it. Both enjoyed the mysterious privilege of medical reputation in roughly equal measure, and concealed their contempt for each other's abilities behind elaborate etiquette. Considering themselves Middlemarch institutions, they were ready to unite against innovators and interfering laymen. On those grounds both privately disliked Mr. Bulstrode equally, although Dr. Minchin had never opposed him openly and never disagreed without explaining himself fully to Mrs. Bulstrode, who believed he alone understood her constitution. A layman who investigated doctors' professional conduct and continually thrust reforms upon them offended the profession's nostrils as such, even if he embarrassed the two physicians less directly than the surgeon-apothecaries contracted to treat paupers. Dr. Minchin fully shared the fresh irritation at Bulstrode's apparent determination to patronize Lydgate. The established practitioners, Mr. Wrench and Mr. Toller, stood apart in friendly conversation, agreeing that Lydgate was an upstart perfectly suited to Bulstrode's purposes. Among nonmedical friends they had already agreed in praising the other young practitioner who had arrived after Mr. Peacock's retirement. He brought no recommendation beyond his own merits and whatever evidence of solid professional knowledge could be inferred from his apparently having wasted no time on other subjects. Clearly, Lydgate's refusal to dispense medicines was intended to cast suspicion on his equals and blur the boundary between a general practitioner like himself and the physicians. In the profession's interests the physicians felt obliged to preserve its ranks, especially against a man who had attended neither English university and enjoyed their absence of anatomical and bedside teaching. Instead he came with a slanderous claim to experience in Edinburgh and Paris, where observation might be plentiful but could hardly be sound.

So on this occasion Bulstrode became identified with Lydgate, and Lydgate with Tyke. The chaplaincy question acquired several interchangeable names, allowing very different minds to reach the same conclusion.

As soon as he entered, Dr. Sprague bluntly told the assembled group, “I'm for Farebrother. A salary, by all means. But why take it away from the Vicar? He's hardly overpaid. He has to insure his life as well as maintain a household and meet a vicar's charitable obligations. Put forty pounds in his pocket and you'll do no harm. Farebrother's a good fellow, with just enough parson about him to remain in orders.”

“Ho, ho, Doctor!” said old Mr. Powderell, a retired ironmonger of some standing. His exclamation fell somewhere between a laugh and a parliamentary protest. “We must let you speak your mind. But the question isn't anybody's income. It's the souls of the poor sick people.” Genuine feeling showed in his voice and face. “Mr. Tyke truly preaches the Gospel. I'd be voting against my conscience if I voted against him. I really would.”

“I don't believe Mr. Tyke's opponents have asked anyone to vote against his conscience,” said Mr. Hackbutt, a wealthy and fluent tanner, turning his glittering spectacles and upright hair rather sternly towards the innocent Mr. Powderell. “But as Directors, we ought to consider whether our sole business is to carry out proposals coming from one particular quarter. Can any committee member claim that he would have thought of removing the gentleman who has always served as chaplain here, unless prompted by people inclined to treat every institution in this town as machinery for imposing their own opinions? I accuse no man's motives. Let those rest between himself and a higher Power. But I do say that influences are operating here which cannot coexist with true independence. Crawling servility is usually dictated by circumstances that those gentlemen who practice it could not afford, morally or financially, to admit. I am a layman myself, but I have paid considerable attention to divisions within the Church, and—”

“Oh, damn the divisions!” broke in Mr. Frank Hawley, the lawyer and town clerk. He seldom came to board meetings but had now hurried in, whip in hand. “They have nothing to do with us here. Farebrother has done the work—such as it was—for nothing. If there's going to be pay, he should get it. Taking the job away from him is a damned piece of favoritism.”
“Gentlemen might do better to avoid personal remarks,” said Mr. Plymdale. “I intend to vote for Mr. Tyke, but without Mr. Hackbutt's hint I wouldn't have known that made me a Servile Crawler.”
“I deny making personal remarks. I expressly said, if I may repeat myself, or even finish what I was about to say—”

“Ah, here's Minchin!” said Mr. Frank Hawley. Everyone turned away from Mr. Hackbutt, leaving him to feel how useless superior gifts were in Middlemarch. “Come, Doctor, you'll be on the right side, eh?”
“I hope so,” said Dr. Minchin, nodding and shaking hands around the room, “whatever it costs my feelings.”
“If feelings come into it,” said Mr. Frank Hawley, “they ought to be for the man being turned out.”

“I admit I also have feelings on the other side. My esteem is divided,” said Dr. Minchin, rubbing his hands. “I consider Mr. Tyke exemplary—no man more so—and believe the motives for proposing him are beyond reproach. Personally, I wish I could vote for him. But my view of the case obliges me to give greater weight to Mr. Farebrother's claims. He is an agreeable man, a capable preacher, and has been among us longer.”
Old Mr. Powderell watched sadly without speaking. Mr. Plymdale adjusted his cravat uneasily.

“I hope you're not presenting Farebrother as a model clergyman,” said Mr. Larcher, the prominent carrier, who had just entered. “I've no ill will towards him, but in these appointments we owe something to the public, quite apart from anything higher. I find Farebrother too lax for a clergyman. I don't want to list particular charges, but he'll make as little attendance here as possible serve the purpose.”

“And a damned sight better than too much,” said Mr. Hawley, whose language was notorious in that part of the county. “Sick people can't stand all that praying and preaching. That Methodist sort of religion lowers the spirits—bad for the insides, eh?” He turned briskly to the four assembled medical men.

No answer was needed, because three more gentlemen entered and received greetings of varying warmth: the Reverend Edward Thesiger, rector of St. Peter's; Mr. Bulstrode; and our friend Mr. Brooke of Tipton. Mr. Brooke had recently agreed to take his turn on the board of directors but had never attended before. His presence now was due to Mr. Bulstrode's efforts. Only Lydgate was still expected.

Everyone sat down, with Mr. Bulstrode presiding, pale and controlled as usual. Mr. Thesiger, a moderate Evangelical, advocated his friend Mr. Tyke's appointment. Tyke was zealous and capable, and his duties at an outlying chapel did not involve so many souls that he lacked ample time for the new responsibility. Such chaplaincies should be undertaken with fervent purpose; they offered exceptional opportunities for spiritual influence. Although a salary was desirable, it made careful vigilance still more necessary, lest the position become merely a matter of pay. Mr. Thesiger spoke with such quiet propriety that his opponents could only simmer silently.

Mr. Brooke believed everyone meant well. He had not personally attended to the Infirmary's affairs, though he felt deeply interested in everything that benefited Middlemarch and was delighted to meet the gentlemen present over any public question. “Any public question, you know,” he repeated, nodding with perfect understanding. “My work as a magistrate keeps me rather busy, along with gathering documentary evidence. But I consider my time at the public's disposal. And, in short, my friends have persuaded me that a chaplain with a salary—a salary, you know—is an excellent thing. I'm glad to come here and vote to appoint Mr. Tyke, whom I understand to be entirely suitable, apostolic and eloquent and all that sort of thing. I'm the last man to withhold my vote, under the circumstances, you know.”

“It sounds as if you've been fed only one side of the question, Mr. Brooke,” said Mr. Frank Hawley. He feared nobody and, as a Tory, suspected electioneering motives. “You don't appear to know that one of our worthiest men has served here as chaplain for years without pay, and that Mr. Tyke is being proposed to replace him.”
“Excuse me, Mr. Hawley,” said Mr. Bulstrode. “Mr. Brooke has been fully informed about Mr. Farebrother's character and situation.”
“By his enemies,” Mr. Hawley snapped.
“I hope no personal hostility enters into this,” said Mr. Thesiger.
“I'll swear it does,” Mr. Hawley retorted.

“Gentlemen,” said Mr. Bulstrode quietly, “the merits can be stated very briefly. If anyone doubts that every gentleman about to vote has been fully informed, I can now summarize the considerations on both sides.”

“I see no point,” said Mr. Hawley. “I assume we all know whom we're voting for. A man who wants to be fair doesn't wait until the last moment to hear both sides. I've no time to waste. I propose we vote immediately.”
A short but heated discussion followed. Then each man wrote “Tyke” or “Farebrother” on a slip of paper and dropped it into a drinking glass. Meanwhile, Mr. Bulstrode saw Lydgate arrive.
“I find the votes are at present evenly divided,” said Mr. Bulstrode in a clear, cutting voice. He looked up at Lydgate.
“One deciding vote remains. It is yours, Mr. Lydgate. Would you kindly write it down?”
“That settles it,” said Mr. Wrench, getting up. “We all know how Mr. Lydgate will vote.”
“You seem to attach some particular meaning to that, sir,” said Lydgate rather defiantly, holding his pencil still.
“Only that you're expected to vote with Mr. Bulstrode. Do you find that meaning offensive?”
“Others may. But that won't stop me voting with him.” Lydgate immediately wrote “Tyke.”

And so the Reverend Walter Tyke became the Infirmary's chaplain, and Lydgate continued working with Mr. Bulstrode. He genuinely doubted whether Tyke might not be the better candidate. Yet he knew inwardly that, without indirect influences, he would have voted for Mr. Farebrother. The chaplaincy remained a painful memory, an occasion on which Middlemarch's petty social environment had proved too strong for him. How could anyone be satisfied with a choice between such alternatives in such circumstances? No more than with a hat chosen from the shapes the age happens to offer. At best he wears it with a resignation supported chiefly by comparison.

Mr. Farebrother, however, greeted him with the same friendliness as before. In practice, the character of a publican and sinner is not always incompatible with that of a modern Pharisee. Most of us see our own faulty behavior little more clearly than our faulty reasoning or dull jokes. But the Vicar of St. Botolph's had certainly escaped even the faintest taint of the Pharisee. By admitting to himself that he was all too much like other men, he had become remarkably unlike them in one respect: he could forgive others for thinking poorly of him, and judge their conduct fairly even when it worked against him.

“I know the world has proved too strong for ME,” he told Lydgate one day. “But I'm no mighty man. I'll never be famous. Hercules choosing between virtue and pleasure makes a pretty fable, but Prodicus gives the hero an easy task, as though the first resolutions were enough. Another story has him end up holding a woman's distaff, and finally wearing the poisoned shirt of Nessus. I suppose one good resolution might keep a man on course if everyone else's resolution helped him.”

The Vicar's conversation was not always encouraging. He had escaped becoming a Pharisee, but not the low estimate of what is possible that we rather hastily infer from our own failures. Lydgate thought Mr. Farebrother suffered from a pitiable weakness of will.

chapters.title: Book II: Old And Young — Chapter XIX
paragraphs:
“See the other, sighing, who has made
A resting place for his cheek upon his palm.”
—Purgatorio, VII.

While George the Fourth still reigned over Windsor's private world, the Duke of Wellington was Prime Minister, and Mr. Vincy was mayor of Middlemarch's old corporation, Mrs. Casaubon, born Dorothea Brooke, went to Rome on her honeymoon. The world then had forty years less knowledge of good and evil than it has now. Travelers seldom carried a thorough understanding of Christian art, either in their heads or in their pockets. Even the day's most brilliant English critic mistook the flower-filled tomb of the Virgin after her Assumption for an ornamental vase invented by the painter. Romanticism, which has helped fill some dull empty spaces with love and knowledge, had not yet spread its leaven through the age and entered everyone's daily food. In Rome it was still fermenting as a distinct and vigorous enthusiasm among certain long-haired German artists. Young people from other nations who worked or idled near them were sometimes swept into the growing movement.

One fine morning a young man with abundant curls, though not excessively long hair, and otherwise English in appearance, had just turned from the Belvedere Torso in the Vatican. From the adjoining circular vestibule he was looking out at the magnificent mountain view. He was so absorbed that he did not notice a lively, dark-eyed German approaching. The German laid a hand on his shoulder and said in a strong accent, “Come quickly, before she changes her pose!”

The call met a ready response. The two hurried lightly past the Meleager towards the hall containing the reclining Ariadne, then known as Cleopatra. She lay in the marble luxuriance of her beauty, drapery folding about her with the gentle ease of petals. They arrived just in time to see another figure standing against a pedestal near the statue: a living, blooming girl, her form unembarrassed by comparison with Ariadne, dressed in plain gray like a Quaker. Her long cloak, fastened at the neck, was thrown back from her arms. One beautiful bare hand supported her cheek, pushing back slightly the white beaver bonnet that made a sort of halo around her face and simply braided dark-brown hair. She was not looking at the sculpture and probably was not thinking about it. Her large eyes rested dreamily on a shaft of sunlight across the floor. Then she became aware of the two strangers who had suddenly stopped as though to study the Cleopatra. Without looking at them, she immediately turned away to join a maid and a traveling attendant who were lingering farther down the hall.

“What do you think of that for a splendid contrast?” the German asked, searching his friend's face for answering admiration but continuing rapidly without waiting for a reply. “There lies ancient beauty, not corpse-like even in death, but caught in complete satisfaction with its own sensuous perfection. And here stands living, breathing beauty, carrying the consciousness of centuries of Christianity in her heart. But she ought to wear a nun's habit. She almost looks like what you call a Quaker. I'd paint her as a nun. She's married, though. I saw the wedding ring on that wonderful left hand; otherwise I'd have taken the sallow clergyman for her father. I saw him leave her some time ago, and just now I found her in that magnificent pose. Think of it! Perhaps he's rich and would like her portrait painted. Ah, no use gazing after her—there she goes! Let's follow her home!”
“No, no,” his companion said with a slight frown.
“You're behaving strangely, Ladislaw. You look thunderstruck. Do you know her?”
“I know she's married to my cousin,” said Will Ladislaw, walking slowly down the hall, preoccupied, while his German friend stayed beside him and watched eagerly.
“What, the clergyman? He looks more like an uncle—a more useful relation.”
“He isn't my uncle. I told you, he's my second cousin,” Ladislaw said irritably.
“Very well, very well. Don't snap. You're not angry because I think Mrs. Second Cousin the most perfect young Madonna I've ever seen?”

“Angry? Don't be absurd. I've only seen her once before, for a couple of minutes, when my cousin introduced us just before I left England. They weren't married then. I didn't know they were coming to Rome.”
“But now you'll visit them. You can find their address, since you know the name. Shall we try the post office? And you could mention the portrait.”
“Damn it, Naumann! I don't know what I'll do. I'm not as shameless as you.”

“Bah! That's because you're a dabbler, an amateur. If you were an artist, you'd see Mistress Second Cousin as classical form brought to life by Christian feeling—a kind of Christian Antigone, sensuous strength governed by spiritual passion.”

“Yes, and you'd think your painting her was the main purpose of her existence: divinity reaching a higher perfection and almost spending itself in the effort to cover your little canvas. Call me an amateur if you like. I DON'T believe the whole universe is straining towards the obscure meaning of your pictures.”

“But it is, my dear fellow, insofar as it strains through me, Adolf Naumann. That is indisputable,” said the good-natured painter, laying a hand on Ladislaw's shoulder, entirely untroubled by the inexplicable irritation in his voice. “Look! My existence presupposes the existence of the whole universe, doesn't it? My purpose is to paint. As a painter, I have a positively inspired conception of your great-aunt or second grandmother as a subject. Therefore the universe is striving towards that picture through the particular hook or claw it has extended in the form of me. Isn't that so?”
“But what if another claw, in the form of me, is trying to prevent it? That makes the case less simple.”
“Not at all. Whatever the struggle produces, a picture or no picture, the result is the same thing, logically.”
Will could not resist such unshakable good humor. The cloud on his face dissolved into sunny laughter.
“Come, my friend, you'll help?” Naumann asked hopefully.

“No, Naumann, it's nonsense. English ladies aren't available to everyone as models. And you're trying to express too much in paint. All you'd produce would be a better or worse portrait with a background every connoisseur would praise or blame for a different reason. What is a woman's portrait, after all? Your painting and sculpture are poor things. They muddle and deaden our ideas instead of elevating them. Language is a finer medium.”
“Yes, for people who can't paint,” said Naumann. “There you're perfectly right. I didn't advise you to paint, my friend.”
The friendly artist had a sting, but Ladislaw chose not to seem wounded. He continued as though he had not heard.

“Language creates a fuller image, improved by its very vagueness. True vision is inward, after all. A painting stares back at you with insistent imperfection. I feel that especially in pictures of women. As if a woman were nothing but a colored surface! You have to wait for movement and tone. Even their breathing differs. They change from moment to moment. Take the woman you just saw: how would you paint her voice? Yet her voice is far more divine than anything you've seen of her.”
“I understand, I understand. You're jealous. No man may presume he can paint your ideal. This is serious, my friend! Your great-aunt! The Nephew as Uncle, turned tragic—monstrous!”
“We'll quarrel, Naumann, if you call that lady my aunt again.”
“What should I call her, then?”
“Mrs. Casaubon.”
“Good. Suppose I get to know her despite you, and discover she'd very much like to be painted?”

“Yes, suppose!” Will Ladislaw said in a scornful undertone meant to end the subject. He knew ridiculously small things were irritating him, half of them of his own making. Why was he making such a fuss about Mrs. Casaubon? Yet he felt as if something concerning her had happened to him. Some people continually create clashes and complications for themselves in dramas no one else is prepared to perform with them. Their sensitivities collide with objects that remain innocently still.

chapters.title: Book II: Old And Young — Chapter XX
paragraphs:
“An abandoned child wakes suddenly,
Its frightened gaze roaming all around,
And sees only that it cannot find
The answering eyes of love.”
Two hours later Dorothea sat in an inner room, a boudoir, of an elegant apartment in the Via Sistina.

I am sorry to say she was sobbing bitterly. She surrendered to the relief of an overburdened heart as a woman usually restrained by personal pride and consideration for others will sometimes allow herself to do when she knows she is alone. Mr. Casaubon was certain to remain at the Vatican for some time.

Yet Dorothea had no clear grievance she could explain even to herself. Amid her tangled thoughts and feelings, the idea struggling towards clarity was an accusation against herself: her desolation must arise from her own spiritual poverty. She had married the man she chose. Unlike most girls, she had chiefly looked forward to marriage as the beginning of new duties. From the outset she had considered Mr. Casaubon's mind so far above her own that studies she could not fully share must often occupy him. Besides, after the brief, narrow experience of her girlhood, she was seeing Rome, the city of visible history, where a whole hemisphere's past seems to move in a funeral procession, bearing strange ancestral images and trophies gathered from distant lands.

But those tremendous fragments only deepened the dreamlike strangeness of her married life. Dorothea had spent five weeks in Rome. On the gentle mornings when autumn and winter seemed to walk hand in hand like a happy elderly couple, one of whom would soon survive in colder loneliness, she had driven out, at first with Mr. Casaubon and more recently chiefly with Tantripp and their experienced traveling attendant. She had been guided through the finest galleries, taken to the principal viewpoints, shown the grandest ruins and most glorious churches. In the end she most often chose to drive onto the Campagna, where she could feel alone with earth and sky, away from the oppressive masquerade of centuries in which her own life too seemed to become a pageant in puzzling costumes.

For those who have seen Rome through knowledge that gives life and a growing soul to every historical form, tracing the hidden transitions that join its contrasts, the city may remain the world's spiritual center and interpreter. But let them imagine one further historical contrast. The huge, broken revelations of that imperial and papal city were thrust suddenly upon the understanding of a girl raised in English and Swiss Puritanism, fed on scant Protestant histories and art chiefly of the kind used to decorate hand screens. Her passionate nature turned every scrap of knowledge into a principle and shaped her actions in its mold; her quick feelings made even the most abstract things sources of pleasure or pain. Newly married, she had passed from an enthusiastic welcome for untried duty into a turbulent preoccupation with her own fate. Unintelligible Rome might rest lightly on bright young nymphs who used it as the backdrop for the glittering picnic of English society abroad. Dorothea had no such protection from profound impressions. Ruins and basilicas, palaces and colossal statues stood amid a shabby present, where living, warm-blooded humanity seemed sunk in the degradation of superstition emptied of reverence. A dimmer but still eager life of titanic figures stared and struggled on walls and ceilings. Long avenues of white statues looked out with marble eyes that seemed to hold the monotonous light of an alien world. This vast wreckage of ambitious ideals, sensual and spiritual, mingled confusedly with signs of living forgetfulness and decay. At first it jarred her like an electric shock; then it pressed upon her with the ache of too many tangled ideas blocking the flow of feeling. Figures pale and glowing took possession of her young senses and settled into memory even when she was not thinking of them, forming strange associations that stayed with her for years. Our moods often bring images that follow one another like projected pictures seen while dozing. All her life, in certain states of dull loneliness, Dorothea would continue to see the immense interior of St. Peter's, its enormous bronze canopy, the urgent purpose in the poses and robes of the prophets and evangelists in the mosaics overhead, and the red hangings being put up for Christmas, spreading everywhere like a disorder of the eye.

Dorothea's inward bewilderment was hardly exceptional. Many souls, still naked in youth, are tumbled into a world of inconsistencies and left to find their footing while their elders attend to business. Nor do I imagine anyone will consider it tragic to discover Mrs. Casaubon crying six weeks after her wedding. Some discouragement, some sinking of the heart when an actual future replaces the imagined one, is common enough. We do not expect people to be deeply moved by ordinary things. The tragedy contained in their very frequency has not yet entered humanity's coarse feelings; perhaps our bodies could scarcely bear much of it. If we could see and feel ordinary human life acutely, it would be like hearing grass grow and a squirrel's heart beat. We would die of the roar on the other side of silence. As things are, even the most sensitive of us move about comfortably padded with stupidity.

Still, Dorothea was crying. Asked why, she could only have answered in the general terms I have already used. To press her for particulars would have been like asking for a history of lights and shadows. The real future replacing her imagined one was being formed from endless tiny details. Through them, her understanding of Mr. Casaubon and of herself as his wife was changing as imperceptibly as a watch hand moves, away from her unmarried dream. It was too soon for her fully to recognize, or at least admit, the change; still less could she have redirected the devotion so essential to her inner life that she was almost certain to recover it sooner or later. Lasting rebellion, the disorder of a life without some loving and reverent purpose, was impossible for her. But she was passing through an interval in which her nature's very strength intensified its confusion. The first months of marriage often bring such critical turbulence, whether in a shrimp pool or deeper waters, before settling into cheerful peace.

Yet was Mr. Casaubon not as learned as before? Had his manner of speaking changed, or his principles become less admirable? Oh, the fickleness of women! Had his command of dates failed, or his ability to state both a theory and the names of its supporters, or his readiness to outline any subject on request? And where better than Rome to display those accomplishments? Besides, had Dorothea's enthusiasm not centered on easing the burden, perhaps the sadness, that great tasks impose upon the person charged with completing them? That such a burden weighed on Mr. Casaubon was merely clearer than before.

These questions are crushing. But whatever else stayed the same, the light had changed, and you cannot find the pearly dawn at noon. One fact remains unavoidable: a fellow human being known only through brief appearances and departures during a few imaginative weeks called courtship may, in the continuous companionship of marriage, prove better or worse than expected, but will certainly not seem exactly the same. The speed of that change would astonish us if we had no similar changes for comparison. Sharing rooms with a brilliant dinner companion, or seeing a favorite politician enter government, can transform our judgment just as quickly. There too we begin by knowing little and believing much, and sometimes end with the quantities reversed.

Those comparisons could mislead, however. No one was less capable of dazzling pretense than Mr. Casaubon. He was as genuine as any cud-chewing animal and had done nothing actively to create illusions about himself. Why, then, in the weeks since her marriage, had Dorothea felt, without clearly observing it, that the wide views and fresh air she had expected in her husband's mind were replaced by waiting rooms and winding corridors leading nowhere? The feeling oppressed her almost to suffocation. I suppose that during courtship everything appears provisional and preliminary. The smallest sample of virtue or accomplishment guarantees delightful reserves that the broad leisure of marriage will reveal. Once across marriage's threshold, however, expectation fixes on the present. Having embarked on the marital voyage, one cannot help noticing that the vessel makes no progress and the sea is nowhere in sight; that one is, in fact, exploring an enclosed basin.

Before their marriage, Mr. Casaubon had often lingered over explanations or disputed details whose relevance Dorothea could not see. She attributed the imperfect connection to the interruptions in their time together. Faith in their future sustained her, and she listened with passionate patience as he recited possible objections to his entirely new theory of the Philistine god Dagon and other fish deities. Later, she thought, she would see this subject, so close to his heart, from the same high ground that had surely made it important to him. Likewise, when he treated thoughts that stirred her deeply as obvious matters to be dismissed, she could explain his manner by the haste and distraction she too felt during their engagement. But now, in Rome, with her deepest feelings in tumult and new experiences making life itself a new problem, she became increasingly and fearfully aware that her mind kept slipping into inward bursts of anger and aversion, or into lonely exhaustion. She had no way of knowing how the judicious Hooker or any other hero of learning might have behaved at Mr. Casaubon's age, so he gained nothing by comparison. Her husband's comments on the strangely powerful objects around them had begun to send a kind of shiver through her mind. He might earnestly intend to perform his part creditably, but merely to perform it. What was fresh to her had long been worn out for him. Whatever capacity for thought and feeling the general life of humanity had once awakened in him had long ago dried into a preserved specimen, a lifeless embalming of knowledge.

When he said, “Does this interest you, Dorothea? Shall we remain a little longer? I am willing to stay if you wish,” staying and leaving seemed equally dreary. Or he might ask, “Would you care to visit the Farnesina, Dorothea? It contains celebrated frescoes designed or painted by Raphael, which most people consider worth seeing.”
“But do YOU care about them?” Dorothea always asked.

“They are highly regarded, I believe. Some depict the story of Cupid and Psyche, probably a romantic invention of a literary age rather than a genuine product of mythology. But if these wall paintings appeal to you, we can easily drive there. You will then, I think, have seen Raphael's principal works, any of which it would be unfortunate to miss on a visit to Rome. He is considered the painter who most perfectly combines grace of form with sublimity of expression. At least, I understand that to be the experts' opinion.”

Such answers, delivered in a measured official tone like a clergyman reading exactly as directed, did nothing to vindicate the Eternal City's glories. Nor did they give her hope that greater knowledge would illuminate the world with joy. Few encounters depress a passionate young person more than contact with a mind in which years of accumulated knowledge seem to have produced a blank absence of interest or sympathy.

On other subjects, certainly, Mr. Casaubon showed the persistence and eagerness usually taken as signs of enthusiasm. Dorothea longed to follow the natural direction of his thoughts rather than feel she was dragging him away from them. Yet she was gradually losing her former joyful confidence that following him would lead to any broad opening. Poor Mr. Casaubon himself was lost among small cupboards and twisting stairways. In his agitated obscurity about the Cabeiri, or his exposure of other mythologists' careless comparisons, he easily lost sight of whatever purpose had first driven his labors. With a candle fixed before him, he forgot the lack of windows. Writing bitter manuscript comments on other men's theories of sun gods, he had ceased to care about sunlight.

These traits, as fixed and unchangeable in Mr. Casaubon as bone, might have escaped Dorothea's notice longer if he had encouraged her to pour out her feelings as a girl and a woman. He might have held her hands in his and listened with tender, understanding pleasure to the little histories making up her experience, then offered the same intimacy in return, so that each person's past became part of their shared knowledge and affection. Or she might have nourished her love with those childlike caresses natural to every affectionate woman who began by kissing the hard, bald head of her doll, creating a happy soul inside the wood from the abundance of her own love. That was Dorothea's inclination. For all her longing to understand distant things and spread goodness widely, she had enough passion for what was near to kiss Mr. Casaubon's sleeve or caress the fastening of his shoe. She only needed some sign of acceptance beyond his impeccably proper declaration that she possessed a most affectionate and truly feminine nature, while politely drawing up a chair to indicate that he found these displays somewhat crude and startling. Once he had carefully dressed in his clerical clothes each morning, he was prepared only for those civilities suited to the period's neatly adjusted stiff cravat and a mind burdened with unpublished material.

By a sad contradiction, Dorothea's ideas and resolutions seemed like melting ice, floating and vanishing in the warm flood of which they had merely been another form. She was ashamed to find herself helpless before feeling, as though it were the only means by which she could know anything. Her strength scattered itself in bursts of agitation, struggle, and despair, then in visions of more complete self-denial that would turn every hardship into duty. Poor Dorothea! She was certainly troublesome, chiefly to herself. But that morning, for the first time, she had troubled Mr. Casaubon.

Over coffee she had begun by resolving to shake off what she privately called selfishness. She turned towards her husband with cheerful attention when he said, “My dear Dorothea, we must now consider everything that remains to be done before our departure. I would gladly have returned sooner, so that we might spend Christmas at Lowick, but my inquiries here have lasted longer than expected. I trust, however, that your time has not passed unpleasantly. Among Europe's sights, Rome has always been considered one of the most impressive and, in some respects, instructive. I well remember regarding my first visit as a landmark in my life. It was after Napoleon's fall, which reopened the Continent to travelers. Indeed, I believe Rome is one of several cities to which that extreme exaggeration has been applied: ‘See Rome and die.’ In your case, though, I would amend it: See Rome as a bride, and live afterwards as a happy wife.”

Mr. Casaubon delivered this little speech with the most conscientious intentions, blinking slightly, moving his head up and down, and finishing with a smile. He had not found marriage a state of rapture. But he intended to be nothing less than a husband beyond reproach, making a charming young woman as happy as she deserved.
“I hope you're completely satisfied with our stay—with what you've accomplished in your studies, I mean,” said Dorothea, trying to keep her thoughts on what mattered most to him.
