“Yes,” Mr. Casaubon replied in that particular tone that makes the word half a refusal. “I have been drawn farther than I anticipated. Various subjects requiring notes have presented themselves, which I could not pass over although I have no immediate use for them. Even with my secretary's assistance, the task has been rather laborious. Happily, your company has prevented the excessive continuation of thought beyond working hours that has so often ensnared my solitary life.”

“I'm very glad my presence has made any difference,” said Dorothea. She vividly remembered evenings when she had supposed his mind had sunk too deeply during the day to reach the surface again. I fear her answer held a little irritation. “When we return to Lowick, I hope I can be more useful and share more of what interests you.”
“Certainly, my dear,” said Mr. Casaubon with a slight bow. “The notes I have made here will require sorting. If you wish, you may make extracts under my direction.”

“And all your other notes,” Dorothea said. Her heart had already burned over this subject, and now her tongue could not remain silent. “All those rows of volumes—won't you do what you used to talk about? Won't you decide which parts to use and begin the book that will make your immense knowledge useful to the world? I'll take your dictation, or copy and extract whatever you ask. I can be useful in no other way.” With that inexplicable behavior so mysteriously attributed to women, Dorothea ended in a little sob, her eyes full of tears.

The intensity of her feeling alone would have disturbed Mr. Casaubon considerably. But there were further reasons why these words were among the most wounding and irritating she could have chosen. She was as unaware of his inward troubles as he was of hers. She had not yet learned the hidden conflicts in him that call for our pity. She had not listened patiently to his heartbeat, only felt her own beating violently. To Mr. Casaubon's ears her voice loudly repeated those muffled suggestions of his own awareness that he could otherwise explain away as imagination, as the illusion of excessive sensitivity. When such suggestions are unmistakably repeated from outside, we always resist them as cruel and unjust. Even complete agreement with our humiliating confessions can anger us. How much worse to hear a close observer speak, in hard, clear syllables, the confused murmurs we try to dismiss as unhealthy and fight against as though they were the onset of numbness! And this cruel outside accuser was his wife—his young bride. Instead of regarding his abundant pen marks and masses of paper with the uncritical awe of a refined canary, she seemed to stand before him as a spy, watching everything with a malicious gift for inference. On this particular point Mr. Casaubon was as sensitive as Dorothea, and just as quick to imagine more than the facts. Earlier he had approvingly noticed her capacity to worship the proper object. Now he suddenly feared that presumption might replace it, that worship might turn into the most irritating criticism of all: the kind that vaguely sees many splendid goals without the least understanding of what reaching them costs.
For the first time since Dorothea had known him, anger flushed Mr. Casaubon's face.

“My love,” he said, keeping his irritation within the reins of propriety, “you may trust me to know the appropriate times and stages of a work that cannot be measured by the easy guesses of ignorant spectators. I could readily have created a passing impression with a mirage of unsupported opinion. But the painstaking investigator must always endure the impatient contempt of talkers who attempt only the smallest achievements, being equipped for nothing greater. It would be well if such people learned to distinguish between judgments whose subject lies entirely beyond their understanding and those whose elements can be grasped in a narrow, superficial survey.”

He spoke with an energy and fluency unusual for him. The speech was not entirely improvised. It had formed in inward conversation and now burst out like round seeds from a fruit split by sudden heat. Dorothea was more than his wife: she embodied the shallow world surrounding the appreciated or discouraged author.
Now Dorothea was angry too. Had she not suppressed everything in herself except the desire to share her husband's main interests?

“My judgment WAS superficial, as any judgment I can form must be,” she replied with an immediate resentment that needed no rehearsal. “You showed me the rows of notebooks. You've often spoken about them and said they needed arranging. But I've never heard you speak of writing anything for publication. Those were simple facts, and my judgment went no further. I only asked you to let me be of some use.”

Dorothea rose from the table. Mr. Casaubon did not answer, but picked up a letter beside him as though to reread it. Both were shocked by their position: each had shown anger towards the other. At home, settled into ordinary life among their neighbors at Lowick, the clash would have been less awkward. On a honeymoon, whose express purpose is to isolate two people because they are everything to each other, disagreement is at the least bewildering and discrediting. To travel far across the globe and place yourselves in emotional solitude, only to have small explosions, struggle for conversation, and pass a glass of water without meeting eyes, can scarcely seem a satisfactory result even to the toughest minds. To Dorothea's inexperienced sensitivity it felt like a catastrophe altering every prospect. For Mr. Casaubon it was a new kind of pain. He had never been on a honeymoon or entered this close union, which involved more subjection than he had imagined. The charming young bride not only required much consideration, which he had diligently provided; she also proved capable of distressing him cruelly at the very point where he most needed comfort. Instead of gaining a soft barrier against the cold, shadowy, unapproving audience of his life, had he merely given that audience a more solid presence?

Neither felt able to speak again just then. Canceling their planned outing would have displayed a continuing anger from which Dorothea's conscience recoiled, especially as she was already beginning to feel guilty. However justified her indignation, her ideal was to offer tenderness rather than demand justice. So when the carriage arrived, she drove with Mr. Casaubon to the Vatican and walked beside him through the stone avenue of inscriptions. At the Library entrance they parted, and she continued through the Museum from sheer indifference to her surroundings. She lacked the energy to turn and say she wanted to drive somewhere. Naumann had first seen her as Mr. Casaubon left her, and had entered the long sculpture gallery at the same time. There he had to wait for Ladislaw, with whom he was to settle a bet of champagne over a puzzling figure of medieval appearance. They examined it and walked on, finishing their dispute, then separated. Ladislaw lingered behind while Naumann went into the Hall of Statues. There he saw Dorothea again, lost in the brooding abstraction that made her pose remarkable. She no more saw the sunlight on the floor than she saw the statues. Inwardly she was seeing the light of future years in her own home and across the English fields, elms, and hedge-lined roads. She felt less certain than before how those years could be filled with joyful devotion. But her mind contained a current into which all thought and feeling sooner or later flowed: the whole of her awareness reaching towards the fullest truth and the good least confined to self. Clearly there was something better than anger and despair.

chapters.title: Book II: Old And Young — Chapter XXI
paragraphs:
“Her speech was womanly and plain;
She used no artificial terms
To make herself seem wise.”
—CHAUCER.

That was how Dorothea came to be sobbing once she knew she was alone. Soon a knock roused her. She hurriedly dried her eyes before calling, “Come in.” Tantripp brought a visiting card. A gentleman was waiting in the entrance hall. The traveling attendant had told him that only Mrs. Casaubon was at home, but he said he was related to Mr. Casaubon. Would she receive him?

“Yes,” Dorothea said immediately. “Show him into the sitting room.” Her strongest memories of young Ladislaw were of learning, when she saw him at Lowick, how generous Mr. Casaubon had been to him, and of taking an interest in his uncertainty about a career. She welcomed anything that offered a chance to put sympathy into action. At this moment the visit seemed to have come to shake her out of self-absorbed dissatisfaction, remind her of her husband's goodness, and make her feel her new right to help him in every act of kindness. She waited a minute or two. When she entered the next room, just enough traces of crying remained to make her open face seem younger and more appealing than usual. She greeted Ladislaw with that exquisite smile of goodwill untouched by vanity and held out her hand. He was several years older, but at that moment looked much younger. His clear complexion flushed suddenly, and he spoke with a shyness entirely unlike his easy indifference with his male companion. Dorothea grew calmer still, wondering and wanting to put him at ease.

“I didn't know you and Mr. Casaubon were in Rome until I saw you this morning in the Vatican Museum,” he said. “I recognized you at once, but—I mean, I assumed the post office would have Mr. Casaubon's address, and I wanted to pay my respects to you both as soon as possible.”

“Please sit down. He isn't here just now, but I'm sure he'll be pleased to hear about you,” said Dorothea. Without thinking, she seated herself between the fire and the light from the tall window, indicating a chair opposite with the calm kindness of an older married woman. The traces of girlish sorrow in her face stood out all the more. “Mr. Casaubon is very busy. But you'll leave your address, won't you? Then he can write to you.”

“You're very kind,” said Ladislaw, beginning to forget his shyness in his interest in the signs of tears that had changed her face. “My address is on the card. But if I may, I'll call again tomorrow when Mr. Casaubon is likely to be at home.”

“He reads in the Vatican Library every day, so you're unlikely to see him without an appointment. Especially now. We're about to leave Rome, and he's very busy. Usually he's away almost from breakfast until dinner. But I'm sure he'll want you to dine with us.”

Will Ladislaw was speechless for a moment. He had never liked Mr. Casaubon, and without his sense of obligation would have laughed at him as a bat living in the darkness of learning. But to think that this dried-up pedant, this manufacturer of little explanations about as valuable as the stock of fake antiquities in a dealer's back room, had first persuaded this adorable young creature to marry him and then spent his honeymoon away from her, fumbling after his moldy trifles—Will tended to exaggerate—filled him with a kind of comic disgust. He was torn between laughing aloud and bursting into contemptuous abuse, both equally inappropriate.
For an instant he felt the struggle twisting his expressive face oddly. With an effort, he turned it into nothing more offensive than a cheerful smile.

Dorothea wondered, but the smile was irresistible and shone back from her own face. Unless you were already angry with him, Will Ladislaw's smile was delightful. It was a rush of inward light illuminating his clear skin as well as his eyes, playing over every line and curve as though an Ariel had touched them with fresh charm and banished every trace of moodiness forever. Its reflection inevitably carried a little laughter too, even beneath Dorothea's still-damp dark lashes, as she asked, “Something amuses you?”
“Yes,” said Will, quick to find an explanation. “I'm remembering the figure I cut when we first met and you demolished my poor sketch with your criticism.”
“My criticism?” Dorothea asked, more puzzled than ever. “Surely not. I always feel especially ignorant about painting.”

“I suspected you knew so much that you could choose exactly the most cutting thing to say. You said—I don't suppose you remember it as I do—that you couldn't see any connection between my sketch and nature. At least, that was the implication.” Will could now laugh as well as smile.

“That truly was ignorance,” said Dorothea, admiring his good humor. “I must have said it because I could never find beauty in the pictures my uncle told me all the experts admired. I've been going about Rome in just the same ignorance. There are relatively few paintings I can really enjoy. When I first enter a room covered in frescoes or rare pictures, I feel something like awe, like a child at a great ceremony with splendid robes and processions. I feel in the presence of a life higher than my own. But as soon as I examine the pictures separately, the life leaves them, or becomes something violent and unfamiliar. It must be my own dullness. I'm seeing so much at once and understanding less than half. That always makes one feel stupid. It's painful to be told something is very fine and be unable to feel its beauty—rather like being blind while people talk about the sky.”

“Oh, a great deal of appreciation for art has to be learned,” said Will. He could no longer doubt her confession's sincerity. “Art is an old language with many artificial, affected styles. Sometimes the chief pleasure in knowing them is simply the feeling that one knows. I enjoy all kinds of art here enormously. But if I took that enjoyment apart, I imagine I'd find many different strands. Dabbling in paint yourself and understanding something of the process makes a difference.”
“Perhaps you intend to become a painter?” Dorothea asked, her interest taking a new direction. “To make it your profession? Mr. Casaubon will be glad to hear you've chosen a career.”

“No, certainly not,” said Will rather coldly. “I've definitely decided against it. The life is too one-sided. I've seen a great deal of the German artists here; I traveled from Frankfurt with one of them. Some are splendid, even brilliant fellows. But I wouldn't want to acquire their habit of seeing the whole world from the studio.”

“I can understand that,” said Dorothea warmly. “Here in Rome there seem to be so many things the world needs more than pictures. Still, if you have a genius for painting, shouldn't you let it guide you? Perhaps you could make better things than these, or different ones, so there wouldn't be so many almost identical pictures in one place.”

Her sincerity was unmistakable, and it drew Will into frankness. “It takes a very rare genius to change things that way. I'm afraid mine wouldn't even let me do well what others have already done—at least, not well enough to justify it. And I could never succeed through sheer drudgery. If something doesn't come easily, I never master it.”
“I've heard Mr. Casaubon say he regrets your lack of patience,” Dorothea said gently. She was rather shocked by this way of treating all life as a holiday.
“Yes, I know his opinion. We disagree.”
The faint streak of contempt in this quick answer offended Dorothea. The morning's distress made her especially sensitive about her husband.
“You certainly differ,” she said rather proudly. “I wasn't comparing you. Mr. Casaubon's capacity for sustained, devoted work is uncommon.”

Will saw he had offended her, but that only sharpened his newly stirred, underlying dislike of Mr. Casaubon. Dorothea's worship of her husband was intolerable. No man enjoys that weakness in a woman except the husband she worships. We mortals are easily tempted to pinch the life out of a neighbor's buzzing glory and persuade ourselves such killing is no murder.

“Uncommon indeed,” he answered at once. “Which makes it a pity to waste it, as so much English scholarship is wasted, through ignorance of what the rest of the world is doing. Mr. Casaubon could save himself a great deal of trouble if he read German.”
“I don't understand,” said Dorothea, startled and anxious.

“I only mean,” Will said casually, “that the Germans lead the way in historical research. They laugh at results obtained by wandering through woods with a pocket compass when they've already built good roads. When I was with Mr. Casaubon, I saw how he shut his ears to them. He would scarcely read even a Latin treatise by a German. I was very sorry about it.”

Will was thinking only of delivering a sharp pinch to destroy that much-praised industry. He could not imagine how his words would wound Dorothea. Young Mr. Ladislaw was far from deeply read in German authors himself. But it takes very little achievement to pity another man's deficiencies.

Poor Dorothea felt such pain at the thought that her husband's life's work might be worthless that she had no energy left to consider whether this young relative, so indebted to him, should have kept his observation to himself. She said nothing, only looked at her hands, absorbed by the thought's pitiable sadness.

After delivering his crushing pinch, however, Will felt ashamed. He took her silence to mean he had offended her further, and his conscience also troubled him over plucking the tail feathers from a benefactor.

“I was particularly sorry,” he resumed, following the usual path from disparagement to insincere praise, “because of my gratitude and respect for my cousin. It would matter less in someone whose abilities and character were less distinguished.”

Dorothea looked up, her eyes brighter than usual with stirred feeling, and said in her saddest, musical tone, “How I wish I'd learned German at Lausanne! There were so many German teachers. But now I can't help at all.”

These last words cast a new, though still mysterious, light for Will. When he first saw her, he had answered the question of how she came to accept Mr. Casaubon by deciding she must be disagreeable despite her looks. That quick, easy explanation would no longer do. Whatever else she was, she was not disagreeable. She was not coldly clever or slyly satirical, but adorably direct and full of feeling. She was an angel deceived. It would be a unique delight to wait and watch for the musical fragments in which her heart and soul revealed themselves so plainly and innocently. Once again he thought of an Aeolian harp.

She must have invented some unusual romance for herself in marrying him. If Mr. Casaubon had been a dragon who simply seized her in his claws and carried her to his cave without legal formalities, rescuing her and falling at her feet would have been an unavoidable act of heroism. But he was harder to manage than a dragon. He was a benefactor with the whole of society behind him. At that moment he entered the room in all the faultless correctness of his manner. Dorothea's face was alive with newly awakened alarm and regret, while Will's was animated by his admiring guesses about her feelings.

Mr. Casaubon's surprise contained no pleasure, but he maintained his customary polite greeting as Will stood and explained his visit. He was less happy than usual, which may have made him seem still dimmer and more faded. Otherwise the contrast with his young cousin could easily have produced that effect. Will's first impression was one of sunny brightness, adding to the elusiveness of his shifting expression. Surely his very features changed shape: his jaw looked large one moment and small the next, and the little curve in his nose seemed ready for transformation. When he turned his head quickly, his hair appeared to scatter light. Some people saw definite genius in that sparkle. Mr. Casaubon, by contrast, gave out no rays.

Dorothea watched her husband anxiously. Perhaps she noticed the contrast, but it merely joined the other causes deepening her new anxiety for him. This was the beginning of a compassionate tenderness nourished by his real circumstances rather than her own dreams. Yet Will's presence gave her greater freedom. The equality of his youth was pleasant, and perhaps so was his willingness to be persuaded. She felt an immense need for someone to talk to. Never before had she met anyone who seemed so quick and flexible, so likely to understand everything.

Mr. Casaubon gravely hoped Will was spending his time in Rome usefully as well as pleasantly. He had thought Will intended to remain in southern Germany. But he invited him to dinner the following day, when they could talk more fully; just now he was rather tired. Ladislaw understood, accepted, and immediately took his leave.

Dorothea's anxious eyes followed her husband as he sank wearily onto the end of a sofa, supported his head on one hand with his elbow resting beside him, and looked at the floor. Flushed a little, her eyes bright, she sat next to him and said:
“Forgive me for speaking so hastily this morning. I was wrong. I'm afraid I hurt you and made your day harder.”
“I am glad you recognize that, my dear,” said Mr. Casaubon. His voice was quiet and he bent his head slightly, but his eyes still looked uneasy as he regarded her.

“But you do forgive me?” Dorothea asked with a sudden sob. Needing some display of feeling, she was ready to exaggerate her fault. Wouldn't love see returning repentance from far away, run to embrace it, and kiss it?

“My dear Dorothea, ‘who with repentance is not satisfied, is not of heaven nor earth.’ You surely do not consider me deserving of banishment under that severe sentence,” said Mr. Casaubon, making an effort both to speak strongly and to smile faintly.
Dorothea did not answer, but a tear that had risen with the sob insisted on falling.

“You are overwrought, my dear. I too feel some unpleasant effects from excessive mental disturbance,” said Mr. Casaubon. He had actually been thinking of telling her she should not have received young Ladislaw while he was absent. He held back partly because introducing a new complaint during her repentant confession would be ungracious, partly because speaking would agitate him further, and partly because pride prevented him from revealing his jealous disposition. His scholarly rivals had not exhausted it so completely that none remained for other directions. There is a kind of jealousy that needs very little fire. It is scarcely passion at all, but a blight bred in the cloudy, damp discouragement of anxious self-concern.
“I think we should dress now,” he added, consulting his watch. They both stood up. Neither ever again referred to what had happened that day.

Dorothea, however, remembered it to the end of her life with the vividness we give to turning points when a cherished expectation dies or a new motive is born. That day she began to see how wildly mistaken she had been in expecting Mr. Casaubon to answer her feelings. She also felt the first intimation that his life might contain a painful awareness creating a need as great as her own.

We are all born morally stupid, treating the world as an udder to nourish our supremely important selves. Dorothea had begun early to emerge from that stupidity. Yet it had been easier to imagine devoting herself to Mr. Casaubon and becoming strong and wise through his strength and wisdom than to understand that he possessed an equally central self, from which light and shadow must always fall differently. She had not yet grasped this with the clarity that turns reflection into feeling, an idea made as immediate to the senses as the solidity of objects.

chapters.title: Book II: Old And Young — Chapter XXII
paragraphs:
“We talked for a long time; she was simple and kind.
Knowing nothing of evil, she did good;
From the riches of her heart she gave me charity,
And as I listened, as a heart gives itself,
I gave her mine without daring to think of it.
She carried my life away and never knew.”
—ALFRED DE MUSSET.

At dinner the following day, Will Ladislaw was delightful company and gave Mr. Casaubon no occasion to disapprove. On the contrary, Dorothea thought she had never seen anyone draw her husband into conversation so successfully or listen to him with such respectful attention. Admittedly, the listeners around Tipton were not especially gifted. Will spoke a good deal himself, but his comments came so quickly and with such an air of incidental unimportance that they seemed a cheerful little chime following a great bell. Whatever his failings at other times, this was certainly one of his good days. He described small incidents among Rome's poor that only someone free to roam could have witnessed. He agreed with Mr. Casaubon about Middleton's unsound opinions on the relationship between Judaism and Catholicism. Then he moved easily into an account, half enthusiastic and half playful, of his pleasure in Rome's very mixture of things. Constant comparison made the mind flexible and prevented one from seeing the world's successive ages as separate boxes with no living connection. Mr. Casaubon's studies, Will remarked, had always been too broad for that, so perhaps he had never experienced such a sudden change. For himself, though, Rome had given him a wholly new sense of history as a whole. Its fragments stirred his imagination and made him build connections. From time to time, though not too often, he appealed to Dorothea and discussed her replies as though her feelings deserved a place in the final judgment even of the Madonna di Foligno or the Laocoön. Feeling that one helps form the world's opinion makes conversation especially cheerful. Mr. Casaubon, too, took some pride in his young wife, who spoke better than most women, as he had recognized when choosing her.

Everything was going so pleasantly that, when Mr. Casaubon said his work in the Library would pause for two days and, after one brief return, leave him no further reason to stay in Rome, Will ventured to urge a visit to a studio or two before Mrs. Casaubon left. Wouldn't Mr. Casaubon take her? It was something not to be missed, something distinctive: a form of life growing like fresh little vegetation, with its population of insects, on enormous fossils. Will would gladly guide them, not through anything tiring, just a few examples.

Seeing Dorothea look earnestly towards him, Mr. Casaubon could hardly avoid asking whether such visits would interest her. He was at her service for the entire day now. They agreed that Will would return the next morning and drive with them.

Will could not leave out Thorwaldsen, a living celebrity about whom even Mr. Casaubon asked. But before much of the day had passed, he led them to his friend Adolf Naumann's studio. He described Naumann as a leading renewer of Christian art, one of those who had not merely revived but enlarged the grand conception of supreme events as sacred mysteries watched by successive ages, bringing the great souls of all periods into a kind of shared present. Will added that for the time being he had made himself Naumann's pupil.

“I've been doing some oil sketches under his guidance,” Will said. “I hate copying. I must add something of my own. Naumann has been painting the Saints Drawing the Chariot of the Church, and I've been sketching Marlowe's Tamburlaine Driving the Conquered Kings in His Chariot. I'm less ecclesiastical than Naumann, and sometimes tease him about cramming in too much meaning. But this time I intend to surpass him in the breadth of my purpose. To me, Tamburlaine in his chariot represents the tremendous course of the world's physical history, whipping the harnessed dynasties onward. I think that's a good mythical interpretation.” He looked at Mr. Casaubon, who received this casual handling of symbolism very uneasily and gave a noncommittal bow.
“It must be a very grand sketch to convey so much,” said Dorothea. “I'd need an explanation even of your explanation. Is Tamburlaine meant to represent earthquakes and volcanoes?”
“Oh yes,” Will said, laughing, “and the migrations of peoples, the clearing of forests, America, and the steam engine. Anything you can imagine!”
“What difficult shorthand!” said Dorothea, smiling at her husband. “It would take all your knowledge to read it.”
Mr. Casaubon blinked furtively at Will, suspecting he was being mocked. But he could not include Dorothea in that suspicion.

They found Naumann hard at work, though without a model. His pictures were arranged to advantage, and a dove-gray smock and maroon velvet cap set off his plain but lively appearance. Everything was as fortunate as though he had expected the beautiful young Englishwoman at precisely that moment.

In confident English the painter gave short explanations of his finished and unfinished subjects, apparently observing Mr. Casaubon as closely as Dorothea. Will broke in now and then with enthusiastic praise, pointing out particular strengths in his friend's work. Dorothea began to gain entirely new ideas about Madonnas seated beneath inexplicable canopied thrones against simple countryside, and saints holding models of buildings or with knives seemingly lodged by accident in their skulls. Things that had appeared monstrous were becoming understandable, even natural in meaning. But this was evidently a field of knowledge Mr. Casaubon had never cared to explore.
“I think I'd rather feel a painting's beauty than have to solve it like a riddle,” Dorothea told Will. “Still, I could learn to understand these pictures sooner than yours with its enormous meaning.”
“Don't mention my painting in front of Naumann,” said Will. “He'll tell you it's all botchwork. That's his strongest insult!”
“Is that true?” Dorothea asked, turning her honest eyes towards Naumann. He made a slight face and answered:
“Oh, he isn't serious about painting. Literature must be his field. That is wi-ide.”

The way Naumann stretched the vowel made the word sound satirical. Will rather disliked it, but managed a laugh. Mr. Casaubon, though somewhat repelled by the painter's German accent, began to respect his discriminating severity.
That respect did not lessen when Naumann drew Will aside briefly, glanced from a large canvas to Mr. Casaubon, then approached again and said:

“My friend Ladislaw thinks you will forgive me, sir, if I say that a sketch of your head would be invaluable for the St. Thomas Aquinas in that picture. It's too much to ask, but I so rarely see exactly what I need: the ideal embodied in reality.”

“You astonish me, sir,” said Mr. Casaubon, a glow of pleasure improving his appearance. “But if my poor features, which I have always considered entirely ordinary, could supply any traits for the Angelic Doctor, I would feel honored. Provided, that is, that the process is not lengthy and Mrs. Casaubon does not object to waiting.”
Nothing could have pleased Dorothea more, unless a miraculous voice had declared Mr. Casaubon the wisest and worthiest of men. Then her wavering faith would have become firm again.

Naumann's equipment was astonishingly ready, and both sketching and conversation began at once. Dorothea sat down in peaceful silence, happier than she had been for a long time. Everyone around her seemed good. She told herself that, had she only been less ignorant, Rome would have been full of beauty; its sadness would have taken flight on wings of hope. No one was less suspicious by nature. As a child she had believed wasps could feel gratitude and sparrows respond to honor, and her indignation had matched her faith when their baseness became clear.
The skillful painter asked Mr. Casaubon about English political institutions, drawing lengthy replies. Meanwhile Will perched on a set of steps at the back, overlooking the scene.
Presently Naumann said, “Now, if I could set this aside for half an hour and return to it—come and look, Ladislaw—I think it's perfect so far.”
Will uttered those emphatic exclamations which suggest admiration too strong for grammar. Naumann then said with pitiable regret:
“Ah, if only I could have a little longer. But you have other engagements. I couldn't ask it, or even ask you to return tomorrow.”
“Oh, let's stay!” said Dorothea. “We have nothing planned today except going about, do we?” She looked pleadingly at Mr. Casaubon. “It would be a pity not to make the head as good as possible.”
“I am at your service, sir,” said Mr. Casaubon with gracious condescension. “Since I have surrendered the inside of my head to idleness, its outside may as well work in this fashion.”

“You are extraordinarily kind. Now I'm happy!” said Naumann. He continued in German to Will, pointing at different places in the sketch as though discussing it. Setting it aside, he looked vaguely around, apparently seeking something to occupy his guests. Then he turned to Mr. Casaubon.
“Perhaps the beautiful bride, the gracious lady, would allow me to fill the interval by attempting a small sketch of her. Not for that picture, of course, as you see. Just a separate study.”
Bowing, Mr. Casaubon said he was sure Mrs. Casaubon would oblige. Dorothea immediately asked, “Where should I stand?”

Naumann apologized repeatedly as he asked her to stand and allowed himself to arrange her pose. She complied without the artificial gestures and laughter often thought necessary on such occasions. “I want you as Santa Clara,” he said. “Leaning like this, your cheek against your hand. Like that. Please look at that stool. There!”
Will was torn between wanting to fall at the saint's feet and kiss her robe, and wanting to knock Naumann down as he adjusted her arm. It was all insolence and desecration. He regretted bringing her.

The painter worked diligently. Recovering himself, Will moved about and entertained Mr. Casaubon as ingeniously as possible. In the end, however, he could not prevent the gentleman from finding the time long; Mr. Casaubon made this clear by worrying that his wife would become tired. Naumann understood the hint.
“Now, sir, if you would oblige me again, I can release your lady wife.”

Mr. Casaubon's patience endured a little longer. When it finally appeared that St. Thomas Aquinas's head would benefit from another sitting, he agreed to return the next day. Santa Clara, too, received more than one touch-up on that visit. Mr. Casaubon was so far from displeased with the result that he arranged to buy the picture in which St. Thomas Aquinas sat among the Church's learned doctors in a debate too abstract to depict, attended with varying degrees of interest by an audience overhead. When the Santa Clara was mentioned afterwards, Naumann declared himself dissatisfied. He could not conscientiously promise to make a worthy picture of it. The arrangement concerning Santa Clara therefore remained conditional.

I will not linger over Naumann's jokes about Mr. Casaubon that evening, or his ecstatic praises of Dorothea's charm. Will joined in both, but with a difference. As soon as Naumann named any detail of her beauty, Will grew angry at his presumption. Even his most ordinary words seemed coarse. What business had he discussing her lips? She was not a woman to be spoken of like other women. Will could not say exactly what he meant, but he became irritable. Yet when, after some resistance, he had agreed to bring the Casaubons to the studio, he had been tempted by the pride of being able to grant Naumann a chance to study her loveliness—or rather, her divinity, since phrases applicable to mere physical prettiness could not apply to her. Certainly everyone in Tipton and the surrounding area, as well as Dorothea herself, would have been surprised at such attention to her beauty. There, Miss Brooke had merely been a “fine young woman.”
“Do me a favor and drop the subject, Naumann. Mrs. Casaubon isn't to be discussed as though she were a model,” said Will. Naumann stared.

“Very well! I'll discuss my Aquinas. Not a bad type of head, after all. I suspect the great scholar himself would have been flattered by a request for his portrait. Nobody equals these stiff scholars for vanity! Just as I expected, he cared much less about her portrait than his own.”

“He's a damned bloodless, pedantic fool,” Will burst out through clenched teeth. Naumann knew nothing of his debt to Mr. Casaubon, but Will was thinking of it himself and wishing a check could settle it all.
Naumann shrugged. “A good thing they're leaving soon, my dear fellow. They're ruining your pleasant temper.”

All Will's hopes and schemes now centered on seeing Dorothea alone. He wanted only to make a stronger impression, to occupy a more special place in her memory than he could yet expect. Her open, eager goodwill, which he recognized as her usual disposition, made him rather impatient. Worshiping a woman enthroned beyond reach plays a large part in men's lives. Yet most worshipers long for some royal acknowledgment, some approving gesture with which their soul's sovereign can encourage them without descending from her throne. That was precisely what Will wanted. But his imagination made contradictory demands. It was beautiful to see Dorothea's eyes turn towards Mr. Casaubon with wifely anxiety and entreaty. Without that dutiful concern, she would have lost some of her halo. The next moment, however, her husband's absorption of such nectar, like water sinking into sand, became unbearable. Will's longing to say damaging things about him was perhaps all the more tormenting because he had such strong reasons to restrain it.
Will had no invitation to dinner the following day. He therefore persuaded himself that he ought to call, and that the only suitable time was midday, when Mr. Casaubon would be out.

Dorothea did not know that her earlier reception of Will had displeased her husband. She had no hesitation in receiving him, especially as he might have come to say goodbye. When he entered, she was examining cameos she had bought for Celia. She welcomed him as though his visit were perfectly natural and, holding a cameo bracelet, immediately said:

“I'm so glad you've come. Perhaps you know about cameos and can tell me whether these are really good. I wanted you with us when we chose them, but Mr. Casaubon thought there wasn't time. He finishes his work tomorrow, and we leave in three days. I've been worried about the cameos. Please sit down and examine them.”
“I'm no expert, but you can't go far wrong with these little scenes from Homer. They're exquisitely carved. And the color is lovely. It will suit you perfectly.”

“Oh, they're for my sister, whose coloring is quite different. You saw her with me at Lowick. She's fair-haired and very pretty, at least I think so. We've never been apart so long before. She's a darling and has never done anything wrong in her life. Before leaving, I discovered she wanted me to buy her some cameos. I'd be sorry if they weren't good examples of their kind.” Dorothea smiled as she added the last qualification.
“You don't seem very fond of cameos,” said Will, sitting some distance away and watching her close the cases.
“No. Frankly, I don't consider them a great purpose in life,” said Dorothea.
“I'm afraid you're a heretic about art in general. Why? I would have expected you to respond strongly to beauty everywhere.”

“I suppose I'm slow to understand many things,” Dorothea said simply. “I'd like to make life beautiful—everyone's life, I mean. And all this enormous expenditure on art, which somehow seems to stand outside life and do nothing to improve it for the world, is painful. My pleasure in anything is spoiled when I'm reminded that most people are shut out of it.”

“That's sympathy turned fanatical,” Will said impulsively. “You could say the same about landscape, poetry, every refinement. Follow the idea through, and you ought to be miserable about your own goodness and turn wicked to avoid having an advantage over others. The best piety is enjoyment, when you can manage it. That's how you do most to preserve the earth's reputation as an agreeable planet. Enjoyment spreads. Trying to take care of the whole world is useless. You're already helping it when you take delight in art or anything else. Would you turn all the world's young people into a tragic chorus, wailing and moralizing over misery? I suspect you mistakenly believe suffering is virtuous and want to make your life a martyrdom.” He had gone further than intended and stopped himself. Dorothea's thoughts, however, were not following the same course. She answered without particular emotion:

“You really misunderstand me. I'm not a sad, melancholy person. I never stay unhappy for long. I'm angry and naughty, unlike Celia. I have a great outburst, and then everything seems glorious again. I can't help believing blindly in glorious things. I'd gladly enjoy the art here, but there's so much I don't understand, so much that seems to make ugliness sacred instead of beauty. The painting and sculpture may be wonderful, but the feeling is often low and brutal, sometimes even ridiculous. Here and there something strikes me immediately as noble, something I could compare to the Alban Mountains or sunset from the Pincian Hill. That only makes it more regrettable that so little of the best kind exists among all these things men have labored over.”
“Of course there's always plenty of poor work. The rare things need that soil to grow in.”

“Oh dear,” said Dorothea, drawing that thought into the main current of her anxiety. “I can see how difficult it must be to do anything good. Since coming to Rome, I've often thought that most of our lives would look uglier and more clumsy than the pictures if they could be hung on a wall.”
She opened her lips as though to continue, then changed her mind and stopped.

“You're too young for those thoughts. They're out of place at your age,” Will said forcefully, with his habitual quick shake of the head. “You speak as if you'd never had any youth. It's monstrous, as though you'd seen Hades in childhood, like the boy in the legend. You've been raised among those dreadful ideas that choose the sweetest women to devour, like Minotaurs. And now you'll be shut up in that stone prison at Lowick, buried alive. The thought makes me furious. I'd rather never have met you than imagine such a future for you.”

Again Will feared he had gone too far. But the meaning we give words depends on our feelings. His angry regret carried so much kindness for Dorothea's heart, which had always poured out warmth and received so little from those around her, that she felt a new gratitude. With a gentle smile she answered:
“It's very kind of you to worry about me. It's because you disliked Lowick yourself. You had your heart set on a different life. But Lowick is the home I've chosen.”

The last words came with an almost solemn rhythm. Will did not know what to say. Kneeling to embrace her slippers and declaring he would die for her would be useless; plainly she required nothing of the sort. They were silent briefly. Then Dorothea began again, as though finally approaching what had been in her thoughts all along.

“I wanted to ask about something you said the other day. Perhaps it was partly your lively way of speaking. I've noticed you like putting things strongly. I often exaggerate myself when I speak hastily.”
“What was it?” asked Will, noticing an unfamiliar hesitation in her voice. “My tongue is given to exaggeration. It catches fire as it goes. I expect I'll have to take it back.”

“What you said about the need to know German, for the subjects Mr. Casaubon studies. I've been thinking about it. With his learning, surely he must have the same materials available as the German scholars?” Her hesitation came from a dim awareness of the strange position she occupied: consulting someone else about the adequacy of her husband's scholarship.

“Not exactly the same materials,” said Will, intending to be properly restrained. “He isn't a specialist in Eastern languages and cultures, you know. He doesn't claim more than secondhand knowledge there.”

“But there are valuable books on antiquity written long ago by scholars who knew nothing of these modern developments, and people still use them. Why shouldn't Mr. Casaubon's work be valuable too?” Dorothea asked, with greater energy in her protest. She felt compelled to argue aloud the case she had been arguing in her mind.

“That depends on the field,” Will replied, his tone also becoming argumentative. “Mr. Casaubon's subject changes as much as chemistry. New discoveries keep creating new perspectives. Who wants a system based on the four elements, or a book refuting Paracelsus? Don't you see that there's no point now in crawling a little way behind last century's men, people like Bryant, and correcting their mistakes? Living in a storeroom of junk, polishing broken-legged theories about Chus and Mizraim?”

“How can you speak so lightly?” Dorothea asked, looking both sorrowful and angry. “If you're right, what could be sadder than so much devoted work wasted? I'm surprised it doesn't hurt you more, if you really believe a man as good, able, and learned as Mr. Casaubon might fail in the work of his best years.” She was beginning to feel shocked that she had allowed even this possibility and angry with Will for leading her to it.

“You asked me about facts, not feelings,” said Will. “But if you want to punish me for the facts, I submit. I'm in no position to express my feelings about Mr. Casaubon. At best it would sound like praise from someone he supports.”

“Please forgive me,” Dorothea said, blushing deeply. “As you say, it was my fault for raising the subject. Indeed, I'm entirely wrong. Failing after long perseverance is much nobler than never making an effort worthy of the name of failure.”

“I agree completely,” Will said, determined to change the situation. “So completely that I've decided not to risk never achieving even a failure. Mr. Casaubon's generosity may have been dangerous for me. I mean to give up the freedom it has allowed. I'll return to England soon and make my own way, relying on nobody but myself.”
“That's admirable. I respect the feeling,” said Dorothea, her warmth returning. “But I'm certain Mr. Casaubon has never considered anything in the matter except your best interests.”
“Now she's married him, she has enough stubbornness and pride to take the place of love,” Will thought. Getting up, he said aloud:
“I won't see you again.”
“Oh, stay until Mr. Casaubon returns,” said Dorothea earnestly. “I'm so glad we met in Rome. I wanted to know you.”
“And I've made you angry,” said Will. “I've made you think badly of me.”

“Oh no. My sister says I'm always angry with people who don't say exactly what I want. But I hope I don't usually think badly of them. Afterwards I'm generally forced to think badly of myself for being impatient.”
“Still, you don't like me. I've made the thought of me unpleasant to you.”
“Not at all,” Dorothea said with completely open kindness. “I like you very much.”
Will was not entirely satisfied. Apparently he might have mattered more if she disliked him. He said nothing, but looked dejected, if not sulky.

“And I'm very interested to see what you do,” Dorothea continued brightly. “I firmly believe people have different natural callings. Without that belief I suppose I'd be very narrow-minded. There are so many things besides painting that I know nothing about. You'd hardly believe how little I've absorbed of music and literature, which you know so well. I wonder what your calling will prove to be. Perhaps a poet?”

“That depends. Being a poet means having a soul so quick to perceive that no shade of quality escapes it, and so quick to feel that perception becomes a hand playing delicately varied music on the strings of emotion. Knowledge turns instantly into feeling, and feeling flashes back as a new instrument of knowledge. A person may reach that state only at moments.”

“But you've left out the poems,” said Dorothea. “I think they're needed to complete a poet. I understand what you mean about knowledge turning into feeling, because that's just what seems to happen to me. But I'm certain I could never write a poem.”

“You ARE a poem. That's the best part of being a poet: what fills the poet's awareness in the finest moments,” said Will, displaying the originality we all share with morning, spring, and other endlessly recurring renewals.
“I'm very glad to hear it,” said Dorothea, her words lilting through laughter like birdsong, her eyes showing playful gratitude. “You say such kind things to me!”
“I wish I could ever do something you'd call kind, ever be of the smallest service to you. I'm afraid I'll never have the chance.” Will spoke passionately.

“Oh yes,” Dorothea said warmly. “The chance will come, and I'll remember your good wishes. I hoped from the first that we would be friends, because you're related to Mr. Casaubon.” A watery brightness filled her eyes, and Will felt his own filling too in obedience to a law of nature. Mentioning Mr. Casaubon would have spoiled everything if anything could then have broken the softening power and sweet dignity of her noble, unsuspecting inexperience.

“And there is something you can do even now,” said Dorothea. A returning impulse made her rise and walk a few steps. “Promise never to speak to anyone about that subject again, about Mr. Casaubon's writings, I mean, in that way. I led you into it. It was my fault. But promise me.”
She came back from her brief walk and stood facing Will, looking at him seriously.

“Certainly. I promise,” said Will, though he reddened. If he never said another cutting word about Mr. Casaubon and stopped accepting his favors, it would plainly be permissible to hate him all the more. A poet must know how to hate, Goethe says, and Will at least possessed that accomplishment. He said he must leave without waiting for Mr. Casaubon, but would call to say goodbye at the last opportunity. Dorothea held out her hand, and they exchanged a simple farewell.

Going out through the carriage entrance, however, he met Mr. Casaubon. After expressing good wishes for his cousin, that gentleman politely declined the pleasure of another farewell visit the next day, which would already be crowded with preparations for departure.

“There's something about our cousin Mr. Ladislaw I think will improve your opinion of him,” Dorothea told her husband that evening. As soon as he had come in, she had mentioned Will's visit and his intention to return. Mr. Casaubon had replied, “I met him outside, and I believe we said our final goodbyes,” with the manner and tone used to indicate that a subject, private or public, holds too little interest to invite another remark. Dorothea had therefore waited.
“What is it, my love?” asked Mr. Casaubon. He always said “my love” when his manner was coldest.

“He's decided to stop wandering immediately and no longer depend on your generosity. He means to return to England soon and earn his own way. I thought you'd see that as a good sign,” said Dorothea, looking pleadingly into her husband's expressionless face.
“Did he specify the precise occupation to which he intends to devote himself?”
“No. But he said he recognized the danger your generosity held for him. He'll write to you about it, of course. Don't you think better of him for deciding?”
“I shall wait for his letter on the subject,” said Mr. Casaubon.

“I told him I was certain you had considered only his welfare in everything you'd done. I remembered how kindly you spoke of him when I first saw him at Lowick,” Dorothea said, placing her hand on her husband's.

“I had a duty towards him,” said Mr. Casaubon, laying his other hand over hers in conscientious acceptance of her caress. He could not prevent an uneasy look. “Otherwise, I confess, the young man is of no particular interest to me. Nor need we discuss his future, which is not ours to determine beyond the limits I have sufficiently explained.” Dorothea did not speak of Will again.

chapters.title: Book III: Waiting For Death — Chapter XXIII
paragraphs:
“Your horses of the Sun,” he said,
“And Apollo, that first-rate driver!
Whatever they're like, I'll eat my head
If I don't beat them by a mile.”

As we have seen, Fred Vincy had a debt on his mind. Although no such intangible burden could weigh down that buoyant young gentleman for many hours together, the circumstances of this debt made it unusually persistent in his thoughts. His creditor was Mr. Bambridge, a local horse dealer whose company was much sought by Middlemarch's young men reputedly “devoted to pleasure.” During university holidays Fred had naturally needed more amusement than he had cash to pay for. Mr. Bambridge had obligingly extended credit for hiring horses and for the accidental ruin of a fine hunter, and had also lent a little money to cover billiard losses. The total was a hundred and sixty pounds. Bambridge did not fear losing his money, sure that young Vincy had people behind him, but he wanted a document to show for it. Fred first signed a promissory note himself; three months later he renewed it with Caleb Garth's signature as security. On both occasions he had felt certain he would pay it himself, possessing ample funds in his own optimism. You will hardly insist that his confidence needed a basis in external facts. Such confidence, as we know, is less coarse and materialistic. It is a comfortable disposition that expects Providence's wisdom or our friends' foolishness, the mysteries of luck or the still greater mystery of our own immense importance in the universe, to produce agreeable outcomes consistent with our good taste in clothes and general preference for the best of everything. Fred was certain his uncle would give him money, that luck would run his way, or that by successive swaps he would gradually transform a forty-pound horse into one worth a hundred at any moment. “Judgment” always counted as some unspecified quantity of ready cash. And even if things failed in ways only an unhealthy distrust could imagine, his father's pocket remained, at that time, a last resort. His assets in optimism thus had a magnificent abundance. He had only a vague idea of what that pocket could hold. Wasn't trade elastic? Wouldn't one year's surplus cover another's shortfall? The Vincys lived easily and lavishly, without any new display, simply following family custom. The children therefore had no measure of economy. The older ones retained something of their childhood belief that their father could pay for anything if he chose. Mr. Vincy himself had expensive Middlemarch habits, spending on coursing, wine, and dinner parties. Their mother kept running accounts with shopkeepers, which brought the pleasant feeling of obtaining whatever one wanted without questions of payment. But Fred knew that fathers naturally bullied their children over expenses. Confessing a debt always brought a little storm over his extravagance, and he disliked bad weather indoors. Too dutiful to treat his father disrespectfully, he endured the thunder knowing it would pass. Meanwhile, though, it was unpleasant to see his mother cry and to have to look sulky instead of enjoying himself. Fred was so good-natured that his gloomy face under a scolding was chiefly a concession to propriety. Renewing the note with a friend's signature was plainly easier. Why not? With such abundant securities in hope, he could have increased other people's liabilities without limit, except that men whose names were worth anything tended to be pessimists. They were unwilling to believe that the universal order must necessarily please a pleasant young gentleman.

When we need a favor, we review our friends, appreciate their finer qualities, forgive their little offenses, and try to conclude of each in turn that he will be eager to help. Our eagerness to be helped is as communicable as any other warmth. Still, we always set some people aside as only moderately eager until the others have refused. Fred happened to cross off every friend but one because asking them would be unpleasant. He implicitly believed that whatever might be said of humanity in general, he at least had a right to escape unpleasantness. The idea of his ever occupying a thoroughly disagreeable position—wearing trousers shrunk in the wash, eating cold mutton, walking because he had no horse, or having to lower himself in any way—was absurd, incompatible with the cheerful intuitions nature had planted in him. He also winced at the thought of being looked down on for lacking money to pay small debts. Thus the friend he chose was both the poorest and the kindest: Caleb Garth.

The Garths loved Fred, and he loved them. When he and Rosamond were small and the Garths better off, the distant family connection through Mr. Featherstone's two marriages—first to Mr. Garth's sister, then to Mrs. Vincy's—had produced a friendship maintained more by the children than the parents. They drank tea from toy cups and spent whole days playing together. Mary was a little tomboy, and at six Fred thought her the nicest girl in the world. He married her with a brass ring cut from an umbrella. Throughout his education he retained his affection for the Garths and the habit of treating their house as a second home, though contact between them and his parents had long since ended. Even during Caleb's prosperity, the Vincys had treated him and his wife condescendingly. Middlemarch observed fine distinctions of rank. Established manufacturers, like dukes, could not limit their connections to equals, but they knew themselves inherently superior in a social sense defined with great precision in practice, however difficult to explain in theory. Since then Mr. Garth had failed in the building business he had unfortunately added to his work as surveyor, valuer, and agent. For a time he had carried it on entirely for his creditors' benefit, living frugally and exerting himself to the utmost so he could eventually repay every penny. He had now succeeded. Everyone who did not think this a bad precedent gave his honorable efforts due respect. Yet nowhere in the world are fashionable visits founded on respect without suitable furniture and a complete dinner service. Mrs. Vincy had never felt comfortable with Mrs. Garth, whom she often described as a woman who had worked for her bread, meaning she had taught before marriage. Familiarity with Lindley Murray's grammar and Mangnall's Questions then resembled a draper's knowledge of calico trademarks or a courier's knowledge of foreign countries: no woman with better circumstances needed it. Since Mary had begun keeping house for Mr. Featherstone, Mrs. Vincy's dislike of the Garths had hardened through fear that Fred might become engaged to this plain girl whose parents “lived so modestly.” Fred knew this and never mentioned his visits to Mrs. Garth at home. Lately he had visited more often, his growing love for Mary drawing him closer to everyone belonging to her.

Fred took his request to Mr. Garth's small office in town and obtained consent without much difficulty. All Caleb's painful experience had failed to make him careful about his own affairs or suspicious of people who had not proved untrustworthy. He thought very highly of Fred and was “certain the lad would turn out well—a frank, affectionate fellow, sound at bottom—you could trust him with anything.” That was Caleb's psychological reasoning. He was one of those rare men strict with themselves and lenient with others. He felt a kind of shame about his neighbors' mistakes and disliked mentioning them. He was therefore unlikely to turn his mind from the best way to harden timber and other ingenious practical matters in order to anticipate such mistakes. Before he could blame anyone, he had to move all the papers within reach, draw several diagrams with his stick, or calculate with the loose change in his pocket. He would rather do another man's work than criticize how it was done. I fear he was poor at enforcing discipline.

Fred explained the debt, his wish to pay without troubling his father, and his certainty that the money would be ready in time to inconvenience nobody. Caleb pushed up his spectacles, listened, looked into his favorite's clear young eyes, and believed him. He did not distinguish confidence about the future from truthfulness about the past. Still, he thought the occasion required a friendly hint about conduct and that a fairly stern warning should precede his signature. He took the paper, lowered his spectacles, examined the available space, reached for his pen and inspected it, dipped it in ink and inspected it again. Then he pushed the paper a little away, raised his spectacles once more, and let the outer ends of his bushy eyebrows droop further, giving his face its distinctive gentleness. Forgive these details for once; had you known Caleb Garth, you would have learned to love them. In a reassuring voice he said:
“Bad luck, eh, damaging the horse's knees? And these swaps don't pay when you're dealing with sharp horse traders. You'll be wiser next time, my boy.”

Then Caleb lowered his spectacles and wrote his signature with his customary care. Whatever business he undertook, he did properly. For a moment he tilted his head and studied the large, well-proportioned letters and final flourish. He handed the paper to Fred, said goodbye, and immediately returned to his absorption in plans for Sir James Chettam's new farm buildings.
Whether his interest in the work drove the signature from his memory, or for some reason more conscious, Caleb left Mrs. Garth entirely unaware of the affair.

Since then Fred's sky had changed, altering his view of the distance. That was why Mr. Featherstone's gift had mattered enough to make his color come and go, first through an expectation too precisely formed and then through a matching disappointment. His failed examination had made his accumulated college debts still less forgivable to his father, and an unprecedented storm had broken at home. Mr. Vincy swore that if there was any more of the same, Fred could leave and earn his living however he could. He had never quite recovered his cheerful manner towards his son, who had especially enraged him by announcing at that point that he did not want to become a clergyman and would rather not continue in that direction. Fred knew he would have been treated more severely if the family had not shared his private belief that he was Mr. Featherstone's heir. The old gentleman's pride and apparent fondness served in place of exemplary conduct, just as a young nobleman's theft of jewels is called kleptomania and discussed with a philosophical smile. Nobody thinks of sending him to a reformatory like a ragged boy who steals turnips. In fact, unspoken expectations of Uncle Featherstone's intentions determined how most of Middlemarch viewed Fred. In his own mind, what the uncle might do in an emergency—or simply as luck embodied—always formed an immeasurable depth of airy perspective. But a gift of banknotes, once given, could be measured. Set against the debt, it left a shortfall still to be supplied by Fred's judgment or luck in another form. The episode of the alleged borrowing, when he had used his father to obtain Bulstrode's certificate, provided a fresh reason not to ask him for money towards the real debt. Fred was perceptive enough to foresee that anger would blur distinctions. His denial of borrowing expressly against his uncle's will would be treated as a lie. He had told his father one troublesome matter and concealed another. In such cases full disclosure always makes the earlier account seem deceitful. Fred prided himself on avoiding lies, even little fibs. He often shrugged and grimaced at what he called Rosamond's fibs—only brothers can connect such ideas with a beautiful girl. He would accept some trouble and self-restraint rather than be accused of falsehood. That inward pressure had driven him to the sensible act of leaving eighty pounds with his mother. It was unfortunate he had not handed it directly to Mr. Garth. But he intended to complete the sum with another sixty. To that end he had kept twenty in his pocket as seed grain which, planted with judgment and watered by luck, might yield more than three times itself. A poor rate of increase, when the field is a young gentleman's boundless soul with every number at its command.

Fred was not a gambler in the special, diseased sense: he did not need to hang all his nervous energy upon a chance or risk as a drunkard needs spirits. He merely tended towards that more general form of gambling which has no alcoholic intensity, but circulates with the healthiest, well-nourished blood. It sustains a cheerful activity of imagination, shaping events to desire. Certain of fair weather for itself, it sees only the advantage to others of coming aboard. Optimism enjoys any throw because success seems assured, and finds a still more generous pleasure in offering as many people as possible a share in the stake. Fred liked games, especially billiards, as he liked hunting or steeplechasing. Needing money and hoping to win only increased the attraction. But his twenty pounds of seed grain had been sown fruitlessly on the seductive green field, at least whatever had not already scattered along the roadside. With payment almost due, he had nothing left except the eighty pounds kept by his mother. The broken-winded horse he rode represented a gift Uncle Featherstone had made long before. His father always allowed him to keep a horse; Mr. Vincy's own habits made that seem a reasonable requirement even for a rather exasperating son. The horse was Fred's property, then, and anxiety over the approaching payment made him resolve to sacrifice a possession without which life would be scarcely worth living. He felt heroic in making the resolution, driven to heroism by fear of breaking his word to Mr. Garth, by love for Mary, and by awe of her judgment. He would go to Houndsley horse fair the following morning and simply sell the horse, returning with the money by coach? Well, it would scarcely fetch thirty pounds, and who knew what might happen? Refusing luck in advance would be foolish. It was a hundred to one that some good opportunity would appear. The longer he considered it, the less possible it seemed that none would, and the less reasonable to go without the ammunition needed to secure it. He would ride with Bambridge and Horrock, the veterinary surgeon. Without asking outright, he would effectively gain the benefit of their opinions. Before leaving, he collected the eighty pounds from his mother.

Most people who saw Fred riding out with Bambridge and Horrock, obviously bound for Houndsley horse fair, assumed young Vincy was chasing pleasure as usual. Without his unusual awareness of serious business, he too would have felt he was indulging himself and doing what one expected of a lively young fellow. Fred was not coarse. He rather looked down on the speech and manners of men who had not attended university, and had written verses as pastoral and innocent of sensuality as his flute playing. His attraction to Bambridge and Horrock was therefore interesting. Love of horses alone could not explain it without the mysterious power of Naming that directs so much human choice. Under any label except “pleasure,” their company would surely have seemed monotonous. Arriving with them at Houndsley on a drizzly afternoon, dismounting at the Red Lion on a street darkened by coal dust, and dining in a room furnished with a county map glazed in dirt, a bad portrait of an unidentified horse in a stable, His Majesty George the Fourth complete with legs and cravat, and several lead spittoons might have seemed hard work. Only the sustaining force of a name made pursuing these things “gay.”

Mr. Horrock did possess an apparent unfathomable depth that gave the imagination scope. His clothes instantly suggested a thrilling connection with horses. The hat brim alone was enough: it tilted upward just sufficiently to avoid any suspicion of turning down. Nature had given him narrow eyes, with nose, mouth, and chin seeming to follow the same moderate upward slope as the brim. The result was a faint, unchanging, skeptical smile. No expression exercises greater tyranny over an impressionable mind. Accompanied by enough silence, it creates a reputation for unbeatable understanding, an inexhaustible store of humor too dry to flow and probably hardened into a motionless crust, and a critical judgment which, if you could ever obtain it, would be the one definitive opinion. This face appears in every occupation, but perhaps nowhere has it held more power over England's young men than in an expert on horses.

When Fred asked about his horse's fetlock, Mr. Horrock turned sideways in the saddle and watched its movement for three minutes. Then he faced ahead, twitched his reins, and remained silent, his profile no more or less skeptical than before.

This contribution to conversation was devastatingly effective. It stirred conflicting passions in Fred: a mad wish to beat an opinion out of Horrock, restrained by his eagerness to preserve the advantage of Horrock's friendship. There was always the chance that, at the right moment, Horrock might say something priceless.

Mr. Bambridge was more forthcoming and seemed to spend his opinions freely. Loud and robust, he was sometimes described as “given to indulgence,” chiefly in swearing, drinking, and beating his wife. Some people who had lost money through him called him vicious. He regarded horse dealing as the finest of the arts and might plausibly have argued that morality had nothing to do with it. Undeniably prosperous, he bore his drinking better than others bore moderation and flourished, on the whole, like a green bay tree. His conversation had a narrow range. Like the fine old tune “Drops of Brandy,” it eventually gave the feeling of circling back on itself in a way that could make weaker heads dizzy. Yet several Middlemarch circles felt that a small dose of Bambridge lent them tone and character. He was a distinguished presence in the Green Dragon's bar and billiard room. He knew stories about racing heroes and clever tricks played by marquesses and viscounts, apparently proving that noble blood asserted its superiority even among swindlers. But his memory's precise tenacity was chiefly devoted to horses he had bought and sold. Years later he still passionately asserted how many miles one could trot in no time without sweating, helping his listeners imagine it by solemnly swearing they had never seen the like. In short, Mr. Bambridge was a man of pleasure and a lively companion.

Being subtle, Fred did not tell his friends he meant to sell his horse. He wanted to discover their real estimate of its value indirectly, unaware that a real opinion was the last thing likely to be extracted from such eminent judges. Mr. Bambridge had no weakness for offering praise freely. Never before had he been so struck by the unfortunate bay's noisy breathing, a defect so extreme that only the roundest word for damnation could convey it.

“You made a bad swap when you went to anyone but me, Vincy! You never rode a finer horse than that chestnut, and you traded him for this brute. Put him into a canter and he sounds like twenty men sawing wood. I've heard only one worse roarer in my life, a roan belonging to Pegwell, the corn dealer. He drove it in his gig seven years ago and tried to sell it to me. I said, ‘No thanks, Peg. I don't deal in wind instruments.’ That's what I said. The joke went all round the county. But what the hell! That horse was a penny trumpet beside yours.”
“You just said his was worse,” said Fred, more irritable than usual.
“Then I told a lie,” Mr. Bambridge said emphatically. “There wasn't a penny's difference.”
Fred spurred his horse, and they trotted on for a while. When they slowed again, Mr. Bambridge added:
“Mind you, the roan was a better trotter.”
“I'm satisfied with his paces,” said Fred, needing all the support he could draw from the knowledge that this was lively company. “I'd say his trot is remarkably clean, wouldn't you, Horrock?”
Mr. Horrock gazed ahead as neutrally as a portrait by an old master.

Fred abandoned the mistaken hope of an honest opinion. On reflection, however, he decided Bambridge's criticism and Horrock's silence were both encouraging: they must think better of the horse than they cared to admit.

That very evening, before the fair began, Fred believed he saw a profitable chance to dispose of his horse, one that made him congratulate himself on bringing the eighty pounds. A young farmer acquainted with Bambridge came into the Red Lion and began discussing the sale of a hunter. He called it Diamond at once, as though it were a public figure. About to marry and give up hunting, he wanted only a useful riding horse that could also pull a vehicle when required. Diamond was in a friend's stable a little way off, and there was still time to inspect him before dark. They reached it through a back street where poisoning without the expense of drugs would have been as easy as in any grim street of that unsanitary age. Fred had no brandy to protect him from disgust, unlike his companions. But the hope that he had finally found a horse on which he could make money excited him enough to take him back first thing the next morning. He was certain that, if he did not strike a bargain with the farmer, Bambridge would. Pressure, he felt, was sharpening his intelligence and giving suspicion all its powers of invention. Bambridge had criticized Diamond in a way he never would have done to a friend's horse unless he meant to buy it. Everyone who examined the animal, even Horrock, was plainly impressed. To benefit fully from the company of such men, one must draw inferences rather than be a simpleton taking their words literally. Diamond was dapple gray, and Fred happened to know that Lord Medlicote's man was looking for exactly such a horse. After all his criticism, Bambridge let slip later, while the farmer was absent, that he had seen worse horses sell for eighty pounds. Certainly he contradicted himself twenty times, but when you knew what was likely to be true, you could test a man's admissions. Fred also had to give some value to his own judgment of horses. The farmer had examined his respectable, if broken-winded, mount long enough to show interest. Probably he would take it and twenty-five pounds in exchange for Diamond. Selling the new horse for at least eighty would then leave Fred fifty-five pounds ahead and a hundred and thirty-five towards the debt. The temporary shortfall falling on Mr. Garth would be no more than twenty-five pounds. By the time Fred dressed hurriedly the next morning, he saw the importance of seizing this rare opportunity so clearly that, even if both Bambridge and Horrock had advised against it, he would not have mistaken their words for their real intentions. He would have known those deep operators held other interests besides a young man's welfare. With horses, distrust was the only guide. But skepticism can never, as we know, be applied completely, or life would stop. We must believe in something and act. Whatever we call that something, it is effectively our own judgment, even when it looks like the most slavish reliance on someone else. Fred trusted his excellent bargain. Before the fair was properly underway, he owned the dapple gray, in exchange for his old horse and thirty pounds, only five more than he had expected.

He felt somewhat anxious and tired, perhaps from the mental debate. Without waiting for the fair's further pleasures, he set off alone on the fourteen-mile journey home, intending to ride quietly and keep the horse fresh.

chapters.title: Book III: Waiting For Death — Chapter XXIV
paragraphs:
“The wrongdoer's sorrow offers little comfort
To the one who carries the burden of the wrong.”
—SHAKESPEARE, Sonnets.

I am sorry to report that just three days after the promising events at Houndsley, Fred Vincy was more dejected than he had ever been. The expected buyer for his horse had not failed him. Rather, before the sale to Lord Medlicote's man could be completed, Diamond, in whom eighty pounds' worth of hope had been invested, suddenly displayed a vicious passion for kicking in the stable. He narrowly missed killing the groom and finally caught a leg in a rope hanging over the stall partition, badly laming himself. Fred had no more remedy than someone who discovers a spouse's bad temper after marriage, a temper old acquaintances naturally knew beforehand. For some reason he showed none of his usual resilience under this misfortune. He knew only that he had fifty pounds, no prospect of getting more at present, and a bill for a hundred and sixty due in five days. Even if he appealed to his father to spare Mr. Garth a loss, Fred felt painfully certain of the response. His father would angrily refuse to rescue Garth from the consequences of what he would call encouraging extravagance and deceit. Fred was so utterly cast down that he could think of nothing but going straight to Mr. Garth with the truth, taking the fifty pounds and at least getting that safely out of his own hands. His father was at the warehouse and did not yet know of the accident. Once told, he would rage about the vicious animal being brought into his stable. Before facing that lesser trouble, Fred wanted to leave with all his courage intact for the greater one. He took his father's horse, having decided that after Mr. Garth he would ride to Stone Court and confess everything to Mary. Indeed, without Mary and his love for her, his conscience would probably have been much less active, both in bringing the debt continually to mind and in urging him now not to spare himself in his usual way by postponing an unpleasant task, but to act as directly and simply as possible. Even people far stronger than Fred Vincy keep half their honesty in the mind of the person they love most. “The theater of all my actions has fallen,” said an ancient figure when his closest friend died. Those whose audience demands their best are fortunate in their theater. At that time it would certainly have made a considerable difference to Fred if Mary Garth had held no firm ideas about admirable character.

Mr. Garth was not at his office, so Fred rode to the house a little outside town: a plain, rambling, old-fashioned timber-framed building with an orchard in front. It had been a farmhouse before the town expanded; now private gardens surrounded it. We grow fonder of houses when they have faces of their own, like friends. The large Garth family—Mary had four brothers and a sister—loved the old house, although its best furniture had long since been sold. Fred loved it too. He knew every part, even the attic with its delicious smell of apples and quinces. Until today he had never approached it without pleasant expectations. Now his heart beat uneasily at the likelihood of having to confess before Mrs. Garth, whom he feared rather more than her husband. She was not prone to sarcasm and impulsive remarks as Mary was. At least in her present, matronly years she never committed herself by speaking hastily. As she said, she had borne the yoke in youth and learned self-control. She had the rare good sense to recognize what could not be changed and submit without complaint. Adoring her husband's virtues, she had accepted early his inability to protect his own interests and had faced the consequences cheerfully. She was generous enough to surrender all pride in teapots or children's frills. She never confided mournfully to neighboring women about Mr. Garth's imprudence and how much money he might have had if only he resembled other men.
