Those neighbors consequently considered her proud or eccentric and sometimes spoke to their husbands of “your fine Mrs. Garth.” She criticized them in return, being better educated than most Middlemarch matrons and—where is the faultless woman?—inclined to severity towards her own sex, which she believed intended for complete subordination. Men's failings, on the other hand, received disproportionate indulgence; she often called them natural. It must also be admitted that she resisted what she considered foolishness a little too emphatically. The move from governess to housewife had impressed itself too deeply on her self-awareness. She seldom forgot that, although her grammar and accent surpassed local standards, she wore a plain cap, cooked the family dinner, and darned every stocking. Sometimes she taught pupils as she moved around, having them follow her through the kitchen with books or slates. She thought it wholesome for them to see her making excellent soapsuds while correcting their mistakes without looking: to know that a woman with sleeves above her elbows could understand the subjunctive mood or the tropical zone. In short, a woman could possess “education” and other admirable things ending in “tion,” worthy of emphatic pronunciation, without being a useless doll. Delivering such improving observations, she wore a firm little frown that did not prevent her face from looking kind. Her words marched out in procession in a warm, pleasant contralto. Certainly the exemplary Mrs. Garth had comic aspects, but her character supported her peculiarities as a very fine wine supports a taste of the skin.

She felt motherly towards Fred and had always excused his mistakes, though she would probably not have forgiven Mary for becoming engaged to him. Her daughter came under the stricter judgment she applied to women. The very unusualness of her indulgence made it harder for Fred to know he must now fall in her estimation. His visit proved still more uncomfortable than expected. Caleb had gone out early to inspect repairs nearby. At certain hours Mrs. Garth was always in the kitchen, and that morning she was managing several tasks at once. She made pies at a well-scrubbed pine table along one side of the airy room, watched Sally at the oven and dough tub through an open door, and taught her youngest boy and girl, who stood opposite with books and slates. A tub and drying rack at the other end showed that small items of washing were being dealt with between times.

Mrs. Garth, sleeves rolled above the elbows, deftly rolling pastry and pinching decorative edges while explaining with grammatical fervor how verbs and pronouns should agree with “collective nouns, or words signifying many,” was a pleasantly amusing sight. Like Mary, she had curly hair and a square face, but she was handsomer, with finer features, pale skin, a solid matronly figure, and a remarkably steady gaze. In her cap with its snowy frill, she recalled that delightful Frenchwoman we have all seen shopping with a basket on her arm. Looking at the mother, one could hope the daughter would grow like her, a future advantage equal to a dowry. Too often a mother stands behind her daughter like a threatening prophecy: “What I am, she will soon be.”

“Now, once more,” said Mrs. Garth, pinching an apple pastry that appeared to distract Ben, an energetic boy with a heavy brow, from the lesson. “‘With attention to whether the word conveys an idea of unity or plurality.’ Tell me again what that means, Ben.”
Like more celebrated educators, Mrs. Garth favored certain old paths. In a general shipwreck of society, she would have tried to hold her Lindley Murray grammar above the waves.
“Oh, it means you have to think what you mean,” Ben replied peevishly. “I hate grammar. What's it for?”
“To teach you to speak and write correctly so people can understand you,” Mrs. Garth said with stern precision. “Would you like to speak like old Job?”
“Yes,” Ben answered firmly. “It's funnier. He says ‘Yo goo.’ That's as good as ‘You go.’”
“But he says ‘There's a ship in the garden’ instead of ‘a sheep,’” Letty said with superiority. “You might think he meant a ship from the sea.”
“Not unless you were silly,” Ben said. “How would a ship from the sea get there?”

“That's only pronunciation, the smallest part of grammar,” said Mrs. Garth. “That apple peel is for the pigs, Ben. If you eat it, I'll have to give them your slice of pie. Job only has to discuss very simple matters. How would you speak or write about anything difficult if you knew as little grammar as he does? You'd choose the wrong words and put them in the wrong places. Instead of understanding you, people would turn away because you were tiresome. What would you do then?”
“I wouldn't care. I'd stop,” said Ben, feeling this a pleasant way out where grammar was concerned.

“I see you're growing tired and foolish, Ben,” said his mother, accustomed to such obstructive reasoning from her sons. Having finished the pies, she moved towards the drying rack. “Come here and tell me Wednesday's story about Cincinnatus.”
“I know! He was a farmer,” Ben said.
“Ben, he was a Roman. Let ME tell it,” said Letty, pushing with her elbow.
“Silly, he was a Roman farmer, and he was plowing.”
“Yes, but something happened before that. It wasn't the beginning. People wanted him,” said Letty.
“First you have to say what sort of man he was,” Ben insisted. “He was wise, like father, so people wanted his advice. And brave, and able to fight. Father could fight too, couldn't he, mother?”
“Let me tell it straight through, Ben, the way mother did,” said Letty, frowning. “Mother, please tell Ben to be quiet.”

“Letty, I'm ashamed of you,” her mother said, wringing caps out of the tub. “Your brother began. You should have waited to see whether he could tell it. How rude you look, shoving and frowning as if you meant to conquer people with your elbows! I'm sure Cincinnatus would have been sorry to see his daughter behave like that.” She pronounced this terrible sentence with such majesty that Letty felt life already painful, between being forbidden to talk and being held in general disapproval, even by the Romans. “Now, Ben.”
“Well—oh—there was lots of fighting, and they were all blockheads, and—I can't tell it exactly as you did—but they needed someone to be captain and king and everything—”
“Dictator,” Letty interrupted with an injured look and some wish to make her mother sorry.
“All right, dictator!” Ben said scornfully. “But that's a bad word. He wasn't dictating things for them to write on slates.”
“Come, Ben, you know better than that,” Mrs. Garth said, carefully keeping a serious face. “Listen, someone's knocking. Run and open the door, Letty.”

It was Fred. When Letty said her father was still out but her mother was in the kitchen, he had no choice. He always went to see Mrs. Garth there if she was working, and could hardly change his habit now. Silently putting an arm round Letty's neck, he led her in without his usual jokes and affectionate gestures.
Mrs. Garth was surprised to see him so early, but she rarely expressed surprise. Continuing her work calmly, she merely said:
“You, Fred, at this hour? You're very pale. Has something happened?”

“I need to speak to Mr. Garth,” Fred said, not yet ready for more. After a pause he added, “And to you.” He assumed she knew all about the note. In the end he must mention it before her, if not to her alone.

“Caleb will be back in a few minutes,” said Mrs. Garth, imagining trouble between Fred and his father. “He can't be long. He has work at his desk that must be finished this morning. Would you mind staying with me while I finish here?”
“We don't have to go on with Cincinnatus, do we?” asked Ben, who had taken Fred's whip and was testing it on the cat.
“No, you may go out. But put down that whip. How cruel to whip poor old Tortoise! Please take it from him, Fred.”
“Come on, old fellow, hand it over,” Fred said, holding out his hand.
“Can I ride your horse today?” Ben asked, surrendering the whip with an air of doing so freely.
“Not today. Another time. This isn't my horse.”
“Will you see Mary today?”
“Yes, I think so,” said Fred, feeling an unpleasant pang.
“Tell her to come home soon, play forfeits, and make us laugh.”
“That's enough, Ben. Run along,” said Mrs. Garth, noticing Fred's discomfort.

“Are Letty and Ben your only pupils now?” Fred asked once they had gone and something was needed to pass the time. He still could not decide whether to wait for Caleb or seize an opening in the conversation to confess to Mrs. Garth, give her the money, and ride away.

“I have one other, just one. Fanny Hackbutt comes at half past eleven. I'm not earning much now,” Mrs. Garth said with a smile. “Pupils are scarce. But I've saved my little fund for Alfred's apprenticeship fee: ninety-two pounds. He can go to Mr. Hanmer now. He's just the right age.”

This was no promising introduction to the news that Mr. Garth was about to lose more than ninety-two pounds. Fred remained silent. “Young gentlemen at university cost rather more,” Mrs. Garth innocently continued, straightening the edging on a cap. “Caleb thinks Alfred will become a distinguished engineer. He wants to give the boy a good chance. There he is! I hear him. Shall we go to him in the parlor?”
When they entered, Caleb had put down his hat and seated himself at the desk.

“Why, Fred, my boy!” he said with mild surprise, holding his pen before dipping it. “You're here early.” Missing the customary cheerful greeting in Fred's face, he immediately added, “Trouble at home? Is something wrong?”

“Yes, Mr. Garth. I've come to tell you something I'm afraid will make you think badly of me. I have to tell you and Mrs. Garth that I can't keep my word. I can't find the money for the bill after all. I've had bad luck. I've only these fifty pounds towards the hundred and sixty.”

As he spoke, Fred took out the notes and placed them on the desk. He had blurted out the bare facts, miserable as a boy and unable to find helpful words. Mrs. Garth, silently astonished, looked to her husband for an explanation. Caleb blushed. After a short pause he said:
“Oh, Susan, I didn't tell you. I signed a bill for Fred, for a hundred and sixty pounds. He was certain he could pay it himself.”
Mrs. Garth's face plainly changed, but like a change beneath water whose surface stays smooth. Fixing her eyes on Fred, she said:
“I suppose you've asked your father for the rest and he's refused.”
“No,” Fred said, biting his lip and finding speech harder. “But I know asking would be useless. Unless it could help, I wouldn't want to bring Mr. Garth's name into it.”

“It's come at a bad time,” Caleb said hesitantly, looking at the notes and nervously fingering the paper. “Christmas here, and money rather tight. You see, I have to cut everything out like a tailor with too little cloth. What can we do, Susan? I'll need every penny in the bank. It's a hundred and ten pounds, damn it!”

“I must give you the ninety-two pounds I've saved for Alfred's apprenticeship,” said Mrs. Garth gravely and firmly, though a sensitive ear might have detected a slight tremor in some words. “And Mary must have saved twenty pounds from her salary by now. She will lend it.”

She had not looked at Fred again and was not calculating which words would wound him most. Eccentric woman that she was, she was absorbed in deciding what to do and did not imagine bitter comments or explosions would help. Yet for the first time she made Fred feel something like the bite of remorse. Strangely, his earlier distress had consisted almost entirely of knowing he must appear dishonorable and lose the Garths' respect. He had not dwelt on the inconvenience and possible harm his failure would cause them. Optimistic young gentlemen seldom exercise their imaginations on other people's needs. Indeed, most of us are raised to think that the highest reason for avoiding wrongdoing has nothing to do with those who would suffer it. But now Fred suddenly saw himself as a contemptible scoundrel robbing two women of their savings.
“I'll certainly repay everything, Mrs. Garth—eventually,” he stammered.

“Yes, eventually,” she replied. Having a particular dislike of fine words on ugly occasions, she could not resist one sharp saying. “But boys can't conveniently be apprenticed eventually. They need to be apprenticed at fifteen.” Never had she felt less inclined to excuse Fred.

“The greater fault was mine, Susan,” said Caleb. “Fred felt certain he'd find the money. But I had no business putting my hand to bills. You've looked everywhere and tried every honest means, I suppose?” he added, turning his compassionate gray eyes on Fred. He was too tactful to name Mr. Featherstone.

“Yes, I've tried everything. I really have. I'd have had a hundred and thirty pounds but for an accident with a horse I was about to sell. My uncle had given me eighty. I traded my old horse and thirty pounds for another that I meant to sell for eighty or more. I intended to do without a horse. But it's turned out vicious and lamed itself. I wish I'd gone to the devil, horses and all, before bringing this on you. Nobody matters more to me. You and Mrs. Garth have always been so kind. But saying that is useless. You'll always think me a scoundrel now.”
Fred turned and hurried from the room, aware of becoming rather tearful and vaguely feeling that his sorrow did the Garths little good. They watched him mount and ride quickly through the gate.

“Fred Vincy disappoints me,” said Mrs. Garth. “I would never have believed he'd involve you in his debts. I knew he was extravagant, but not that he'd be mean enough to put his risks on his oldest friend, the person least able to afford a loss.”
“I was a fool, Susan.”

“You were,” his wife said, nodding and smiling. “But I wouldn't have announced it in the marketplace. Why keep such things from me? It's the same with your buttons. You let them come off without telling me and go out with your cuff dangling. If I'd known, I might have had a better plan ready.”
“I know you're deeply upset, Susan,” Caleb said, looking at her tenderly. “I can't bear your losing the money you've scraped together for Alfred.”

“It's fortunate I HAD scraped it together. And you'll be the one to suffer, because you'll have to teach the boy yourself. You must give up your bad habits. Some men take to drink; you've taken to working for nothing. You must indulge yourself less in that. And you must ride over to Mary and ask what money she has.”
Caleb had pushed his chair back. He leaned forward, slowly shaking his head and carefully fitting his fingertips together.
“Poor Mary!” he said. Then, more quietly, “Susan, I'm afraid she may love Fred.”
“Oh no. She's always laughing at him. And he's unlikely to think of her as anything but a sister.”
Caleb did not answer. Presently he lowered his spectacles, pulled his chair up to the desk, and said, “Damn the bill! I wish it were in Hanover. These things interrupt business terribly.”

The first part exhausted his vocabulary of curses and came out in a slight snarl, easy enough to imagine. But anyone who had never heard him say “business” could scarcely understand the special fervent reverence, almost religious devotion, in which he wrapped that word, as a sacred object is wrapped in gold-fringed linen.

Caleb Garth often shook his head while contemplating the value and indispensable power of the labor, with its countless heads and hands, that feeds, clothes, and houses society. It had captured his imagination in boyhood. The ringing of great hammers building roofs or ships' keels, workers' shouted signals, the furnace's roar, the engine's thunder and splash—all were sublime music to him. Timber felled and loaded, a huge trunk trembling star-like far down the road, a crane working on the wharf, produce stacked in warehouses, the precision and variety of muscular effort wherever exact work was required: these youthful sights had given him poetry without poets, a philosophy without philosophers, a religion without theology. His early ambition was to take the most effective possible part in this magnificent labor, which he dignified in his own special way as “business.” Though briefly trained by a surveyor and otherwise largely self-taught, he knew more about land, building, and mining than most specialists in the county.

His division of human occupations was rather rough. Like the classifications of more famous men, it would not satisfy these advanced times. He divided them into “business, politics, preaching, learning, and amusement.” He had nothing against the last four, but regarded them as a reverent pagan regards gods other than his own. Similarly, he respected every social rank, yet would not have wanted to belong to one that prevented sufficiently close contact with business to earn the honorable marks of dust and mortar, engine moisture, or the sweet soil of woods and fields. He always considered himself an orthodox Christian and would discuss grace preceding human action if the subject arose. Nevertheless, I think his real gods were sound practical plans, accurate work, and faithful completion of a task. His prince of darkness was a careless worker. Caleb had no spirit of rejection in him, however. The world seemed so marvelous that he would accept any number of systems, like any number of heavens, provided they did not plainly obstruct good drainage, solid building, correct measurement, and sensible drilling for coal. He possessed, in fact, a reverent soul and strong practical intelligence. But he could not handle finance. He understood values, yet lacked the sharp imagination that calculates monetary profit and loss. Having learned this at a cost, he resolved to abandon every branch of his beloved business requiring that talent. He devoted himself entirely to the many kinds of work he could do without managing capital. Within his district he became one of those precious men everyone wants to employ: he worked well, charged little, and often refused payment altogether. No wonder the Garths were poor and lived modestly. They did not mind, however.

chapters.title: Book III: Waiting For Death — Chapter XXV
paragraphs:
“Love does not seek to please itself,
Nor care for its own comfort,
But gives up ease for someone else
And builds a heaven in hell's despair.
. . . . . . .
Love seeks to please itself alone,
To bind another to its pleasure,
Delights in someone else's loss of ease,
And builds a hell in spite of heaven.”
—W. BLAKE, Songs of Experience.

Fred wanted to reach Stone Court when Mary would not expect him and his uncle was still upstairs. Then she might be alone in the paneled parlor. He left his horse in the yard to avoid sounding on the gravel in front and entered without warning beyond the turn of the door handle. Mary sat in her usual corner, laughing over Mrs. Piozzi's memories of Johnson. The amusement was still on her face as she looked up. It gradually faded when Fred approached without a word and stood before her, looking ill, his elbow on the mantelpiece. She remained silent too, merely raising her eyes in a question.
“Mary,” he began, “I'm a worthless scoundrel.”
“One of those descriptions at a time should be enough,” she said, attempting a smile but feeling alarmed.
“I know you'll never think well of me again. You'll think I'm a liar, dishonest, that I didn't care for you or your parents. You always think the worst of me anyway.”
“I can't deny I'll think all that if you give me good reasons, Fred. But please tell me immediately what you've done. I'd rather hear the painful truth than imagine it.”

“I owed a hundred and sixty pounds. I asked your father to sign a bill as security. I thought it wouldn't affect him. I was certain I'd pay it myself, and I've tried as hard as I could. But I've been so unlucky. A horse turned out badly, and I can only pay fifty pounds. I can't ask my father; he wouldn't give me a penny. My uncle gave me a hundred not long ago. What can I do? Your father has no money to spare, so your mother will have to use the ninety-two pounds she's saved. She says your savings must go too. You see what a—”

“Oh, poor mother! Poor father!” Mary's eyes filled, and a small sob rose which she tried to suppress. She stared ahead without attending to Fred as all the consequences at home came before her. He too was silent for a while, more miserable than ever. Finally he said, “I wouldn't have hurt you for anything, Mary. You'll never forgive me.”

“What difference does my forgiveness make?” Mary asked passionately. “Would it make things easier for mother to lose the money she's earned by teaching for four years so she could send Alfred to Mr. Hanmer? Would you find all that pleasant enough if I forgave you?”
“Say anything you want. I deserve it.”
“I don't want to say anything,” Mary replied more quietly. “My anger won't help.” She wiped her eyes, put aside the book, and went to fetch her sewing.
Fred watched her, hoping she would meet his eyes and give his pleading remorse a way in. But no; she could easily avoid looking up.

“I do care about your mother losing her money,” he said once she was seated and sewing quickly. “I wanted to ask, Mary—don't you think Mr. Featherstone might advance the money if you told him? About Alfred's apprenticeship, I mean.”

“My family doesn't like begging, Fred. We'd rather earn our money. Besides, you say Mr. Featherstone recently gave you a hundred pounds. He seldom gives presents, and has never given any to us. Father certainly won't ask him for anything. Even if I wanted to beg, it would do no good.”
“I'm so miserable, Mary. If you knew how miserable, you'd pity me.”
“There are things more deserving of pity. But selfish people always consider their own discomfort more important than anything in the world. I see enough of that every day.”
“It's hardly fair to call me selfish. If you knew what other young men do, you'd think me far from the worst.”
“I know that people who spend a great deal on themselves without knowing how they'll pay must be selfish. They're always thinking about what they can get, never what others may lose.”
“Anyone can have bad luck and be unable to pay despite intending to, Mary. There's no better man than your father, yet he got into difficulties.”

“How dare you compare yourself with my father?” Mary asked in a deep voice of indignation. “He didn't get into trouble by thinking about idle pleasures. He was always thinking about work for other people. And he lived hard and worked hard to repay everyone's loss.”

“And you think I'll never try to make anything good. It's ungenerous to believe the worst of a man. When you have influence over him, you might try using it to improve him, but you never do. Anyway, I'm leaving,” Fred finished wearily. “I'll never speak to you about anything again. I'm very sorry for all the trouble I've caused. That's all.”

Mary let her sewing fall and looked up. Even a girl's love often contains something motherly, and Mary's hard experience had made her sensitive in a way very different from the brittle, shallow thing we call girlishness. Fred's final words sent a sudden pang through her, like a mother's at imagining the cries of her naughty, wandering child who might get lost and hurt. When she met his dull, hopeless gaze, pity overcame her anger and every other anxiety.

“Oh, Fred, you look so ill! Sit down a moment. Don't leave yet. Let me tell uncle you're here. He's been wondering why he hasn't seen you all week.” She spoke quickly, saying whatever came first without quite knowing the words, her voice half soothing, half pleading. She rose as if to fetch Mr. Featherstone. Naturally Fred felt as if the clouds had parted to let in light. He moved into her path.
“Say one word, Mary, and I'll do anything. Say you won't think the worst of me, won't give me up completely.”

“As though thinking badly of you gave me pleasure,” Mary said sadly. “As though seeing you idle and frivolous didn't hurt. How can you bear to be so contemptible while others work and struggle and so much needs doing? How can you bear to be useful for nothing? And with so much goodness in your nature, Fred. You could be worth a great deal.”
“I'll try to become anything you want, if you'll tell me you love me.”

“I'd be ashamed to say I loved a man who was always depending on others and counting on what they'd do for him. What will you be at forty? Like Mr. Bowyer, I suppose: just as idle, living in Mrs. Beck's front parlor, fat and shabby, hoping someone invites you to dinner, spending the morning learning a comic song. Oh no, learning a tune on the flute.”

Her lips had begun to curve into a smile as soon as she asked about his future—young spirits change quickly—and by the end her face shone with amusement. Her ability to laugh at him relieved Fred like the ending of pain. With a yielding little smile he tried to take her hand. She slipped quickly towards the door. “I'll tell uncle. You MUST see him for a minute or two.”

Secretly, Fred felt his future was protected against Mary's mocking predictions, quite apart from the “anything” he stood ready to do if she would only specify it. He never dared mention his expectations from Mr. Featherstone in her presence, and she always ignored them as though everything depended on Fred himself. But if he actually inherited the property, she would have to acknowledge his altered position. These thoughts passed rather sluggishly through him before he went upstairs. He stayed only briefly, pleading a cold. Mary did not return before he left. Riding home, however, he began to feel more aware of being ill than of being unhappy.

Caleb arrived at Stone Court shortly after dusk. Mary was not surprised, although he seldom had time to visit and disliked having to talk with Mr. Featherstone. The old man, in turn, felt uncomfortable with a brother-in-law he could not irritate, who did not mind being thought poor, wanted nothing from him, and understood every branch of farming and mining better than he did. Mary had been sure her parents would want to see her. If her father had not come, she would have asked leave to visit home for an hour or two the next day. After discussing prices over tea with Mr. Featherstone, Caleb rose to leave and said, “I need a word with you, Mary.”

She carried a candle into another large parlor where no fire was lit, set its weak light on the dark mahogany table, then turned and put her arms around his neck. She kissed him with the childish affection he delighted in. Beneath his broad brows his expression softened as a great, beautiful dog's does when petted. Mary was his favorite child. Whatever Susan said, and however right she was about everything else, Caleb thought it entirely natural that Fred or anyone should find Mary more lovable than other girls.
“I've something to tell you, my dear,” he began hesitantly. “Not very good news, though it could be worse.”
“About money, father? I think I know.”

“Do you? How could you? You see, I've been a bit foolish again and signed a bill, and now it must be paid. Your mother has to give up her savings. That's the worst part, and even they won't quite cover it. We need a hundred and ten pounds. She has ninety-two, and I've nothing to spare at the bank. She thinks you may have saved something.”
“Oh yes, more than twenty-four pounds. I thought you'd come, so I put it in my bag. Look! Lovely white notes and gold.”
Mary took the folded money from her small bag and placed it in his hand.

“But how—we need only eighteen. Here, put the rest back, child. How did you know?” Caleb asked. His incurable indifference to money was already giving way to a greater concern about what this might mean for Mary's affections.
“Fred told me this morning.”
“Ah. Did he come specially?”
“I think so. He was very upset.”

“I'm afraid Fred can't be trusted, Mary,” her father said with hesitant tenderness. “Perhaps he means better than he behaves. But I'd be sorry to see anyone's happiness tied to his, and so would your mother.”
“So would I, father,” Mary said without looking up, pressing the back of his hand against her cheek.

“I don't mean to pry, my dear. But I feared there might be something between you and Fred and wanted to warn you. You see, Mary”—his voice grew more tender; after pushing his hat about on the table and studying it, he finally looked at her—“however good a woman is, she must endure the life her husband makes for her. Your mother has endured a great deal because of me.”
Mary lifted the back of his hand to her lips and smiled at him.

“Well, nobody's perfect, but—” Mr. Garth shook his head to supply what words could not. “I'm thinking of what it must be like for a wife who can never rely on her husband, because there's no principle in him that makes him fear wronging others more than having his own toes trodden on. That's the whole of it, Mary. Young people may fall in love before they understand life and imagine it all a holiday if only they can be together. But it soon becomes a working day, my dear. Still, you have more sense than most and haven't been wrapped in cotton wool. Perhaps there's no need to tell you. But a father fears for his daughter, and you're alone here.”

“Don't worry about me,” Mary said, meeting his eyes seriously. “Fred has always been very kind to me. He's affectionate and good-hearted, and despite his self-indulgence I don't think he's false. But I'll never promise myself to a man without an adult's independence, who idles his time away hoping other people will support him. You and mother have taught me too much pride for that.”
“That's right. Quite right. Now I'm reassured,” said Mr. Garth, picking up his hat. “Still, it's hard to take away your earnings, isn't it, child?”
“Father!” Mary protested in her deepest voice. Her last words before he closed the outer door were, “Take pocketfuls of love home to everyone as well.”

“Your father wanted your wages, I suppose,” said old Mr. Featherstone when she returned, with his usual gift for unpleasant guesses. “He has a tight enough time, I reckon. You're of age now. You ought to save for yourself.”
“I consider my parents the best part of myself, sir,” Mary answered coldly.

Mr. Featherstone grunted. He could hardly deny that an ordinary girl like her might be expected to make herself useful, so he found another remark, unpleasant enough to suit any occasion. “If Fred Vincy comes tomorrow, don't keep him chatting. Send him up to me.”

chapters.title: Book III: Waiting For Death — Chapter XXVI
paragraphs:
He beats me and I curse him. What splendid satisfaction! I wish it were
the other way round, so I could beat him while he cursed me.
—Troilus and Cressida.

Fred did not return to Stone Court the next day, for reasons that allowed no choice. His visits to Houndsley's filthy streets in pursuit of Diamond had brought back more than a bad bargain in horseflesh. He had also caught an illness which for a day or two seemed merely low spirits and a headache. After his visit to Stone Court it grew so much worse that he went into the dining room and collapsed on the sofa. When his mother anxiously questioned him, he said, “I feel terribly ill. I think you'd better send for Wrench.”

Wrench came but suspected nothing serious. He described a “slight upset” and said nothing about returning the following day. He valued the Vincys' custom properly, but even the most watchful men can be dulled by routine and, on harassed mornings, go through their duties with the enthusiasm of someone ringing the same bell every day. Mr. Wrench was a small, neat, bilious man with a carefully dressed wig, a demanding practice, an irritable temper, a sluggish wife, and seven children. He was already late for a four-mile drive to meet Dr. Minchin beyond Tipton. Hicks, a country practitioner, had died, increasing business for Middlemarch doctors in that direction. Great statesmen make mistakes; why shouldn't small medical men? Wrench did not forget to send the usual white packets, which this time contained dark, powerful purgatives. They brought poor Fred no relief. Still unwilling, as he said, to believe he was “in for an illness,” he got up at his usual leisurely hour the next morning and came down intending to eat breakfast. Instead he could do nothing but sit shivering by the fire. They sent for Wrench again, but he was out on his rounds. Seeing her darling's altered face and general misery, Mrs. Vincy began to cry and said she would call Dr. Sprague.
“Don't be silly, mother. It's nothing,” said Fred, reaching his hot, dry hand towards her. “I'll soon be well. I must have caught cold on that horrible wet ride.”

“Mamma!” said Rosamond, sitting near the window. The dining room overlooked the highly respectable street called Lowick Gate. “There's Mr. Lydgate, stopping to talk to someone. I'd call him in if I were you. He cured Ellen Bulstrode. People say he cures everyone.”

Mrs. Vincy sprang to the window and threw it open, thinking only of Fred and nothing of medical etiquette. Lydgate stood only two yards away beyond the iron railings. He turned at the sudden sound of the sash before she called. Within two minutes he was in the room. Rosamond withdrew after waiting just long enough to show a pretty anxiety struggling with her sense of propriety.

Lydgate listened to an account in which Mrs. Vincy's mind instinctively fastened on every minor detail, especially what Wrench had and had not said about returning. He immediately saw that trouble with Wrench might follow, but the seriousness of the case put that consideration aside. He was convinced Fred had reached the pink-spotted stage of typhoid fever and had received exactly the wrong medicines. He must go straight to bed, have a regular nurse, and be given various treatments and precautions about which Lydgate was precise. These signs of danger terrified Mrs. Vincy, whose fear poured out in whatever words came easiest. It was “very bad treatment from Mr. Wrench, whom they'd employed for so many years instead of Mr. Peacock, though Peacock was just as much a friend. Why should Wrench neglect her children more than anyone else's? She couldn't understand it. He hadn't neglected Mrs. Larcher's children when they had measles, nor would Mrs. Vincy have wanted him to. And if anything happened—”

Here she broke down completely, her beautiful throat and good-natured face painfully convulsed. They were in the hall, beyond Fred's hearing, but Rosamond had opened the drawing-room door and now approached anxiously. Lydgate defended Wrench. Yesterday's symptoms might have been misleading; this kind of fever was very uncertain at first. He would go immediately to the chemist and have a prescription prepared to avoid delay, then write to Wrench explaining what had been done.

“But you must come back. You must keep treating Fred. I can't leave my boy to someone who may come or may not. Thank God I bear nobody ill will, and Mr. Wrench saved me when I had pleurisy. But he'd better have let me die if—if—”
“Shall I meet Mr. Wrench here, then?” Lydgate asked, genuinely believing Wrench ill-equipped to handle such a case wisely.
“Please arrange it, Mr. Lydgate,” said Rosamond, coming to her mother's help and supporting her arm to lead her away.

When Mr. Vincy came home he was furious with Wrench and did not care if he ever entered the house again. Lydgate would continue, whether Wrench liked it or not. Fever in the house was no joke. Everyone must be told not to come to Thursday's dinner. Pritchard need not bring up wine; brandy was best against infection. “I shall drink brandy,” Mr. Vincy declared emphatically, as though this were no time for blank cartridges. “Fred's an extraordinarily unlucky boy. He'll need a good turn of luck later to make up for this. Otherwise I don't know who'd want an eldest son.”
“Don't say that, Vincy,” his wife said, her lip trembling, “unless you want him taken from me.”

“The worry will kill you, Lucy. I can see that,” he said more gently. “Still, Wrench shall hear what I think.” His confused feeling was that proper concern for his family—the Mayor's family—might somehow have prevented the fever. “I'm the last man to join the fuss about new doctors, or new parsons either, whether they're Bulstrode's men or not. But Wrench shall hear my opinion, however he takes it.”

Wrench took it badly. Lydgate was as polite as his casual manner allowed, but politeness from someone who has put you at a disadvantage only makes matters worse, especially if you disliked him already. Country practitioners used to be an irritable breed, touchy about their honor, and Wrench ranked among the most irritable. He agreed to meet Lydgate that evening, but the occasion tried his temper. He had to hear Mrs. Vincy exclaim:
“Oh, Mr. Wrench, what have I done to deserve this? Going away and never coming back! My boy might have been lying dead!”
Mr. Vincy had kept up a brisk attack on the enemy Infection and was considerably heated by it. Hearing Wrench arrive, he jumped up and went into the hall to deliver his opinion.

“I'll tell you, Wrench, this is beyond a joke,” said the Mayor. Lately accustomed to rebuking offenders in an official manner, he now made himself broader by hooking his thumbs into his waistcoat armholes. “Letting fever steal into a house like this! Some things ought to be grounds for a lawsuit and aren't. That's my opinion.”

Yet unreasonable accusations were easier to bear than being taught, or rather sensing that a younger man like Lydgate privately thought he needed teaching. For “the fact was,” Wrench later said, Lydgate paraded fanciful foreign ideas that would not last. He swallowed his anger for the moment but afterwards wrote declining further attendance. The household might be valuable, but he would not bow to anyone over a professional matter. With considerable probability on his side, he reflected that sooner or later Lydgate would make a mistake too. His ungentlemanly attacks on other practitioners' sale of medicines would eventually rebound upon him. Wrench made cutting remarks about Lydgate's tricks, worthy only of a quack, for building an artificial reputation among gullible people. Sound practitioners never stirred up that kind of cant about cures.

On this point Lydgate was as sore as Wrench could wish. Promotion by ignorant admirers was not merely humiliating but dangerous, no more enviable than a weather prophet's reputation. The foolish expectations surrounding every kind of work made him impatient. His unprofessional frankness could easily harm him as much as Wrench hoped.

Nevertheless, Lydgate became the Vincys' doctor, and Middlemarch discussed the event widely. Some said the family had behaved disgracefully: Vincy had threatened Wrench, and Mrs. Vincy had accused him of poisoning her son. Others thought Lydgate's passing had been providential, that he was exceptionally skilled with fevers, and that Bulstrode was right to promote him. Many believed Bulstrode had been responsible for his coming to town at all. Mrs. Taft, always counting stitches and collecting information in misleading fragments between rows of knitting, had acquired the notion that Lydgate was Bulstrode's illegitimate son. This seemed to confirm her suspicions about Evangelical laymen.
One day she passed this information to Mrs. Farebrother, who duly told her son, remarking:
“Nothing about Bulstrode would surprise me, but I'd be sorry to believe it of Mr. Lydgate.”
After a burst of laughter, Mr. Farebrother replied, “Mother, you know perfectly well that Lydgate comes from a good northern family. He'd never heard of Bulstrode before arriving here.”
“That's satisfactory as far as Mr. Lydgate is concerned, Camden,” the old lady said with an air of exactness. “But as for Bulstrode, the report may be true about some other son.”
